questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician for recurrent prolonged bleeding after minor injuries, including a small knee cut that bled for several hours. His mother's brother reportedly has similar problems. Laboratory studies show a prolonged partial thromboplastin time (PTT) with a normal prothrombin time (PT) and decreased factor VIII activity. Which of the following inheritance patterns best explains this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked dominant

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive

explanation.summary: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is a classic X-linked recessive disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The findings of prolonged PTT with normal PT and decreased factor VIII activity diagnose hemophilia A. It is X-linked recessive: an affected male carries a single pathogenic X allele (hemizygous), and the disease is transmitted through unaffected female carriers, which fits the affected maternal uncle who inherited it through the mother's line.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal dominant conditions show affected individuals in every generation with male-to-male transmission, not disease traced only through the maternal line and males.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive disease requires two pathogenic alleles and affects males and females equally, whereas this predominantly affects males via carrier females.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial disorders are maternally inherited and affect high-energy tissues (neuromuscular), not a coagulation factor deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: In X-linked dominant inheritance all daughters of an affected male are affected and females are affected more often, which does not match a boy affected through carrier females.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A woman is an obligate carrier for hemophilia A, an X-linked recessive disorder, and her partner is an unaffected man. They are counseled about the risk to their future daughters. What is the probability that any given daughter will be a carrier of the pathogenic allele?

explanation.summary: A carrier mother passes her variant X to half of her daughters.
explanation.whyCorrect: The carrier mother is X-wt/X-v and each daughter receives the father's normal X plus one of the mother's two X chromosomes. Half of the daughters inherit the mother's X-v (becoming carriers) and half inherit her X-wt, giving a 50% chance a daughter is a carrier.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A carrier mother has a pathogenic X to pass on, so the risk is not zero.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 25% would apply if both parents contributed a variant allele at random, but the father contributes only a normal X here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 75% overstates the risk; the mother passes the variant X to only half of her offspring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 100% would require the mother to be homozygous for the variant (affected), not a carrier.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A geneticist is describing the status of a male patient with respect to a gene located on his X chromosome. Because he has only one copy of that gene, which of the following terms most accurately describes his genetic status at that locus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemizygous

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterozygous

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wild-type

explanation.summary: An individual with only a single allele for a gene is hemizygous.
explanation.whyCorrect: Males have only one X chromosome, so they carry a single allele for X-linked genes and are described as hemizygous. This is why a male expresses an X-linked recessive disorder with just one pathogenic allele.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A carrier has one pathogenic and one wild-type allele without disease, which requires two alleles and describes only females for X-linked genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heterozygous means having two different alleles at a locus, again requiring two copies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Homozygous refers to having two identical alleles at a locus, which requires two copies of the gene.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wild-type describes the common non-disease form of an allele, not the number of alleles present.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with progressive muscle weakness undergoes a muscle biopsy. Molecular analysis of the tissue reveals that some copies of the mitochondrial DNA carry a pathogenic mutation while others are wild-type. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aneuploidy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consanguinity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemizygosity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heteroplasmy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Heterozygosity

explanation.summary: A mixture of mutant and wild-type mitochondrial DNA within a cell is heteroplasmy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because each cell contains many mitochondria and each mitochondrion has multiple mtDNA copies, replication and random sorting during cell division can leave a cell with both mutant and wild-type mtDNA, a state called heteroplasmy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aneuploidy is an abnormal number of whole chromosomes, not a mixture of mitochondrial DNA variants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Consanguinity refers to reproductive partners being biologically related, a pedigree concept unrelated to mtDNA content.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemizygosity refers to having a single allele of a nuclear gene, as in males for X-linked genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Heterozygosity describes two different alleles at a locus in nuclear DNA, not a mixture of mitochondrial genomes.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A child with a mitochondrial DNA mutation is asymptomatic at birth but develops encephalopathy and myopathy over several years as the proportion of mutant mitochondria in his tissues rises. His cells maintained normal function until the mutant load became high enough to impair energy production. Which of the following concepts best explains why the disease became clinically apparent only later?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anticipation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genomic imprinting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Threshold effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-inactivation

explanation.summary: Mitochondrial disease appears once the mutant mtDNA fraction exceeds a critical threshold.
explanation.whyCorrect: When only a small number of mitochondria carry the mutation, cells and tissues still function normally. Once the proportion of mutant mitochondria exceeds a threshold, cell and tissue dysfunction produces the disease phenotype, especially in high-energy tissues that rely on oxidative phosphorylation, such as neuromuscular tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticipation is the worsening or earlier onset of a disorder across successive generations, not the accumulation of mutant mtDNA within one person.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Genomic imprinting is parent-of-origin-dependent gene expression, unrelated to mitochondrial mutant proportions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Incomplete penetrance describes some individuals with a genotype never showing the phenotype, not a threshold of mutant load.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-inactivation is the silencing of one X chromosome in females and explains milder female phenotypes in X-linked conditions, not mitochondrial thresholds.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A man is diagnosed with a disorder caused by a mutation in his mitochondrial DNA. He and his unaffected wife are counseled about the risk of the condition in their children. Which of the following statements about transmission is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All of his children will inherit the mutation from him

choices.label: B
choices.text: Half of his children will inherit the mutation from him

choices.label: C
choices.text: None of his children will inherit the mutation from him

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only his daughters will inherit the mutation from him

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only his sons will inherit the mutation from him

explanation.summary: Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited, so affected fathers do not transmit the mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sperm mitochondria are generally not present in the fertilized embryo, so mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the mother. An affected male therefore does not transmit a mitochondrial DNA mutation to any of his children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Children of an affected female inherit the mutation, but an affected male transmits it to none of his children.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no 50% split from a father; paternal mitochondrial transmission does not occur.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fathers do not transmit mtDNA to daughters either, because mtDNA comes from the mother.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transmission is not sex-selective toward sons; fathers transmit mtDNA to no offspring at all.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A pedigree is analyzed for a genetic disorder. Affected individuals are present in every generation, males and females are affected in roughly equal numbers, and there are several instances in which an affected father has an affected son. Which of the following inheritance patterns is most consistent with this pedigree?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: X-linked dominant

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked recessive

choices.label: E
choices.text: Y-linked

explanation.summary: Affected individuals in every generation, equal sex ratio, and male-to-male transmission indicate autosomal dominant inheritance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autosomal dominant pedigrees show affected individuals in multiple generations and affect males and females equally. Male-to-male transmission is a key clue that the gene is not on the X chromosome, because a father passes his Y to his sons; only one pathogenic allele is needed to express the phenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive disease typically appears in only one generation and often arises from unaffected carrier parents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: X-linked dominant conditions cannot show father-to-son transmission because fathers pass only the Y to sons.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-linked recessive pedigrees show mostly affected males with skipped generations and no male-to-male transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Y-linked traits affect only males and cannot affect females, so an equal sex ratio excludes it.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A pedigree shows an affected girl whose parents are unaffected first cousins. No one else in the previous two generations is affected, and the disorder affects males and females equally. Which of the following inheritance patterns is most consistent with these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked dominant

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive

explanation.summary: An affected child of unaffected consanguineous parents points to autosomal recessive inheritance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autosomal recessive conditions require two pathogenic alleles, so affected individuals often have unaffected carrier parents, affect males and females equally, and tend to appear in only one generation. Consanguinity increases the chance both parents inherited the same recessive allele from a shared ancestor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal dominant disease would show affected individuals in every generation, typically with an affected parent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial disease is maternally inherited through an affected mother, not seen in an affected child of two unaffected carriers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-linked dominant disease would affect the parent generation and show more affected females across generations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked recessive disease affects predominantly males, not a girl born to unaffected parents.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A pedigree shows an affected man whose every daughter is affected but whose sons are all unaffected. Affected females tend to have milder disease than affected males. Which of the following inheritance patterns best explains this pedigree?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: X-linked dominant

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked recessive

choices.label: E
choices.text: Y-linked

explanation.summary: An affected male transmitting to all daughters but no sons is the hallmark of X-linked dominant inheritance.
explanation.whyCorrect: In X-linked dominant inheritance, all daughters of an affected male are affected because they all inherit his single X chromosome, while sons inherit his Y and are unaffected. Affected females are often less severely affected because of X-inactivation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance allows male-to-male transmission and does not affect all daughters exclusively.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive disease usually arises from carrier parents and does not show every daughter of an affected father affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-linked recessive disease affects mostly males, and daughters of an affected male would typically be unaffected carriers.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Y-linked traits pass only father to son and cannot affect daughters at all.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A trait is observed to affect only males in a family. Every affected man has an affected father and an affected paternal grandfather, and each affected man transmits the trait to all of his sons but to none of his daughters. Which of the following inheritance patterns best describes this trait?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: C
choices.text: X-linked dominant

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked recessive

choices.label: E
choices.text: Y-linked

explanation.summary: Transmission only from fathers to all sons and exclusively in males indicates Y-linked inheritance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the Y chromosome is passed only from fathers to sons, Y-linked traits are transmitted and expressed only in males and pass straight down the male line. If a man is affected, his father, paternal grandfather, and sons should also be affected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal dominant traits affect both sexes and can be transmitted by mothers as well as fathers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitochondrial traits are maternally inherited and affect both sexes, not passed father to son.
whyWrongByChoice.C: X-linked dominant traits are transmitted by affected males to all daughters, not to sons.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-linked recessive traits are transmitted through carrier females and skip generations, not straight down the male line to all sons.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A patient is affected by a condition that occurs when only one of the two copies of a particular gene located on chromosome 9 carries a pathogenic variant. Which of the following inheritance patterns would this condition follow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked dominant

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive

explanation.summary: A single pathogenic allele on an autosome causing disease defines autosomal dominant inheritance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chromosome 9 is one of the 22 autosomes, so a condition on it is autosomal. Because only one pathogenic allele is needed to express the phenotype, the pattern is dominant, making this autosomal dominant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive conditions require two pathogenic alleles, not just one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial inheritance involves genes on the mitochondrial DNA, not on chromosome 9.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-linked dominant conditions are located on the X chromosome, not on chromosome 9.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-linked recessive conditions also involve the X chromosome, not an autosome.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: While constructing a family history, a clinician wants to label the affected individual whose diagnosis first brought the family to medical attention. Which of the following terms describes this person?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consultand

choices.label: B
choices.text: First-degree relative

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterozygote

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obligate carrier

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proband

explanation.summary: The proband is the affected individual who first brings the family to medical attention.
explanation.whyCorrect: By convention, the proband is the affected person who first brings the family to medical attention and is often marked in a pedigree with an arrow pointing to a shaded symbol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The consultand is the person consulting the health professional, who may or may not be affected and may or may not be the proband.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A first-degree relative is a parent, sibling, or offspring of the proband, defined by relationship rather than by initiating medical attention.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A heterozygote simply has two different alleles at a locus and is a genotype term, not a pedigree role.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An obligate carrier is an individual who must be heterozygous based on the pedigree, such as the parent of an affected recessive child, not necessarily the first to seek care.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has no symptoms, but a routine blood test shows a markedly abnormal enzyme level that is later traced to a variant in one of his genes. He has no physical findings on examination. Which of the following terms best describes the abnormal enzyme level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genotype

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygote

choices.label: D
choices.text: Locus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phenotype

explanation.summary: A phenotype is any expression of the genotype, including a biochemical trait detectable only by laboratory testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenotype is the expression of genotype as a morphological, clinical, cellular, or biochemical trait. It may be clinically observable or may only be detected by blood or tissue testing, so an abnormal enzyme level found on a blood test is a phenotype even in the absence of physical findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An allele is a variation of a gene or DNA sequence, not the measurable trait it produces.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Genotype is the individual's set of genes (the two alleles at a locus), not the trait those genes produce.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A homozygote is a person with a pair of identical alleles at a locus, a description of genotype rather than of a trait.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A locus is a specific location on a chromosome.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A medical student learns that each chromosome of the fourth homologous pair carries one copy of the FGFR3 gene, so a person has two copies of that gene. Which of the following terms refers to the variant forms of this gene found on the two different homologues?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alleles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genotypes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homologues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loci

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phenotypes

explanation.summary: Alleles are variations of a gene on different homologous chromosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each chromosome in a homologous pair usually carries one copy of a given gene; for FGFR3 on the fourth pair, that gives two alleles. The term allele refers to the variations of a gene present on different homologues.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The genotype is the set of two alleles at a locus, not the individual variants themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homologues are the paired chromosomes themselves, not the gene variants they carry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A locus is the specific location on a chromosome where a gene sits; the two FGFR3 copies occupy the same locus on each homologue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenotype describes the traits produced by the genotype, not gene variants.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: Sequencing of a healthy 25-year-old woman identifies a variant in a gene that is one of the common natural forms of that gene in the population and is not associated with any disease. Which of the following best describes this allele?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dominant allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mutant allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pathogenic variant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recessive allele

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wild-type allele

explanation.summary: Alleles encoding common natural variants of a gene are wild-type alleles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most allelic variation is not related to disease. Alleles that encode common natural variants of a gene are called wild-type alleles, in contrast to a pathogenic variant, which is a variation that results in disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dominant describes a phenotype displayed with only one allele, not whether the allele is the common non-disease form.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mutant allele is another name for a pathogenic variant or mutation, which this common non-disease variant is not.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A pathogenic variant is an allelic variation that results in disease; this variant is not associated with disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recessive describes how a phenotype is expressed (only with no dominant allele present), not whether a variant is a common natural form.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: While reviewing a pedigree for an autosomal recessive disorder, a genetic counselor notices that the parents of the affected child are connected by a double horizontal line rather than a single line. Which of the following does this symbol indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One partner is deceased

choices.label: B
choices.text: One partner was adopted into the family

choices.label: C
choices.text: The couple are monozygotic twins

choices.label: D
choices.text: The couple is consanguineous

choices.label: E
choices.text: The couple is divorced

explanation.summary: A double line between mates in a pedigree denotes a consanguineous union.
explanation.whyCorrect: In standard pedigree symbols, a marriage or union is a single line, while a consanguineous couple (mates who are biologically related) is connected by a double line. Consanguinity is worth noting because related parents are more likely to have both inherited the same recessive allele from a common ancestor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A deceased individual is shown by a diagonal line drawn through the symbol.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adoption into a family is shown with brackets around the sex symbol and a dotted line of descent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monozygotic twins are shown as two symbols joined by lines meeting at a common point with a connecting bar, not a double union line.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Divorce is shown as a single union line broken by two short slashes.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A family with an X-linked dominant disorder is evaluated. Affected males in the family have severe disease, whereas affected females in the same family consistently have milder clinical findings. Which of the following best explains the milder phenotype in the females?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemizygosity for the variant allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Homozygosity for the variant allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: Random sorting of mitochondrial DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Threshold effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-inactivation

explanation.summary: In X-linked dominant pedigrees, affected females tend to have a less severe phenotype because of X-inactivation.
explanation.whyCorrect: X-linked dominant pedigrees tend to show more affected females, but their clinical phenotype is often less severe than that of affected males. This is attributed to X-inactivation: a heterozygous female (X wild-type / X variant) silences one X chromosome in each cell, so only a proportion of her cells express the variant allele, whereas an affected male expresses it in every cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemizygosity applies to males, who have a single X chromosome, and explains their full expression rather than the females' milder disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Homozygosity for a dominant pathogenic variant would be expected to worsen rather than lessen the phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Random sorting of mitochondrial DNA relates to heteroplasmy in mitochondrial disorders, not X-linked disease severity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The threshold effect describes when a proportion of mutant mitochondria becomes high enough to cause mitochondrial disease.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A pedigree in a case report refers to the proband as individual III-5. According to standard pedigree labeling conventions, which of the following correctly identifies this person?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A person in the third generation with five children

choices.label: B
choices.text: A third-degree relative of the fifth affected individual

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fifth affected individual in the third sibship

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fifth person from the left in the third generation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The third person from the left in the fifth generation

explanation.summary: Generations are labeled with Roman numerals and individuals are counted numerically left to right within each generation.
explanation.whyCorrect: By convention, generations in a pedigree are labeled with Roman numerals from the top down, and individuals within each generation are numbered left to right. III-5 therefore denotes the fifth individual counted from the left in generation III.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Arabic number is the individual's position in the row, not the number of offspring.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The label describes position in the diagram, not degree of relationship to another individual.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Numbering counts all individuals in the generation from left to right regardless of affected status or sibship.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The Roman numeral gives the generation and the Arabic number gives the position, not the reverse.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A healthy 28-year-old woman schedules a visit with a genetic counselor because her brother was recently diagnosed with an autosomal recessive disorder and she wants to know her own reproductive risk. She has no symptoms of the disorder. In pedigree terminology, which of the following best describes this woman?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consultand

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemizygote

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygote

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obligate carrier

choices.label: E
choices.text: Proband

explanation.summary: The consultand is the person consulting the health professional, who may or may not be affected and may or may not be the proband.
explanation.whyCorrect: The consultand is your patient, the person who is consulting you as a health professional. This woman is seeking counseling for herself, so she is the consultand; she is not the proband, because her affected brother is the individual who first brought the family to medical attention.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemizygosity refers to having only one allele at a locus, as in males for X-linked genes, and does not apply here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A homozygote has two identical alleles at a locus; an unaffected sibling of an autosomal recessive proband is not known to be homozygous for the pathogenic allele.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An obligate carrier must be heterozygous based on the pedigree, such as the parents of an affected recessive child; an unaffected sibling may or may not carry the allele.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The proband is the affected individual who first brings the family to medical attention, which here is her brother.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A clinician is constructing a family history for a proband with a hereditary condition and wants to classify relatives by degree of relationship. Which of the following relatives of the proband is a second-degree relative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: First cousin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Half-sibling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Offspring

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parent

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sibling

explanation.summary: Second-degree relatives include grandparents, grandchildren, aunts and uncles, nieces and nephews, and half-siblings.
explanation.whyCorrect: Relatives are classified as first degree (parents, siblings, and offspring of the proband), second degree (grandparents and grandchildren, aunts and uncles, nephews and nieces, and half-siblings), or third degree (for example, first cousins). A half-sibling is therefore a second-degree relative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: First cousins are third-degree relatives.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Offspring are first-degree relatives.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parents are first-degree relatives.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Full siblings are first-degree relatives.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman who is affected by an autosomal recessive disorder (homozygous for the pathogenic allele) has four children with an unrelated man who does not carry the pathogenic allele. Which of the following best describes the expected genetic status of her four children?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All four are affected

choices.label: B
choices.text: All four are unaffected non-carriers

choices.label: C
choices.text: All four are unaffected obligate carriers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two are affected and two are carriers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two are carriers and two are non-carriers

explanation.summary: Every child of an affected (homozygous) autosomal recessive parent and a non-carrier partner is an obligate heterozygous carrier.
explanation.whyCorrect: An affected individual is homozygous for recessive pathogenic alleles and so passes a pathogenic allele to every child, while the non-carrier partner passes a wild-type allele to every child. Each child is therefore an obligate carrier, meaning we know they must be heterozygous with one wild-type and one pathogenic allele, exactly as for the generation IV offspring of affected individual III-9 in the brick's autosomal recessive pedigree.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal recessive disease requires a pathogenic allele from each parent; the non-carrier father contributes only wild-type alleles, so no child is affected.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Every child necessarily receives a pathogenic allele from the homozygous mother, so none is a non-carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No child can be affected, because the father cannot contribute a pathogenic allele.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Because the mother has only pathogenic alleles to give, all children (not half) receive one.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: In a large pedigree for an autosomal dominant disorder, a man in generation I has no features of the condition, while his wife and several of their children are affected. Which of the following best describes the man's genotype at the disease locus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemizygous for the pathogenic variant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heterozygous with one pathogenic allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygous for the pathogenic variant

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous for the recessive wild-type allele

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unaffected carrier of a single pathogenic allele

explanation.summary: An unaffected individual in an autosomal dominant pedigree must be homozygous for the wild-type allele.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because only one pathogenic allele is needed to express an autosomal dominant phenotype, anyone who carries even a single pathogenic allele would be affected. A person who does not express the phenotype therefore must be homozygous for the recessive wild-type allele, as the brick deduces for I-1 in its autosomal dominant example pedigree.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemizygosity applies to X-linked genes in males, not to an autosomal locus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A heterozygote with one pathogenic allele would display the dominant phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homozygosity for a dominant pathogenic variant would produce disease (typically severe or lethal), not an unaffected individual.
whyWrongByChoice.E: For a dominant condition there is no unaffected carrier state, because a single pathogenic allele is sufficient to produce the phenotype.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A man and a woman who are each heterozygous for the same autosomal dominant disorder ask a genetic counselor what would happen if a child inherited the pathogenic allele from both of them. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The child would be affected only above a mutant threshold

choices.label: B
choices.text: The child would be an unaffected obligate carrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: The child would be phenotypically identical to the parents

choices.label: D
choices.text: The child would express the phenotype in only one sex

choices.label: E
choices.text: The child would typically have a severe or lethal phenotype

explanation.summary: Having two dominant pathogenic alleles is typically lethal or causes severe phenotypic consequences.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typically, having two dominant alleles that cause disease is lethal to the person. This is why it is relatively rare to be homozygous for a dominant pathogenic variant and why affected individuals in autosomal dominant pedigrees are generally assumed to be heterozygous.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A threshold of mutant load applies to heteroplasmic mitochondrial disorders, not to nuclear autosomal genotypes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no unaffected carrier state for a dominant disorder; even one pathogenic allele produces the phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homozygosity for a dominant pathogenic variant frequently leads to severe consequences or is lethal, not a phenotype identical to the heterozygous parents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The gene is autosomal, so expression is not restricted to one sex.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with an autosomal dominant disorder (heterozygous for the pathogenic allele) and his unaffected wife are expecting a son. What is the probability that the son will be affected?

explanation.summary: In autosomal dominant transmission, each child of a heterozygous affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the trait, regardless of sex.
explanation.whyCorrect: The affected father is heterozygous, so each child has a 50% chance of receiving his pathogenic allele, and one pathogenic allele is enough to produce the phenotype. Because the gene is autosomal, an affected father can transmit to a son (male-to-male transmission), so the son's risk is 50%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Zero risk to sons applies to X-linked disorders, where fathers pass only the Y chromosome to sons; this gene is autosomal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 25% would require a pathogenic contribution from both parents, but only one parent carries a pathogenic allele and one allele suffices.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 75% overstates the risk; the heterozygous father passes the pathogenic allele to half of his offspring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 100% would require the father to be homozygous for the pathogenic variant, which is rare and typically lethal.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A genetics student is comparing pedigrees of two families: one with an autosomal dominant disorder and one with an autosomal recessive disorder. In both, males and females are affected in equal proportions. Which of the following features is most characteristic of the autosomal recessive pedigree and would help distinguish it from the autosomal dominant one?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Affected individuals typically appear in only one generation

choices.label: B
choices.text: All daughters of an affected male are affected, but no sons

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each affected individual has at least one affected parent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Male-to-male transmission is absent from the pedigree

choices.label: E
choices.text: Males are affected far more often than females in each generation

explanation.summary: Autosomal recessive pedigrees typically show affected individuals in only one generation, whereas autosomal dominant pedigrees show affected individuals in every generation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Autosomal recessive conditions require pathogenic variants in both alleles, so affected individuals usually have unaffected carrier parents, and it is more typical to see only one generation with affected individuals (the pedigree may skip generations). In contrast, autosomal dominant pedigrees show affected individuals in multiple generations.

whyWrongByChoice.B: All daughters of affected males being affected is the hallmark of X-linked dominant inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An affected parent for every affected individual is typical of autosomal dominant inheritance, not autosomal recessive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Absence of male-to-male transmission is a clue for X-linked inheritance, not a feature distinguishing the two autosomal patterns.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both autosomal patterns affect males and females at equal rates because the genes are on somatic chromosomes.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A student is comparing the Y chromosome with the autosomes and the X chromosome. Which of the following statements about the Y chromosome is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carries genes largely restricted to gonadal and genital development

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carries genes whose functions are mostly in oxidative phosphorylation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contains a larger number of genes than the X chromosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Is passed from mothers to their sons at fertilization

choices.label: E
choices.text: Specifies several hundred distinct protein products

explanation.summary: The Y chromosome has few genes, and a high proportion of them function in gonadal and genital development.
explanation.whyCorrect: By comparison with the autosomes and the X chromosome, the Y chromosome has relatively few genes: fewer than 100 genes specifying only about 24 distinct proteins. The functions of a high proportion of these genes are restricted to gonadal and genital development, which is why there are very few Y-linked conditions.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Genes for oxidative phosphorylation are the domain of the mitochondrial genome, not the Y chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Y chromosome has relatively few genes compared with the X chromosome and autosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Y chromosome is passed only from fathers to sons; mothers do not have a Y chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The Y chromosome specifies only about 24 distinct proteins, not several hundred.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man and his wife are evaluated for infertility. He is otherwise healthy with normal secondary sexual characteristics, but semen analysis shows a very low sperm count. Which of the following genetic findings is most likely in this man?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deletion of the long arm of the X chromosome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heteroplasmic mutation in mitochondrial DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterozygous pathogenic variant on chromosome 9

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous recessive variant on an autosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Microdeletion of the male-specific region of Yq

explanation.summary: Microdeletions in the male-specific portion of Yq are found in a significant proportion of otherwise healthy men with low sperm count.
explanation.whyCorrect: Y chromosome deletions and microdeletions occur in about 1 in 2000-3000 males in the general population. Microdeletions in the male-specific portion of Yq are found in a significant proportion of otherwise healthy men with low sperm count, because three regions on Yq contain genes important in spermatogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The genes important in spermatogenesis described here lie on the long arm of the Y chromosome, not the X.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitochondrial DNA mutations produce neuromuscular and other high-energy-tissue disease rather than isolated low sperm count in a healthy man.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A chromosome 9 variant is not the classic genetic association with isolated oligospermia described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The recognized association with low sperm count in otherwise healthy men is a Yq microdeletion, not a homozygous autosomal recessive variant.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A biochemistry student is asked to describe the mitochondrial chromosome. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circular molecule of about 24 genes, inherited from the father

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circular molecule of only 37 genes, present in many copies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Circular molecule replicated only once per cell division

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linear molecule of about 100 genes, one copy per cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Linear molecule that pairs with a homologue during meiosis

explanation.summary: The mitochondrial chromosome is a tiny circular molecule containing 37 genes, present in multiple copies per mitochondrion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Human cells contain hundreds to thousands of mitochondria, and each mitochondrion contains a number of copies of a small circular molecule, the mitochondrial chromosome. It is very tiny compared with a nuclear chromosome and contains only 37 genes, whose products function in the mitochondria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 24 distinct proteins is the figure for the Y chromosome, and mitochondrial DNA is maternally, not paternally, inherited.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The multiple mtDNA copies in each mitochondrion replicate and then sort randomly among newly synthesized mitochondria; they are not limited to a single replication per division.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitochondrial DNA is circular, contains 37 genes, and exists in many copies per cell, not a single copy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mitochondrial DNA is circular and cytoplasmic; it does not pair with a homologue like a nuclear chromosome.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has a confirmed pathogenic mitochondrial DNA mutation. He is told that none of his children will inherit the mutation from him. Which of the following best explains why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mutant mitochondria are removed from sperm during meiosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paternal mitochondrial DNA is silenced by X-inactivation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paternal mitochondrial DNA remains below the phenotypic threshold

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sperm mitochondria are generally not present in the fertilized embryo

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Y chromosome carries no genes for mitochondrial proteins

explanation.summary: Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited because sperm mitochondria are generally not present in the fertilized embryo.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sperm mitochondria are generally not present in the fertilized embryo, so the embryo's mitochondria (and their DNA) come from the mother. Children of a female with a mitochondrial DNA mutation inherit it, but males do not transmit it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes maternal inheritance to sperm mitochondria not being present in the embryo, not to selective removal of mutant mitochondria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: X-inactivation silences one X chromosome in females; it has nothing to do with mitochondrial DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The threshold concept concerns the proportion of mutant mitochondria within a cell, not why paternal mtDNA is absent from offspring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The Y chromosome's gene content is irrelevant; mitochondrial genes reside on the mitochondrial chromosome, and their absence in offspring is due to absent sperm mitochondria.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a mitochondrial DNA mutation. She has two sons and one daughter with her unaffected husband. Which of her children are expected to inherit the mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All three children

choices.label: B
choices.text: None of the children

choices.label: C
choices.text: On average, half of the children

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only the daughter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only the two sons

explanation.summary: Children of a female with a mitochondrial DNA mutation inherit the mutation regardless of sex.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited, children of a female with a mitochondrial DNA mutation will inherit the mutation. Both sons and daughters receive their mitochondria from their mother, so all three children inherit it (although the proportion of mutant mtDNA, and thus the phenotype, can vary).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Only an affected father transmits to none of his children; an affected mother transmits to all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 50% split describes a heterozygous nuclear allele, not maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sons receive their mitochondria from the mother just as daughters do, so transmission is not limited to daughters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Daughters inherit maternal mitochondria as well; sex does not determine mitochondrial transmission from a mother.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A woman with a heteroplasmic mitochondrial DNA mutation has two sons. One developed severe myopathy in childhood, while the other is asymptomatic in his 20s, and testing shows very different proportions of mutant mitochondrial DNA in the two brothers. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Different amounts of paternal mtDNA in each fertilized embryo

choices.label: B
choices.text: Different patterns of X-inactivation between the two brothers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inheritance of a wild-type nuclear allele by only one son

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive increase in mutant load across successive generations

choices.label: E
choices.text: Random sorting of mutant and wild-type mtDNA into their cells

explanation.summary: Random segregation of mutant and wild-type mitochondrial DNA during cell division produces cells and individuals with different proportions of mutant mtDNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: During mitosis and meiosis, the multiple copies of mitochondrial DNA in each mitochondrion replicate and then sort randomly among the newly synthesized mitochondria. This random segregation produces daughter cells with heteroplasmy in varying proportions, so two children of the same heteroplasmic mother can carry very different mutant loads; the son whose proportion exceeds the threshold manifests disease while the other does not.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sperm mitochondria are generally not present in the fertilized embryo, so paternal mtDNA does not contribute to either son.
whyWrongByChoice.B: X-inactivation concerns X-linked genes in females and does not apply to mitochondrial DNA in males.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The disorder is caused by a mitochondrial DNA mutation, not by a nuclear allele that segregates between siblings.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Worsening across generations describes anticipation, not the variable mutant load produced within one generation by random mtDNA segregation.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a mitochondrial DNA mutation develops progressive ataxia, retinal degeneration, and loss of function of her external ocular muscles, while her skin and connective tissues appear unaffected. Which of the following best explains why these particular tissues are affected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: These tissues are the only ones that express mitochondrial genes

choices.label: B
choices.text: These tissues contain the fewest mitochondria per cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: These tissues have the highest rate of cell division

choices.label: D
choices.text: These tissues receive mitochondria from the paternal lineage

choices.label: E
choices.text: These tissues rely on oxidative phosphorylation for high energy demands

explanation.summary: Mitochondrial DNA diseases most profoundly affect tissues that depend on oxidative phosphorylation to meet high metabolic energy demands.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diseases resulting from mutations in mitochondrial DNA tend to have the most profound effects in tissues that rely on oxidative phosphorylation to meet high demands for metabolic energy. Neuromuscular disease is the most common outcome, with consequences such as encephalopathy, myopathy, ataxia, retinal degeneration, and loss of function of the external ocular muscles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mitochondrial genes function in mitochondria of almost all cells, not only in nerve, retina, and muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tissues with high energy demands are affected because of their dependence on mitochondrial energy production, not because they have few mitochondria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rapid cell division is not the determinant; nervous and muscle tissue are affected because of their high energy requirements.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitochondria are maternally inherited in all tissues; there is no paternal mitochondrial lineage.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy has an X-linked dominant disorder. His mother is affected and his father is unaffected. Using X(wt) for an X chromosome carrying the wild-type allele and X(v) for one carrying the variant, which of the following is the most likely set of genotypes for the mother, father, and son?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mother X(v)X(v); father X(wt)Y; son X(wt)Y

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mother X(wt)X(v); father X(v)Y; son X(wt)Y

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mother X(wt)X(v); father X(wt)Y; son X(v)Y

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mother X(wt)X(wt); father X(v)Y; son X(v)Y

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mother X(wt)X(wt); father X(wt)Y; son X(v)Y

explanation.summary: An affected son in an X-linked dominant pedigree must be X(v)Y and must have received his X(v) from an affected mother, since fathers pass only the Y to sons.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tracking sex chromosomes with alleles clarifies the genotypes. The affected son expresses the phenotype, so he is X(v)Y, and his X chromosome necessarily came from his mother; because she is affected she carries at least one X(v), most likely as a heterozygote X(wt)X(v). The father is unaffected, so he is X(wt)Y, and in any case he contributes only his Y chromosome to a son.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A son with X(wt)Y would not express the dominant phenotype, contradicting the stem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A son who is X(wt)Y would be unaffected, and the father here is stated to be unaffected, not X(v)Y.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An unaffected mother would be X(wt)X(wt) and could not give her son an X(v); an affected father cannot pass an X to a son at all.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two parents without a variant allele cannot produce an X(v)Y son by inheritance; the mother is stated to be affected.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A small pedigree shows an affected man and his unaffected wife with two affected daughters and one unaffected son. A geneticist notes that the pedigree is consistent with X-linked dominant inheritance. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance has not been excluded

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive inheritance is the most likely pattern

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial inheritance has not been excluded

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pedigree alone confirms autosomal dominant inheritance

choices.label: E
choices.text: The pedigree alone confirms X-linked dominant inheritance

explanation.summary: A pedigree alone often cannot distinguish X-linked from autosomal inheritance; clinical presentation and the pedigree together make the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Often we cannot determine from the pedigree alone whether a disorder is X-linked or autosomal. With an autosomal dominant disorder, it could happen by chance that an affected father and unaffected mother have two affected daughters and no affected sons, exactly mimicking X-linked dominant transmission. The clinical presentation together with the pedigree is needed to make the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Affected individuals in two consecutive generations with an affected parent is not the typical autosomal recessive picture, which usually shows affected children of unaffected carrier parents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited, and an affected father does not transmit it, so paternal transmission to daughters excludes mitochondrial inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pedigree does not confirm autosomal dominant inheritance either; it is equally consistent with X-linked dominant transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Affected daughters and an unaffected son could occur by chance in autosomal dominant inheritance, so the pedigree alone does not confirm X-linkage.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl is diagnosed with an X-linked recessive disorder confirmed by genetic testing to be homozygous for the pathogenic X allele. Which of the following is the most likely genetic status of her parents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Affected father and carrier mother

choices.label: B
choices.text: Affected father and non-carrier mother

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unaffected father and affected mother

choices.label: D
choices.text: Unaffected non-carrier father and carrier mother

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unaffected non-carrier father and non-carrier mother

explanation.summary: An affected female with an X-linked recessive disorder must receive a pathogenic X allele from each parent: a carrier (or affected) mother and an affected father.
explanation.whyCorrect: Females very rarely express X-linked recessive phenotypes because they need two pathogenic X alleles, X(v)X(v). They must have a carrier (X(wt)X(v)) or affected (X(v)X(v)) mother and an affected father (X(v)Y), since a daughter receives one X from each parent and the father's only X is the one he passes to every daughter.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A non-carrier mother is X(wt)X(wt) and would give the daughter a wild-type X, making her a carrier rather than affected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Even with an affected mother, an unaffected father contributes a wild-type X, so the daughter would be an unaffected carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An unaffected father is X(wt)Y and gives every daughter a wild-type X, so she could at most be a carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two non-carrier parents have no pathogenic X allele to transmit.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with hemophilia A, an X-linked recessive disorder, plans to have children with his wife, who has no family history of the condition and is confirmed not to carry the pathogenic allele. Which of the following best describes the expected status of their children?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All daughters carriers; no sons affected

choices.label: B
choices.text: All sons affected; daughters unaffected non-carriers

choices.label: C
choices.text: All sons and all daughters affected

choices.label: D
choices.text: Half of sons affected; half of daughters carriers

choices.label: E
choices.text: No children affected or carriers

explanation.summary: An affected X-linked recessive father passes his X(v) to every daughter (making them carriers) and his Y to every son (who are unaffected).
explanation.whyCorrect: Fathers expressing an X-linked recessive disorder cannot pass the phenotype to their sons, because they pass only their Y chromosome to male offspring. Every daughter, however, inherits her father's single X chromosome, which carries the variant; with a wild-type X from the non-carrier mother, each daughter is a carrier (X(wt)X(v)) but not affected.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sons receive the father's Y chromosome, not his X, so none can be affected through him; and daughters all receive his X(v).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sons cannot be affected, and daughters with one wild-type X from the mother are carriers rather than affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 50% risk to sons and daughters describes a carrier mother, not an affected father with a non-carrier partner.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Every daughter necessarily inherits the father's X(v), so all daughters are carriers.

questions.topicName: Pedigrees and Patterns of Monogenic Inheritance

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy and his 12-year-old sister both carry the same pathogenic NF1 variant and both have neurofibromatosis 1. The boy has only a few small cafe-au-lait spots, whereas his sister has numerous large cafe-au-lait spots, several neurofibromas, and scoliosis. Which of the following best explains the difference in the severity of disease between these two siblings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic anticipation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominant expression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locus (genetic) heterogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced penetrance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable expressivity

explanation.summary: Different severity of the same phenotype among individuals with the same genotype is variable expressivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Expressivity describes the severity of a disease-related phenotype among individuals who share a genotype. Neurofibromatosis 1 is highly penetrant but has highly variable expressivity, so people with the same NF1 variant may show cafe-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, and scoliosis of differing size, number, and location.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticipation refers to earlier onset or worsening across generations, not variation between siblings of one generation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance is the simultaneous expression of both alleles of a heterozygous pair, as in ABO blood groups, not a difference in severity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Locus heterogeneity means the same phenotype arises from mutations in different genes; both siblings share the same NF1 variant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reduced penetrance would mean some carriers show no phenotype at all; here both siblings are clearly affected, so penetrance is complete.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is found to carry a pathogenic BRCA1 variant during cascade testing after her sister developed breast cancer. Despite carrying the same variant, she has never developed breast or ovarian cancer. Which of the following concepts best accounts for the fact that not everyone with this variant develops cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pleiotropy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable expressivity

explanation.summary: When fewer carriers than expected show any phenotype, penetrance is incomplete.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penetrance is the all-or-nothing probability that a genotype produces any phenotype at all. Hereditary cancer syndromes such as BRCA1-related breast cancer are classic examples of incomplete penetrance because not everyone who carries the pathogenic variant develops cancer in their lifetime.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic heterogeneity refers to different mutations in the same gene causing one phenotype, not to a carrier remaining unaffected.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance is the simultaneous expression of two alleles and is unrelated to whether a phenotype appears.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pleiotropy is one gene variant causing multiple unrelated features across organ systems, which is not what this scenario describes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Variable expressivity describes differing severity among individuals who do manifest disease, not the total absence of disease in a carrier.

questions.stem: A person inherits an A allele from one parent and a B allele from the other at the ABO locus. Laboratory typing shows that their red blood cells display both A and B antigens on the surface. Which of the following genetic concepts does this finding best illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modifier gene effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pleiotropy

explanation.summary: The ABO blood group is the classic example of codominance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Codominance occurs when both alleles of a heterozygous pair are expressed and contribute to the phenotype. The A and B alleles each encode an enzyme that modifies red-cell surface sugars, so a heterozygous AB individual expresses both A and B antigens because neither allele is dominant over the other.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Incomplete penetrance concerns whether a phenotype appears at all, not the joint expression of two alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Locus heterogeneity is the same phenotype arising from different genes, which does not apply to a single ABO locus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A modifier gene is a separate gene altering another gene's phenotype; both antigens here come from the two ABO alleles themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pleiotropy is one gene affecting multiple organ systems, not two alleles at one locus being co-expressed.

questions.stem: An untreated infant with phenylketonuria develops microcephaly, developmental delay, eczema, a mousy body odor, and a markedly elevated serum phenylalanine concentration. All of these seemingly unrelated features arise from a variant in the single gene encoding phenylalanine hydroxylase. Which of the following concepts best describes this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pleiotropy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable expressivity

explanation.summary: One gene variant producing many unrelated features across organ systems is pleiotropy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pleiotropy refers to situations where a pathogenic variant in a single gene leads to multiple, seemingly unrelated phenotypic effects across different organ systems. Untreated phenylketonuria illustrates this with neurologic, dermatologic, and metabolic manifestations all stemming from one gene defect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Codominance is joint expression of two alleles at one locus and does not explain multi-system involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Incomplete penetrance concerns whether disease appears at all, not the breadth of features when it does.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Locus heterogeneity is one phenotype produced by variants in different genes; PKU here arises from a single gene.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Variable expressivity describes differing severity of the phenotype among individuals with the same genotype, not multiple features in one patient.

questions.stem: Two unrelated children both have cystic fibrosis, but sequencing shows that each carries a different pair of pathogenic mutations within the CFTR gene. Which of the following concepts best explains how different mutations in the same gene produce the same disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominant expression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modifier gene effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pleiotropic gene effect

explanation.summary: Different mutations at the same locus causing one phenotype is allelic heterogeneity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Allelic heterogeneity occurs when different mutations at the same locus lead to a similar phenotype. Cystic fibrosis is the classic example because it can be caused by many different mutations within the CFTR gene.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance is the co-expression of two alleles and does not describe multiple disease-causing mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Locus heterogeneity involves mutations in genes at different loci; here all mutations are within the single CFTR gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A modifier gene alters the phenotype from a different gene; the scenario concerns variants inside CFTR itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pleiotropy is one variant causing multiple unrelated features, not different variants producing the same disease.

questions.stem: A geneticist notes that Cornelia de Lange syndrome, a developmental disorder, can be caused by a pathogenic variant in any one of three different genes located at separate chromosomal loci. Which of the following concepts does this observation best illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pleiotropy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable expressivity

explanation.summary: One phenotype produced by mutations in different genes is locus heterogeneity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Locus heterogeneity describes the same disorder being caused by mutations in genes at different loci. Cornelia de Lange syndrome, which can be acquired by a mutation in any of three different genes, is an example. Such heterogeneity can complicate diagnosis and cause false-negative genetic testing when not all loci are known.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic heterogeneity involves different mutations within a single gene, not across different genes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance is joint expression of two alleles at one locus and is unrelated to multiple causative loci.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pleiotropy is one gene variant causing multiple features, the opposite direction of this scenario.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Variable expressivity concerns differing severity among affected individuals, not the number of causative genes.

questions.stem: In sickle cell disease, a single base-pair change (GAG to GTG) in the HBB gene substitutes one amino acid in the beta-chain of hemoglobin, converting it to hemoglobin S. Which of the following types of mutation is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromosomal nondisjunction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Frameshift mutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Large gene deletion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Point mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trinucleotide repeat expansion

explanation.summary: A single base-pair substitution altering one codon is a point mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: A point mutation is a single base-pair change. In sickle cell disease this GAG-to-GTG substitution in HBB changes one amino acid in the beta-globin chain to yield hemoglobin S, and a person homozygous for the variant has HbSS disease. This is a clean example of a direct genotype-phenotype correlation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nondisjunction is failure of chromosome separation causing aneuploidy, not a single base-pair change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A frameshift results from insertion or deletion of bases not in multiples of three, shifting the reading frame; only a single base is changed here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A large deletion removes a segment of the gene; here a single nucleotide is substituted, not deleted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trinucleotide repeat expansions underlie disorders such as Huntington disease, not the single substitution in HBB.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man whose father had Huntington disease learns that he carries the same pathogenic variant. He currently has no neurologic symptoms, and his physician explains that manifestations most often appear during the 30s or 40s. Which of the following best characterizes this feature of Huntington disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Age-dependent penetrance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity at one locus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Codominant expression

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modifier gene effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pleiotropic gene effect

explanation.summary: When a genotype expresses only later in life, penetrance is age-dependent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penetrance of some disorders is age-dependent: a person may not express the disorder early in life yet develop signs and symptoms later. Huntington disease most frequently becomes symptomatic when people are in their 30s or 40s, so a young unaffected carrier reflects age-dependent penetrance rather than true absence of disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Allelic heterogeneity is different mutations in the same gene causing one phenotype, not delayed onset.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Codominance is the co-expression of two alleles and has nothing to do with age of onset.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A modifier gene alters a phenotype caused by another gene; the delayed onset here reflects age-dependent penetrance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pleiotropy is one gene producing multiple unrelated features across organ systems.

questions.stem: Two patients with cystic fibrosis carry identical CFTR genotypes, yet one has markedly more severe disease. Investigators determine that a variant in a separate gene at a different locus is responsible for altering the severity of the CFTR-related phenotype. Which of the following best describes the role of this second gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modifier gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pleiotropy

explanation.summary: A separate gene that changes the phenotype produced by another gene is a modifier gene.
explanation.whyCorrect: A modifier gene has the ability to alter the phenotype caused by expression of a different gene elsewhere in the genome, and can affect dominance, penetrance, and expressivity. Cystic fibrosis is a recognized example in which modifier genes can influence disease severity, symptoms, or whether signs appear at all.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic heterogeneity involves different mutations within the same gene; here a distinct, separate gene changes the phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance is the joint expression of two alleles at one locus, not one gene modifying another.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Locus heterogeneity means the same disease arises from different genes independently; here CFTR still causes the disease and a second gene only modifies it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pleiotropy is a single gene causing multiple features, not a second gene influencing severity.

questions.stem: A physician in a Marfan syndrome clinic sees five children who all share the same autosomal dominant condition. All are tall and thin with long fingers, but only one has severe heart disease, two have eye disease, and two have curved spines. A shadowing student asks why patients with the same disorder have different findings. Which of the following concepts best explains this variation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable expressivity

explanation.summary: A range of findings among people with the same disorder reflects variable expressivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: In most genetic disorders a range of signs and symptoms occurs among different affected individuals, a phenomenon called variable expressivity. The Marfan patients all express the disease (complete penetrance) but differ in which features appear and how severe they are, which is variable expressivity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic heterogeneity concerns different mutations in the same gene, not variability in expression among affected patients.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance is co-expression of two alleles at a locus and does not explain the range of findings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Incomplete penetrance would mean some mutation carriers show no disease at all; here all five children are affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Locus heterogeneity means the same phenotype arises from different genes; these patients share one disorder.

questions.stem: Monozygotic twins share an identical genome, yet one develops a particular trait and the other does not because of differences in diet and other non-genetic exposures. Which of the following concepts best accounts for this discordance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Environmental effects

choices.label: D
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pleiotropy

explanation.summary: Non-genetic factors that shape a phenotype are environmental effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Environmental effects are non-genetic factors that can influence a phenotype. When genetically identical twins differ in a trait, factors outside the genome such as diet and exposures can drive the difference, illustrating how the environment modifies genotype-phenotype correlation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic heterogeneity concerns different mutations in one gene; the twins share the same genome, so this cannot be the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance is joint expression of two alleles and does not explain a difference driven by exposures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Locus heterogeneity involves different genes causing one phenotype and cannot apply to twins with an identical genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pleiotropy is one gene producing multiple features, not a non-genetic cause of discordance.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to distinguish penetrance from expressivity. Which of the following statements most accurately defines penetrance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single gene variant causing multiple unrelated phenotypic features

choices.label: B
choices.text: The probability that a genotype produces any phenotypic expression at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: The same phenotype being caused by mutations in different genes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The severity of the disease-related phenotype among individuals with the same genotype

choices.label: E
choices.text: The simultaneous expression of both alleles of a heterozygous pair

explanation.summary: Penetrance is the all-or-nothing probability that a genotype produces any phenotype.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penetrance is the probability that an allele or alleles will have any phenotypic expression at all; it is all-or-nothing, so an individual either shows some clinical manifestation or none. If only 8 of 10 people with a genotype ever show a phenotype, penetrance is 80%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This defines pleiotropy, a single gene variant causing multiple unrelated features.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This defines locus heterogeneity, one phenotype produced by mutations in different genes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This defines expressivity, which describes the severity of the phenotype among individuals who share a genotype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This defines codominance, the joint expression of both alleles of a heterozygous pair.

questions.stem: A geneticist reports that a patient is heterozygous at the CFTR locus. When the geneticist uses the word genotype in this report, which of the following is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The alleles occupying that locus on the two homologous chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: The clinical severity of the patient's lung disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: The expression of the locus as a biochemical trait

choices.label: D
choices.text: The number of different genes that can produce the same disorder

choices.label: E
choices.text: The probability that the patient will develop any symptoms

explanation.summary: Genotype at a locus is the pair of alleles present on the two homologous chromosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genotype at a particular locus in the genome refers to the alleles occupying that locus on the two homologous chromosomes. Reporting a patient as heterozygous at CFTR is a statement about which two alleles are present, not about how they are expressed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Clinical severity is a matter of phenotype and, more specifically, expressivity, not genotype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Expression of the genotype as a biochemical, clinical, morphologic, or cellular trait is the definition of phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The number of different genes that can cause one disorder describes locus heterogeneity, not genotype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The probability that a genotype produces any symptoms is penetrance, not the genotype itself.

questions.stem: A first-year student states that the term phenotype applies only to disease states. Which of the following is the best example of a phenotype as the term is properly defined?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A GAG-to-GTG base change in the HBB gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person's eye color

choices.label: C
choices.text: The chromosomal position 17q11.2

choices.label: D
choices.text: The locus of a modifier gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: The pair of alleles present at the ABO locus

explanation.summary: Phenotype is any expression of genotype as a trait, including non-disease traits such as eye color and height.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenotype is the expression of genotype as a morphologic, clinical, cellular, or biochemical trait.
