Although discussions of genotype-phenotype correlation focus on disease phenotypes, phenotype can refer to many non-disease characteristics such as height and eye color, so the student's claim is too narrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A base change is a mutation in the DNA sequence, part of the genotype rather than its expression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A chromosomal position is a locus, the address of a gene, not an expressed trait.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The locus of a modifier gene is a genomic location, not a trait.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The alleles at a locus are the genotype, not the phenotype.

questions.stem: A physician tells a family that their child's disorder is determined primarily by the alleles at a single locus and is transmitted in fixed, predictable proportions, so the phenotype of relatives who inherit the variant can be predicted. Which of the following terms best describes this type of disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromosomal (cytogenetic) disorder

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominant disorder

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monogenic (Mendelian) disorder

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multifactorial (complex) disorder

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polygenic threshold disorder

explanation.summary: Disorders determined primarily by alleles at a single locus are monogenic, or Mendelian, disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genotype-phenotype correlation is easiest to understand for monogenic disorders, those determined primarily by the alleles at a single locus. They follow the classic inheritance patterns (autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, X-linked), are also called Mendelian disorders after Gregor Mendel, and their transmission occurs in fixed and predictable proportions, which allows the phenotype of individuals who inherit one or two copies of the variant to be predicted.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A chromosomal disorder involves gain or loss of chromosomal material rather than alleles at one locus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance describes both alleles of a heterozygous pair being expressed; it is not a category of disorder defined by single-locus inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A multifactorial disorder involves multiple genes plus environmental contributions, not a single locus with fixed transmission ratios.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A polygenic disorder depends on many loci, not primarily on alleles at a single locus.

questions.stem: A registry follows 40 adults who all carry the same pathogenic variant for an autosomal dominant disorder over their lifetimes. Thirty develop at least one clinical manifestation of the disorder, ranging from a single minor finding to severe multisystem disease, and 10 never show any clinical evidence of the variant. Which of the following is the penetrance of this disorder in this registry?

explanation.summary: Penetrance is the proportion of individuals with a genotype who show any phenotype; 30 of 40 is 75%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penetrance is the proportion of individuals with a certain genotype who express the associated phenotype, and with enough data it can be given a numerical value. It is all-or-nothing, so anyone with some clinical manifestation, no matter what form it takes, counts as penetrant. Here 30 of 40 carriers show a phenotype, so penetrance is 75%; the range of severity among the 30 is expressivity and does not change the calculation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 25% is the proportion of carriers who are non-penetrant, not the penetrance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 30 is the number of affected carriers, not the proportion; penetrance is expressed as a fraction of all carriers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 40 is the total number of carriers in the registry, not a proportion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 100% penetrance would require every carrier to show some manifestation, but 10 never did.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man carries a pathogenic variant for an autosomal dominant disorder. His only finding is a single small skin lesion characteristic of the condition, whereas his sister, who carries the same variant, has severe involvement of several organ systems. For the purpose of determining whether the variant is penetrant in this man, which of the following is the most accurate classification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Non-penetrant until involvement of a second organ system occurs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Non-penetrant, because a single lesion is too minor to count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Partially penetrant, in proportion to the number of lesions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penetrant, because any clinical manifestation counts as expression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unclassifiable until his sister's severity is compared with his

explanation.summary: Penetrance is all-or-nothing: any clinical manifestation, however minor, means the genotype is penetrant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penetrance is described as all or nothing: either there is some clinical manifestation, no matter what form it takes, or there is no clinical evidence of the pathogenic variant. A single characteristic lesion is a clinical manifestation, so the variant is penetrant in this man. The difference between his mild disease and his sister's severe disease is variable expressivity, a separate concept.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no requirement for multiple organ systems; one manifestation of any form is sufficient for penetrance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Penetrance does not depend on how severe the manifestation is; any finding counts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penetrance is not graded within an individual; it is either present or absent. Degree of disease is expressivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penetrance is judged by whether the individual shows any phenotype at all, not by comparison with a relative's severity.

questions.stem: A medical student notes that two phenomena, reduced penetrance and a wide range of variable expressivity, keep appearing together in her review of certain genetic disorders. These two phenomena are most characteristically associated with which of the following inheritance patterns?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal recessive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial

choices.label: D
choices.text: X-linked recessive

choices.label: E
choices.text: Y-linked

explanation.summary: Penetrance is thought of mainly in autosomal dominant disorders, and the greatest variability in expressivity is also found in autosomal dominant conditions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penetrance tends to be associated more with autosomal dominant disorders, and although most genetic disorders have some degree of variable expressivity, the greatest variability tends to be found in autosomal dominant conditions. Examples in this pattern include BRCA1-related breast cancer (incomplete penetrance) and neurofibromatosis 1 and Marfan syndrome (variable expressivity).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autosomal recessive disorders can show some variable expressivity, but reduced penetrance and the widest variability are not their hallmark.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial inheritance is not among the classic monogenic patterns discussed and is not the answer here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-linked recessive inheritance is not the pattern with which reduced penetrance and the greatest expressivity range are most associated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Y-linked inheritance is not the pattern characteristically linked to reduced penetrance and variable expressivity.

questions.stem: A newborn whose mother has Huntington disease undergoes genetic testing and is found to carry the pathogenic variant. The infant has a normal neurologic examination. The parents ask whether the absence of any findings means the variant is non-penetrant in their child. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A modifier gene at a second locus has permanently silenced the variant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Signs may still appear in adulthood, because penetrance is age-dependent

choices.label: C
choices.text: The child shows reduced penetrance and will remain unaffected for life

choices.label: D
choices.text: The child shows variable expressivity with an unusually mild phenotype

choices.label: E
choices.text: The normal examination indicates the test result was a false positive

explanation.summary: A newborn carrier without findings cannot be called non-penetrant when the disorder has age-dependent penetrance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penetrance of some disorders is age-dependent: a newborn may not express the disorder, but the same individual may have signs and symptoms that show up later during childhood or adulthood. Huntington disease is the example given, most frequently becoming symptomatic when people are in their 30s or 40s, so a normal newborn examination does not establish non-penetrance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nothing in the scenario points to a second gene; the delayed appearance of signs is explained by age-dependent penetrance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Non-penetrance can only be judged over a lifetime; a newborn without findings has simply not reached the age at which this disorder manifests.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Variable expressivity describes differing severity among people who already express the disease; this infant expresses no phenotype yet.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A normal examination in a newborn is expected for a disorder that becomes symptomatic decades later and does not indicate a false-positive test.

questions.stem: During a lecture, an instructor compares one genetic concept to a light switch that is either on or off and a second concept to a dimmer that allows a spectrum of brightness between light and dark. Which of the following concepts is represented by the dimmer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expressivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penetrance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pleiotropy

explanation.summary: Penetrance is the on-or-off light switch; expressivity is the dimmer that sets severity.
explanation.whyCorrect: If penetrance is thought of as a light switch, resulting in the light being on or off, then expressivity is like a dimmer, allowing a spectrum of brightness in between. Penetrance relates to the proportion of individuals who display the expected phenotype at all, whereas expressivity describes the severity of disease in those who do.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Codominance is the simultaneous expression of both alleles of a heterozygous pair, unrelated to a severity spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Locus heterogeneity is one phenotype caused by variants in different genes, not a spectrum of disease severity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penetrance is the all-or-nothing switch in the analogy, not the dimmer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pleiotropy is a single-gene variant causing multiple unrelated features, not a gradation of severity.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has multiple cafe-au-lait spots and several neurofibromas, and neurofibromatosis 1 is diagnosed. Which of the following best describes the gene responsible for her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A modifier gene at 4p16 that alters disease severity

choices.label: B
choices.text: A tumor suppressor gene at 17q11.2

choices.label: C
choices.text: A tumor suppressor gene at 7q31

choices.label: D
choices.text: An oncogene at 11p15 that drives cell proliferation

choices.label: E
choices.text: An oncogene at 17q11.2

explanation.summary: Neurofibromatosis 1 results from mutations of the tumor suppressor gene NF1 at 17q11.2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurofibromatosis 1 is an autosomal dominant disease due to mutations of the tumor suppressor gene NF1 located at 17q11.2. The disease is highly penetrant, and the variable size of cafe-au-lait spots and variable size and location of neurofibromas reflect its highly variable expressivity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NF1 is the primary disease-causing gene, not a modifier gene, and it is not located on chromosome 4.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The gene class is right, but NF1 is on chromosome 17 at 17q11.2, not on chromosome 7.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NF1 is neither an oncogene nor located on chromosome 11.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NF1 is a tumor suppressor gene, not an oncogene, although the chromosomal location is correct.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with neurofibromatosis 1 has numerous cafe-au-lait spots, several neurofibromas, and scoliosis. Prenatal testing shows that her fetus has inherited the same NF1 variant. She asks what to expect for the child. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The child has about a 50% chance of showing any feature of the disorder

choices.label: B
choices.text: The child may well be unaffected, because the disorder has low penetrance

choices.label: C
choices.text: The child will almost certainly show disease, but severity is unpredictable

choices.label: D
choices.text: The child will have the same findings as the mother, with the same severity

choices.label: E
choices.text: The child's severity will be milder, because the disorder shows anticipation

explanation.summary: Neurofibromatosis 1 is highly penetrant but has highly variable expressivity, so an inheriting child will be affected to an unpredictable degree.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurofibromatosis 1 is highly penetrant, meaning essentially everyone with the genotype is affected by the disease. However, it has highly variable expressivity: people with the same genotype may have cafe-au-lait spots of variable sizes, neurofibromas of variable size and location, and different degrees of learning disabilities, facial dysmorphism, and scoliosis. The child who inherited the variant will therefore almost certainly be affected, but the severity cannot be predicted from the mother's findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 50% figure describes the chance of inheriting an autosomal dominant variant; this fetus has already inherited it, and once present the variant is highly penetrant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neurofibromatosis 1 is highly penetrant, so a carrier is very unlikely to be entirely unaffected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Highly variable expressivity means the child's findings and severity may differ substantially from the mother's.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticipation is not a feature described for neurofibromatosis 1, and there is no basis to predict a milder course.

questions.stem: A trait is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern in a three-generation family. An affected grandmother has a son who shows no sign of the trait, yet two of his children are affected. Every affected family member has the trait to an identical degree. Which of the following best classifies the penetrance and expressivity of this trait in the family?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Codominant with age-dependent penetrance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Completely penetrant with consistent expressivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Completely penetrant with variable expressivity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incompletely penetrant with consistent expressivity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Incompletely penetrant with variable expressivity

explanation.summary: An obligate carrier with no phenotype means incomplete penetrance; identical severity in all affected members means consistent expressivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The unaffected son must carry the variant because he has an affected parent and transmitted the trait to two children, so the genotype produced no phenotype in him; that is reduced or incomplete penetrance. Among those who do show the trait, the expression is identical in every case, so expressivity is consistent rather than variable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Codominance concerns two alleles being expressed simultaneously and does not describe this pedigree; nothing indicates onset tied to age.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complete penetrance would require every carrier to show the trait, but the son who transmitted it is unaffected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The son's lack of any phenotype rules out complete penetrance, and identical severity among affected members rules out variable expressivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penetrance is incomplete, but expressivity is consistent because all affected members show the trait to the same degree.

questions.stem: In an autosomal dominant family, every individual who inherited the variant over three generations shows at least one feature of the trait, but the manifestations range from a single barely detectable finding in some relatives to severe multisystem disease in others. No obligate carrier is unaffected. Which of the following best classifies this trait?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Codominant with consistent expressivity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Completely penetrant with consistent expressivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Completely penetrant with variable expressivity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incompletely penetrant with consistent expressivity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Incompletely penetrant with variable expressivity

explanation.summary: Every carrier affected means complete penetrance; a spectrum from minimal to severe means variable expressivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penetrance asks whether all individuals with the genotype show some sort of phenotype; here every carrier does, so the trait is completely penetrant. Expressivity describes the severity of disease, and a spectrum from a barely detectable finding to severe multisystem disease is variable expressivity, much like neurofibromatosis 1, which is highly penetrant yet highly variable in expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Codominance is the simultaneous expression of two alleles of a heterozygous pair and does not describe the range of severity in this family.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Penetrance is complete, but the wide range of severity means expressivity is variable, not consistent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both halves are wrong: every carrier is affected (complete penetrance) and severity varies widely (variable expressivity).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Incomplete penetrance would require at least one carrier with no phenotype, but no obligate carrier is unaffected.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old blood donor is homozygous for the O allele at the ABO locus, and his red blood cells display neither A nor B antigen. Which of the following best explains the absence of these antigens at the molecular level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The O allele deletes the entire ABO locus from both homologous chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: The O allele does not result in enzymatic modification of the red cell surface sugars

choices.label: C
choices.text: The O allele encodes an enzyme that removes A and B antigens from the cell surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: The O allele encodes both antigens, which are degraded before reaching the surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: The O allele is dominant over the A and B alleles and suppresses their expression

explanation.summary: The O allele produces no enzymatic modification of red cell surface sugars, so OO individuals lack A and B antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ABO gene has three alleles: A, B, and O. The A and B alleles encode enzymes that modify sugars on the surface of red blood cells, creating A antigen or B antigen. The O allele does not result in enzymatic modification of these sugars, so people who are homozygous for the O allele have neither A nor B antigens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The O allele is an allele at an intact ABO locus, not a deletion of the locus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The O allele does not actively remove antigens; it simply fails to add the sugar modifications that create them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The O allele does not produce either antigen; the absence of antigen reflects a lack of enzymatic modification, not degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The O allele produces no antigen of its own and does not suppress the A or B alleles; in an OO individual there is no A or B allele to suppress.

questions.stem: A laboratory scientist explains why a person with the AB genotype displays two different antigens on red blood cells. The A and B alleles at the ABO locus each encode which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A beta-globin chain variant of adult hemoglobin

choices.label: B
choices.text: A modifier protein acting on a gene at a second locus

choices.label: C
choices.text: A transmembrane chloride channel in epithelial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tumor suppressor protein that regulates Ras signaling

choices.label: E
choices.text: An enzyme that modifies sugars on the red cell surface

explanation.summary: The A and B alleles encode enzymes that modify red cell surface sugars to create the A and B antigens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The A and B alleles of the ABO gene encode enzymes that modify sugars on the surface of red blood cells, thereby creating A antigen or B antigen. In a heterozygous AB person both alleles are expressed, neither is dominant to the other, and the red cells carry both antigens, the classic example of codominance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-globin is encoded by HBB, the gene altered in sickle cell disease, not by the ABO alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The ABO alleles act at their own locus to create antigens; they are not modifier genes acting on another locus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A chloride channel is the product of the CFTR gene, which is discussed in the context of allelic heterogeneity and modifier genes, not ABO.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A tumor suppressor protein is the product of NF1, the gene mutated in neurofibromatosis 1.

questions.stem: A student asks how a modifier gene differs from a recessive allele, since both seem to change what phenotype a person displays. Which of the following is the most accurate distinction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A recessive allele acts only in homozygotes, whereas a modifier gene acts only in heterozygotes

choices.label: B
choices.text: A recessive allele alters penetrance, whereas a modifier gene alters only expressivity

choices.label: C
choices.text: A recessive allele arises by point mutation, whereas a modifier gene arises by deletion

choices.label: D
choices.text: A recessive allele is a non-genetic influence, whereas a modifier gene is inherited

choices.label: E
choices.text: A recessive allele is a variant of the same gene, whereas a modifier gene is a different gene

explanation.summary: Dominant and recessive describe variations of one gene; a modifier gene is a totally different gene elsewhere in the genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: A modifier gene has the ability to alter the phenotype caused by the expression of a different gene elsewhere in the genome. This is different from dominant and recessive alleles because those terms refer to variations of one gene, whereas a modifier gene is a totally different gene. Modifier genes can affect dominance, penetrance, and expressivity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The distinction is not about zygosity; modifier genes are defined by being a separate gene, not by acting only in heterozygotes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Modifier genes can affect dominance, penetrance, and expressivity, not expressivity alone, and recessiveness is not defined by altering penetrance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither term is defined by mutation type; the difference is whether the variant lies in the same gene or a different one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A recessive allele is a genetic variant, not a non-genetic influence; non-genetic factors are environmental effects.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to study how a gene at one locus alters the severity of a disease caused by a variant at a different locus. Which of the following conditions is an example in which modifier genes are known to affect disease severity, the symptoms a patient manifests, or whether any signs appear at all?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ABO blood group

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alkaptonuria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cornelia de Lange syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phenylketonuria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spinal muscular atrophy

explanation.summary: Spinal muscular atrophy is one of the conditions whose phenotype can be influenced by modifier genes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Several genetic conditions have phenotypes that can be influenced by modifier genes in humans. Retinitis pigmentosa, hereditary hemochromatosis, spinal muscular atrophy, and cystic fibrosis are all examples in which modifier genes can affect the severity of disease, the symptoms a patient manifests, or even whether they show any signs or symptoms at all.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ABO blood group is the classic example of codominance, not of modifier gene influence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alkaptonuria illustrates allelic heterogeneity, many different mutations at the same locus causing the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cornelia de Lange syndrome is the example of locus heterogeneity, being caused by a mutation in any of three different genes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phenylketonuria is presented as the example of pleiotropy, a single-gene variant causing multiple unrelated features, not of modifier gene effects.

questions.stem: Two adults carry identical pathogenic CFTR genotypes. One has classic cystic fibrosis, whereas the other has no clinical signs or symptoms at all. Investigators trace the difference to a variant in a gene at a separate locus. Which of the following properties of the CFTR genotype has this second gene altered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dominance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expressivity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Penetrance

explanation.summary: A modifier gene that determines whether a genotype produces any phenotype at all is altering penetrance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Modifier genes can affect dominance, penetrance, and expressivity, and in cystic fibrosis they can influence severity, the symptoms a patient manifests, or even whether they show any signs or symptoms at all. Because the second adult shows no clinical evidence of the CFTR genotype, the modifier is altering penetrance, the all-or-nothing question of whether any phenotype appears.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic heterogeneity refers to different mutations within CFTR causing the same disease; both adults have identical CFTR genotypes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance is the simultaneous expression of both alleles of a heterozygous pair, not the effect of a second gene on phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dominance concerns the relationship between alleles of one gene; the scenario is about whether the genotype is expressed at all.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Expressivity would apply if both adults were affected but to different degrees; here one has no phenotype whatsoever.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with phenylketonuria that was never treated has microcephaly, developmental delay, eczema, and a mousy body odor. Which of the following additional findings is part of the constellation of features that results from this single-gene disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cafe-au-lait spots

choices.label: B
choices.text: Long, thin fingers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neurofibromas

choices.label: D
choices.text: Osteopenia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickled red blood cells

explanation.summary: Untreated phenylketonuria produces a pleiotropic constellation that includes osteopenia along with neurologic, skin, and biochemical findings.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenylketonuria is an example of pleiotropy: if untreated, it is characterized by a constellation of functional and physical signs and symptoms across organ systems, including mousy body odor, microcephaly, developmental delay, osteopenia, dry skin, eczema, epilepsy, scleroderma, and an elevated serum concentration of phenylalanine. Osteopenia is the bone manifestation within this constellation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cafe-au-lait spots are a feature of neurofibromatosis 1, not phenylketonuria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Long, thin fingers are a finding of Marfan syndrome, not phenylketonuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neurofibromas are nerve sheath tumors seen in neurofibromatosis 1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickled red cells result from hemoglobin S in sickle cell disease, a different single-gene disorder.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is diagnosed clinically with alkaptonuria, a disorder in which the body cannot process amino acids properly and which can result from many different mutations at the same locus. A targeted genetic panel that screens only the most common variants at that locus returns a negative result. Which of the following concepts best explains why this negative result does not exclude the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modifier gene effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pleiotropy

explanation.summary: When many different alleles at one locus cause a disease, a panel that misses some of them can give a false-negative result.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alkaptonuria can be caused by many different mutations in the same locus of a chromosome, which is allelic heterogeneity. Allelic heterogeneity can complicate a genetic diagnosis: a false negative can occur if not all alleles for a genetic disease are known or tested, so a panel limited to the most common variants may miss the patient's causative allele.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Incomplete penetrance concerns carriers who show no phenotype; this patient is clinically affected and the issue is the test's coverage of alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Locus heterogeneity would apply if different genes caused the disease; the stem specifies many mutations at the same locus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A modifier gene alters the phenotype produced by another gene; it does not explain a negative test for the causative locus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pleiotropy is one gene variant producing many unrelated features and has no bearing on why a test misses a mutation.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl has developmental delay and dysmorphic features consistent with Cornelia de Lange syndrome. Sequencing of one of the genes associated with the disorder is normal. Which of the following concepts best explains why a normal result at this one gene does not exclude the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Age-dependent penetrance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

explanation.summary: A disorder caused by mutations at any of several loci can give a false-negative result if only one locus is tested.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cornelia de Lange syndrome is an example of locus heterogeneity, a developmental disease that can be acquired by a single mutation in any of three different genes. Locus heterogeneity can complicate a genetic diagnosis, and a false negative can occur if not all loci are known or examined; sequencing only one of the three genes leaves the other two untested.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Age-dependent penetrance refers to delayed onset of signs, not to a negative test in a symptomatic child.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Allelic heterogeneity is different mutations within a single gene; the issue here is that the disease can arise from entirely different genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Codominance is the simultaneous expression of two alleles at one locus and is unrelated to negative genetic testing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Incomplete penetrance concerns carriers without a phenotype, whereas this child is clearly affected.

questions.stem: Investigators sequence the genomes of everyone in an isolated population to estimate the prevalence of an autosomal dominant disorder. They find that the number of people who are clinically affected is substantially lower than the number who carry the pathogenic genotype. Which of the following phenomena have they most likely encountered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codominance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pleiotropy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable expressivity

explanation.summary: Fewer affected people than carriers of the genotype at the population level is incomplete penetrance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Penetrance is the proportion of individuals with a certain genotype who express the associated phenotype. When the proportion who actually express the disease is lower than the number who should according to their genotypes, less than 100% of individuals with the mutation express the expected disease, which is incomplete penetrance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic heterogeneity is different mutations in the same gene producing one disease and does not account for carriers being unaffected.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Codominance occurs when two alleles are simultaneously expressed and does not explain unaffected genotype carriers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pleiotropy refers to many disparate phenotypic effects across organ systems from one gene variant, not to absence of disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Variable expressivity means people with the same variant have phenotypes of differing severity or tissue involvement; it does not refer to the absence of a phenotype in someone with the variant.

questions.stem: A newborn screen identifies hemoglobin S. Follow-up sequencing of the HBB gene is performed to determine whether the infant will have the HbSS form of sickle cell disease. Which of the following genotypes at the HBB locus produces HbSS disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heterozygous for the GAG-to-GTG variant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heterozygous for the variant plus a modifier gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygous for a deletion of the HBB gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous for the GAG-to-GTG variant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Homozygous for the normal GAG codon

explanation.summary: A person homozygous for the GAG-to-GTG HBB variant has the HbSS form of sickle cell disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: A single base-pair point mutation (GAG to GTG) in the HBB gene results in an amino acid substitution in the beta-chain of hemoglobin that changes it to hemoglobin S. When a person is homozygous for this variant, they will have the HbSS form of sickle cell disease, a direct genotype-phenotype correlation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A heterozygote carries one HbS allele and one normal allele, which is not the HbSS genotype.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HbSS disease is defined by the HBB genotype itself, not by the presence of a modifier gene alongside a single variant allele.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The sickle variant is a point mutation that substitutes one amino acid, not a deletion of the gene.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Homozygosity for the normal GAG codon yields normal beta-globin and no hemoglobin S.

questions.stem: A newborn screening test shows a markedly elevated serum concentration of phenylalanine, and phenylketonuria is confirmed. Which of the following best classifies the elevated phenylalanine level itself?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biochemical phenotype

choices.label: B
choices.text: A genotype at the causative locus

choices.label: C
choices.text: A modifier gene effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: A morphologic phenotype

choices.label: E
choices.text: An allele

explanation.summary: Phenotype includes biochemical traits, so an elevated serum phenylalanine is a biochemical phenotype.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phenotype is the expression of genotype as a morphologic, clinical, cellular, or biochemical trait. The elevated serum concentration of phenylalanine in phenylketonuria is one of the phenotypic manifestations of the disorder, expressed as a biochemical trait rather than a physical feature.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The genotype is the pair of alleles at the locus; the phenylalanine level is the expression of that genotype, not the genotype itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nothing indicates a second gene altering the phenotype; the elevated level is a direct manifestation of the disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A morphologic phenotype is a structural feature such as microcephaly; a serum concentration is biochemical.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An allele is a version of a gene at a locus, not a measured trait.

questions.stem: Two siblings have cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder, and carry identical CFTR genotypes, yet one has far more severe disease than the other. A student states that variable expressivity cannot explain this because it occurs only in autosomal dominant disorders. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most genetic disorders show some variable expressivity, not only dominant ones

choices.label: B
choices.text: The difference can only be due to locus heterogeneity between the siblings

choices.label: C
choices.text: The difference must reflect incomplete penetrance rather than expressivity

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student is correct; autosomal recessive disorders always show consistent expressivity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable expressivity is limited to X-linked and autosomal dominant conditions

explanation.summary: Variable expressivity is greatest in autosomal dominant conditions, but most genetic disorders show some degree of it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Variable expressivity is when a disease affects people to different degrees. Though the greatest variability tends to be found in autosomal dominant conditions, most genetic disorders have a degree of variable expressivity. Cystic fibrosis is a specific example in which severity can differ among people with the same genotype, with modifier genes among the factors that can influence it.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Locus heterogeneity means the same disease is caused by different genes; both siblings have identical CFTR genotypes, so it cannot explain their difference.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penetrance is all-or-nothing and both siblings are affected, so the difference in severity is a matter of expressivity, not penetrance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autosomal recessive disorders are not exempt from variable expressivity; the greatest variability is in dominant conditions, but most disorders show some.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Variable expressivity is not confined to particular inheritance patterns; most genetic disorders show it to some degree.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with colorectal cancer. His family history includes multiple relatives with early-onset colorectal and endometrial cancers, raising concern for Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer). To identify a causative mutation, the clinician wants to simultaneously sequence the coding exons and splice sites of MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, and EPCAM. Which molecular technique is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with locus-specific probes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping of cultured peripheral lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Next-generation sequencing using a targeted gene panel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion of a single PCR product

choices.label: E
choices.text: SNP-microarray genotyping with fixed probes

explanation.summary: An NGS gene panel sequences the exons and exon-intron boundaries of several disease genes at once, making it ideal for multigene conditions like Lynch syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lynch syndrome can be caused by mutations in any of several mismatch-repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2) or EPCAM. An NGS panel sequences all of these genes' exons and splice sites simultaneously, efficiently detecting the responsible variant regardless of which gene harbors it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH detects the presence, absence, or location of large chromosomal sequences, not single-nucleotide mismatch-repair gene mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping visualizes whole chromosomes and cannot detect a small point or frameshift mutation within a single gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Restriction enzyme digestion only detects a specific, already-known mutation that alters a restriction site and cannot screen five genes for unknown variants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A SNP-microarray is a targeted approach limited to variants with probes on the array and would miss rare or novel mutations in these genes.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A newborn screening program wants an inexpensive first-line test to detect the F508del mutation in the CFTR gene, which accounts for roughly 70% of cystic fibrosis cases. Which technique offers a rapid, cost-effective way to screen for this common, well-characterized variant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FISH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping

choices.label: C
choices.text: SNP-microarray

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whole-exome sequencing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole-genome sequencing

explanation.summary: SNP-microarrays are a cost-effective, targeted first step for detecting common, high-frequency mutations such as F508del.
explanation.whyCorrect: SNP-arrays function as genotyping panels that efficiently detect known high-frequency mutations. Because they are less expensive than sequencing, they provide a quick, cost-effective screen for common variants like F508del before moving to more comprehensive analyses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH detects large chromosomal changes, not a small single-gene deletion like F508del.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping evaluates chromosome number and structure and cannot detect a 3-base-pair deletion in CFTR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Whole-exome sequencing is an unbiased, costlier exploratory approach reserved for when a common mutation is not suspected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Whole-genome sequencing is comprehensive but far more expensive and data-intensive than needed to screen for one common mutation.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A patient with a strong clinical suspicion of a hereditary disorder has a SNP-microarray performed, which returns negative. The clinician notes that this platform can only interrogate certain positions. Which statement best explains a key limitation of SNP-microarrays?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They can only be used after a restriction enzyme digestion step

choices.label: B
choices.text: They can only detect balanced chromosomal translocations

choices.label: C
choices.text: They can only detect variants for which probes are present on the array

choices.label: D
choices.text: They read every base of the genome and therefore detect all possible mutations

choices.label: E
choices.text: They require a heat-stable polymerase that denatures above 80 degrees C

explanation.summary: SNP-microarrays are a targeted approach limited to the variants their probes cover, so rare or novel variants are missed.
explanation.whyCorrect: SNP-arrays detect only variants for which probes are designed onto the chip. Rare or novel variants that are not represented on the array will be missed, which is why a negative result does not exclude disease and may prompt more comprehensive sequencing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SNP-arrays do not require a restriction enzyme digestion step; that is a feature of RFLP analysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: SNP-arrays detect SNPs, copy number variations, and loss of heterozygosity; balanced translocations are typically missed and are not their defining detection target.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SNP-arrays are targeted, not comprehensive; they do not read every base of the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A heat-stable polymerase is a feature of PCR, not a limitation of SNP-arrays.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A laboratory is running a PCR that repeatedly heats the reaction to 95 degrees C during the denaturation step of every cycle. The enzyme used remains active despite this repeated high-temperature exposure. This heat stability is attributable to the fact that the enzyme was originally purified from which source?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chicken embryo fibroblasts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Escherichia coli grown at 37 degrees C

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human bone marrow cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis cultures

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thermus aquaticus

explanation.summary: Taq polymerase is heat-stable because it comes from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium that lives in hot environments.
explanation.whyCorrect: Taq polymerase was purified from Thermus aquaticus, a thermophilic bacterium living in hot springs (50 to 80 degrees C). Unlike polymerases from animal cells, it remains active even after exposure to temperatures around 95 degrees C, which was the breakthrough that allowed PCR to be automated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chicken embryo cells are a possible DNA sample source but not the source of a thermostable polymerase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli lives at moderate temperatures and its polymerase is not adapted to survive repeated near-boiling exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Polymerases from human (animal) cells are not heat-stable and would be denatured by the 95 degrees C step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M. tuberculosis is a diagnostic PCR target, not the source of the heat-stable polymerase.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: While optimizing a PCR reaction, a technician notes that the buffer supplies a divalent cation that acts as an essential cofactor for the polymerase, along with potassium ions that promote primer annealing. Which component is the essential polymerase cofactor provided by the buffer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dideoxynucleotide (ddNTP)

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fluorochrome label

choices.label: C
choices.text: A restriction endonuclease

choices.label: D
choices.text: MgCl2 (magnesium)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sodium chloride (NaCl)

explanation.summary: The PCR buffer supplies MgCl2, whose magnesium ion is a required cofactor for the polymerase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The buffer creates the optimal chemical environment for enzyme activity: it regulates pH, supplies MgCl2 as a cofactor for the polymerase, and includes potassium ions to promote primer annealing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ddNTPs are chain-terminating nucleotides used in Sanger sequencing, not a polymerase cofactor supplied in a standard PCR buffer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluorochrome labels tag ddNTPs in sequencing and are not the enzyme's cofactor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A restriction endonuclease is a DNA-cutting enzyme used in RFLP, not a PCR cofactor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Potassium ions (not sodium chloride) promote annealing, and the essential cofactor is magnesium, not NaCl.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A PCR product spanning the beta-globin (HBB) region is digested with the restriction enzyme DdeI, which recognizes the sequence C^TNAG present in the normal (HbA) allele. After gel electrophoresis, one patient's sample shows only two smaller digested fragments and no uncut band. Which genotype does this pattern indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chromosomal translocation involving HBB

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failed PCR amplification

choices.label: C
choices.text: HbAA (homozygous wild type)

choices.label: D
choices.text: HbAS (heterozygous carrier)

choices.label: E
choices.text: HbSS (homozygous sickle cell)

explanation.summary: Complete cutting into two fragments means the DdeI site is intact on both alleles, indicating the normal HbAA genotype.
explanation.whyCorrect: The DdeI recognition site is present in the normal HbA allele. In an HbAA individual, both alleles are cut completely, producing only the two smaller digested fragments with no remaining uncut band.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A translocation would not be assessed by this single-fragment restriction digest, and the pattern shown reflects normal cutting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Failed amplification would show no bands at all, not two clean digested fragments.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HbAS carriers show three bands: one uncut (mutant allele) plus two digested fragments (wild-type allele).
whyWrongByChoice.E: In HbSS the A-to-T mutation destroys the DdeI site on both alleles, so the fragment remains uncut as a single band.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: In the same DdeI-based sickle cell assay, a different patient's digested sample displays three bands on the gel: one full-length undigested band plus two smaller digested fragments. Which genotype is most consistent with this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete absence of the HBB gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contamination with a DNA ladder

choices.label: C
choices.text: HbAA (homozygous wild type)

choices.label: D
choices.text: HbAS (heterozygous carrier)

choices.label: E
choices.text: HbSS (homozygous sickle cell)

explanation.summary: A mix of one uncut band and two cut fragments reflects one mutant (uncut) allele and one wild-type (cut) allele, the heterozygous carrier state.
explanation.whyCorrect: A heterozygous HbAS genotype has one allele that retains the DdeI site (cut into two fragments) and one allele carrying the mutation that abolishes the site (remains uncut). The gel therefore shows three bands: the undigested fragment plus the two digested fragments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absence of HBB is not what this assay demonstrates; the three-band pattern reflects two different alleles, not a missing gene.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A DNA ladder is loaded in a separate reference well and would not create this specific three-band digestion pattern in the sample lane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HbAA is fully cut and shows only the two digested fragments, with no uncut band.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HbSS cannot be cut and shows only a single uncut band.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: During Sanger sequencing, a small amount of fluorochrome-labeled dideoxynucleotide (ddNTP) is included with the normal dNTPs. When a ddNTP is incorporated, DNA synthesis stops at that position, generating fragments of many different lengths. What chemical property of ddNTPs causes this chain termination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are heat-stable and resist denaturation

choices.label: B
choices.text: They bind magnesium and deplete the cofactor supply

choices.label: C
choices.text: They carry an extra phosphate group that repels the polymerase

choices.label: D
choices.text: They cut the DNA strand at a specific recognition site

choices.label: E
choices.text: They lack a 3-prime hydroxyl group

explanation.summary: ddNTPs terminate the chain because they lack the 3-prime hydroxyl needed to bond to the next nucleotide.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike dNTPs, dideoxynucleotides lack a 3-prime hydroxyl group. Without it, no phosphodiester bond can form with the following nucleotide, so synthesis terminates at that position. Because ddNTP concentration is much lower than dNTP concentration, termination occurs randomly, producing a ladder of fragments each ending in a labeled base.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heat stability is a property of Taq polymerase, unrelated to why ddNTPs stop synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ddNTPs do not terminate the chain by sequestering magnesium; they lack the 3-prime hydroxyl group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chain termination is due to the missing 3-prime hydroxyl, not an extra phosphate repelling the polymerase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cutting DNA at recognition sites is the function of restriction enzymes, not ddNTPs.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A researcher wants a method that can detect a previously undescribed (novel) point mutation in a single candidate gene of interest. Which technique is capable of identifying such a novel point mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array CGH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sanger sequencing

choices.label: D
choices.text: SNP-array

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standard karyotyping

explanation.summary: Sequencing reads DNA base by base, so it can identify novel point mutations, unlike targeted or chromosome-level methods.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sanger sequencing reads the DNA sequence base by base and can detect novel point mutations and small indels, because it does not require prior knowledge of the specific variant. SNP-arrays and restriction digestion, by contrast, are targeted approaches limited to already-known variants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Array CGH is designed to detect copy number variations, not point mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Restriction enzyme digestion only detects known mutations that alter a restriction site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A SNP-array only detects variants with probes on the chip, so it cannot reveal a truly novel point mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Karyotyping visualizes chromosomes and cannot resolve a single-base change.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: After a restriction digestion, a laboratory loads the DNA into an agarose gel and applies an electric current to separate the fragments. Given the physical principle of gel electrophoresis, how will fragments of different sizes migrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All fragments migrate at the same rate regardless of size

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fragments migrate toward the negative electrode

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larger fragments migrate faster because they carry more charge

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only fragments labeled with a fluorochrome will move through the gel

choices.label: E
choices.text: Smaller fragments migrate faster and travel farther than larger fragments

explanation.summary: In gel electrophoresis, DNA separates by size, with smaller fragments passing through the pores more easily and migrating faster.
explanation.whyCorrect: Electrophoresis relies on charged molecules migrating in an electric field through a gel matrix. Small DNA fragments pass through the pores more easily and migrate faster, while larger fragments move more slowly, allowing separation by size.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fragments do not migrate at the same rate; separation by size is the entire point of the technique.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA is negatively charged and migrates toward the positive electrode, not the negative one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Larger fragments migrate more slowly, not faster; size, not extra charge, dominates their slower movement through the pores.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fluorochrome labels are used in sequencing detection; unlabeled DNA still migrates and can be visualized in a standard gel.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A pathologist suspects a somatic mutation present in only a small proportion of cells within a tumor biopsy (low-level mosaicism). Which feature of next-generation sequencing best enables detection of such a rare, low-frequency variant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deep coverage, in which each base is read many times

choices.label: B
choices.text: Digestion of the sample with DdeI before loading

choices.label: C
choices.text: Limiting the analysis to whole chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reading only a single DNA fragment at a time

choices.label: E
choices.text: Use of a single primer to define the starting point

explanation.summary: Deep coverage reads each base many times, increasing sensitivity for rare low-frequency variants such as those in mosaicism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deep coverage, where each base is read many times, enhances the ability to detect rare mutations such as those seen in mosaicism. Somatic mutations present in only a small fraction of cells could be missed if coverage is insufficient, so high (or ultra-deep) coverage is key.

whyWrongByChoice.B: DdeI digestion is part of RFLP analysis and is not how NGS achieves sensitivity for rare variants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Limiting analysis to whole chromosomes describes karyotyping and would miss a single-base somatic variant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NGS reads millions of fragments simultaneously; reading only one fragment at a time describes the older, less sensitive approach.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single primer defining the start point is a feature of Sanger sequencing setup, not the reason NGS detects low-level mosaicism.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: An electropherogram from a Sanger sequencing run shows, at a single position, two overlapping peaks of different colors superimposed on one another, while the rest of the trace shows clean single peaks. What does this overlapping (double) peak most likely indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A heterozygous point variant

choices.label: B
choices.text: A large chromosomal deletion spanning the gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complete failure of the sequencing reaction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Contamination of the buffer with magnesium

choices.label: E
choices.text: Successful digestion by a restriction enzyme

explanation.summary: Overlapping peaks at one position on a Sanger trace reflect two different bases there, the signature of a heterozygous variant.
explanation.whyCorrect: On an electropherogram, clear non-overlapping peaks give reliable base calls, whereas overlapping peaks indicate a mixed signal. Two different bases occupying the same position, seen as superimposed peaks, is characteristic of a heterozygous point variant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A large chromosomal deletion is not resolved by base-level electropherogram peaks and would not appear as a single overlapping position.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A failed reaction produces a flat or noisy trace with no readable peaks, not a clean trace with one doubled position.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Magnesium is a normal buffer cofactor and does not create overlapping base-call peaks at a single position.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restriction digestion is analyzed by gel banding patterns, not by electropherogram peaks.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia achieves remission and later relapses. SNP-microarray analysis is performed on leukemic cells from both the initial diagnosis and the relapse. At relapse, the total gene dosage line across a region of chromosome 19p13.3-p12 containing JAK3 remains at two copies, but the allele-specific dosage lines diverge so that one parental allele accounts for both copies. This finding was absent in the diagnostic sample. Which of the following best describes the new abnormality detected at relapse?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Balanced translocation involving 19p13.3-p12

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four-copy amplification of JAK3

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterozygous deletion of 19p13.3-p12

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trisomy of chromosome 19

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniparental disomy of 19p13.3-p12

explanation.summary: SNP-arrays detect loss of heterozygosity; when total dosage stays at two copies but one allele accounts for both, the region shows uniparental disomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond SNP genotyping, SNP-arrays identify copy number variations and loss of heterozygosity, which are frequently observed in cancer cells. The blue line reports total gene dosage while the green and red lines report allele-specific dosage. A region where total dosage is unchanged but the allele-specific lines separate indicates uniparental disomy, which in the leukemia example was detected at the 19p13.3-p12 locus only at relapse, showing how arrays can compare initial diagnosis with relapse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A balanced translocation does not change gene dosage or allelic ratio and is typically missed by arrays.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amplification would raise total dosage to four copies, whereas the blue line stayed at two.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A heterozygous deletion would drop the total dosage line to one copy in the region; here it remains at two.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trisomy would raise the total gene dosage line to three copies across the whole chromosome, not leave it at two.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is about to begin a medication known to have highly variable efficacy and a significant rate of adverse drug reactions among patients. Her physician orders a genetic test to personalize the choice and dose of the drug before the first prescription. Which of the following tests is designed for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping of peripheral lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pharmacogenomic SNP-array

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion with DdeI

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole-genome sequencing with deep coverage

explanation.summary: Pharmacogenomic SNP-arrays detect SNPs associated with variable drug responses, allowing treatment to be personalized.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pharmacogenomic SNP arrays are used to detect SNPs associated with variable responses to certain medications. This information is used to personalize treatment, predict drug efficacy, and potentially minimize adverse drug reactions, exactly the goal in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH detects the presence, absence, or location of large chromosomal sequences, not drug-response SNPs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping visualizes whole chromosomes and cannot genotype single-nucleotide drug-response variants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DdeI digestion is a single-site genotyping tool for the sickle cell mutation, not a panel of drug-response SNPs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Whole-genome sequencing is an unbiased, expensive exploratory approach rather than the targeted panel designed to genotype known drug-response SNPs.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A research consortium enrolls 50,000 participants to identify genetic variants across the genome that are associated with an increased risk of type II diabetes, a complex multifactorial disease. Which of the following techniques is most widely used for this type of genome-wide association study?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sanger sequencing of a single candidate gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: SNP-microarray genotyping

explanation.summary: SNP-arrays are the workhorse of genome-wide association studies and can detect susceptibility variants for complex diseases.
explanation.whyCorrect: SNP-arrays evaluate a large number of variants in a single test and are widely used in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to associate genetic variation with diseases or traits. They can detect susceptibility variants for complex diseases such as Alzheimer's or type II diabetes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH detects specific large chromosomal sequences and cannot survey single-nucleotide variation genome-wide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping assesses chromosome number and structure, not single-nucleotide susceptibility variants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RFLP analysis interrogates a single known restriction site, not variation across the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sanger sequencing reads one selected region and is not a genome-wide tool for tens of thousands of participants.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a strong family history of a hereditary disorder has SNP-microarray testing at one laboratory, which reports no pathogenic variant. Because clinical suspicion remains high, a second laboratory runs a SNP-microarray on the same DNA sample and identifies a well-characterized pathogenic variant. Which of the following best explains the discordant results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A new somatic mutation arose between the two tests

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first array omitted the MgCl2 polymerase cofactor

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first sample was degraded by heat at 95 degrees C

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two array platforms differ in probe content

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variant is a balanced translocation missed by arrays

explanation.summary: Probe content varies between SNP-array platforms, so not all arrays test for the same variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: A limitation of SNP-arrays is that probe content varies between platforms, meaning not all arrays test for the same variants, although there is usually overlap for well-characterized mutations. An array can only detect variants for which probes are present, so a variant absent from the first platform's probe set but present on the second platform's would be missed by one and found by the other.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The same DNA sample was tested twice, so a new mutation could not have appeared between the tests.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MgCl2 is a cofactor supplied in the PCR buffer for the polymerase; it is not the explanation for a platform-dependent array result.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeated exposure to 95 degrees C is the normal denaturation step of PCR and does not selectively hide one variant from an array.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A balanced translocation is typically missed by arrays and would not have been detected by the second array either; the finding was a well-characterized variant.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and elevated sodium and chloride concentrations in sweat. SNP-microarray testing shows he is homozygous for the F508del mutation in CFTR. Which of the following additional findings is expected in this patient later in life?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune attack on the myelin sheath of central neurons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased sweat sodium and chloride concentration with age

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infertility from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thin, watery secretions replacing the thick airway mucus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaso-occlusive pain crises with avascular necrosis of the femoral head

explanation.summary: Almost all males with cystic fibrosis are infertile because of congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cystic fibrosis (mucoviscidosis) is characterized by thick mucus leading to the triad of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and elevated sodium and chloride in sweat. Almost all males with CF are infertile due to congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens. Pulmonary phenotype and survival vary greatly even among F508del homozygotes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Attack on the myelin sheath describes multiple sclerosis, a separate multifactorial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elevated sweat sodium and chloride is a defining feature of CF and is not expected to normalize.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CF is characterized by thick mucus; secretions do not become thin and watery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaso-occlusive crises and avascular necrosis are complications of sickle cell disease, not cystic fibrosis.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 6-month-old girl with failure to thrive, steatorrhea, and a positive sweat chloride test undergoes SNP-microarray screening for CFTR mutations, which detects neither F508del nor any other variant represented on the array. The clinical diagnosis of cystic fibrosis remains strongly suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate next test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization for CFTR

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotyping of peripheral blood lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat the SNP-microarray on a new blood sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion of a CFTR PCR product

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sanger sequencing of the entire CFTR gene

explanation.summary: SNP-arrays miss up to 30% of CF-causing variants, so a negative array in a clinically suspected case is followed by Sanger sequencing of the whole CFTR gene.
explanation.whyCorrect: Approximately 70% of cystic fibrosis cases are caused by F508del, which SNP-arrays detect well, but arrays will miss up to 30% of disease-causing variants because they can only detect variants with probes on the chip. Sanger sequencing enables comprehensive analysis of the entire CFTR gene to identify additional pathogenic mutations, including novel point mutations and small indels.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH detects the presence, absence, or location of large sequences and cannot read single-nucleotide changes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotyping resolves chromosome-level abnormalities and cannot detect point mutations or small indels in CFTR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeating the same targeted array cannot find a variant that has no probe on the chip.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Restriction digestion only genotypes known mutations that alter a restriction site; it cannot search a gene for unknown variants.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with a chronic cough, night sweats, and weight loss has a sputum sample sent for PCR-based detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA. Compared with traditional culture-based methods, which of the following is the principal advantage of this PCR-based approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It amplifies the organism's entire genome

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly detects epigenetic changes in the organism

choices.label: C
choices.text: It does not require a thermal cycler

choices.label: D
choices.text: It provides a faster diagnosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: It works without organism-specific primers

explanation.summary: PCR detects M. tuberculosis DNA directly from patient samples, giving a faster diagnosis than culture.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA can be directly detected from patient samples using PCR, offering a faster diagnosis compared to traditional culture-based methods. PCR can also identify drug resistance by detecting mutations in genes associated with resistance to rifampicin and fluoroquinolones, helping to select treatment and monitor response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PCR amplifies a specific segment of DNA defined by the primers, not an entire genome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epigenetic changes are not detected directly by DNA amplification or sequencing methods.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PCR depends on a thermal cycler to drive the denaturation, annealing, and elongation temperature steps.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PCR requires a forward and reverse primer designed to flank the specific target sequence.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A technician sets up a PCR to amplify a 450-bp region of a gene. The reaction contains template DNA, Taq polymerase, buffer with MgCl2, dNTPs, and a single 20-nucleotide oligonucleotide complementary to the 5' end of the target. After 35 cycles, gel electrophoresis shows no band at 450 bp. Which of the following best explains the failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A second primer flanking the opposite end of the amplified region is missing

choices.label: B
choices.text: The oligonucleotide is too short and should be about 200 nucleotides

choices.label: C
choices.text: The oligonucleotide must be labeled with a fluorochrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reaction requires dideoxynucleotides in addition to dNTPs

choices.label: E
choices.text: The template must be digested with a restriction enzyme first

explanation.summary: PCR requires two primers, a forward and a reverse primer, that flank and define the fragment to be amplified.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primers are short oligonucleotides of about 20 nucleotides designed to flank the region of interest. Two primers are required per PCR: a forward primer and a reverse primer. They bind the DNA strands and define the fragment, and PCR amplifies from the first nucleotide of the forward primer to the last nucleotide of the reverse primer. With only one primer, no defined fragment can be exponentially amplified.

whyWrongByChoice.B: About 20 nucleotides is the normal primer length; length is not the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fluorochrome labels are used on ddNTPs in Sanger sequencing; PCR primers do not need a label.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ddNTPs are chain terminators used in sequencing and would stop synthesis rather than enable amplification.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restriction digestion is a genotyping step performed after PCR, not a prerequisite for amplification.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A researcher uses an online genome database to design primers for a region of interest. The 5'-to-3' strand reads 5'-...CATGCA-3' at the downstream end of the target region. Which of the following sequences should be synthesized as the reverse primer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 5'-ACGTAC-3'

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5'-CATGCA-3'

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5'-GCATGC-3'

choices.label: D
choices.text: 5'-GTACGT-3'

choices.label: E
choices.text: 5'-TGCATG-3'

explanation.summary: The reverse primer is the reverse complement of the 5' strand's downstream end.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two primers are selected, one at the 5' (upstream) end of the target and one downstream at the 3' end. The reverse primer has the reverse-complement sequence of the 5' strand end of the sequence. Reversing CATGCA gives ACGTAC, and complementing each base gives TGCATG, which is the reverse primer written 5' to 3'.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is the reversed sequence without complementing the bases, so it would not base-pair with the template.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is identical to the 5' strand; a primer with the same sequence as the 5' strand is the forward primer, and it must sit upstream, not at the downstream end.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This sequence is neither the complement nor the reverse of the target end.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This is the base-by-base complement written without reversing, so it is not antiparallel to the template and would not anneal correctly.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A PCR designed to amplify a single 450-bp fragment is run on an agarose gel alongside a DNA ladder. Instead of one band, the lane shows several bands of different sizes, including the expected 450-bp product. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Taq polymerase was denatured during the 95 degrees C denaturation step

choices.label: B
choices.text: The primer set amplified off-target regions elsewhere in the genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reaction buffer lacked the MgCl2 cofactor entirely

choices.label: D
choices.text: The template carried a homozygous deletion inside the amplicon

choices.label: E
choices.text: Too few cycles were run to reach exponential amplification

explanation.summary: Poor primer specificity leads to off-target amplification, producing extra bands of unexpected sizes.
explanation.whyCorrect: It is crucial to check primer specificity to ensure that the primer set amplifies only the intended region and avoids off-target amplification elsewhere in the genome. Non-specific primers bind additional sites, generating multiple products of different sizes that appear as extra bands on the gel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Taq polymerase is heat-stable and is not denatured at 95 degrees C; loss of enzyme would give no band at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Without the MgCl2 cofactor the polymerase would not function, giving no product rather than extra products.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A homozygous deletion would produce a single smaller band, not multiple bands together with the expected product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Too few cycles would give a faint or absent band, not additional bands of other sizes.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A thermal cycler is programmed with three temperature steps per cycle: 95 degrees C for 20-30 seconds, 50-65 degrees C for 20-40 seconds, and 72 degrees C for a duration based on target length. During which of these steps do the forward and reverse primers bind to the single-stranded template?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 4 degrees C hold after the final cycle

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 37 degrees C incubation before cycling

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 50-65 degrees C step

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 72 degrees C step

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 95 degrees C step

explanation.summary: Primers anneal to the denatured template during the 50-65 degrees C annealing step.
explanation.whyCorrect: One PCR cycle is divided into steps characterized by temperature: denaturation at 95 degrees C (20-30 seconds) separates the strands, annealing at 50-65 degrees C (20-40 seconds) lets the forward and reverse primers bind the single-stranded DNA, and elongation at 72 degrees C lets Taq polymerase extend from the primers for a time based on target length.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A cold hold after cycling simply preserves the product; no annealing step occurs there.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 37 degrees C incubation is not one of the PCR cycle steps.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 72 degrees C is the elongation step, during which Taq polymerase extends primers that have already annealed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 95 degrees C is the denaturation step that separates the double strand; primers cannot bind at this temperature.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A laboratory routinely amplifies a 450-bp fragment. A new assay requires amplification of a 3,000-bp region from the same template. Which of the following protocol parameters should be adjusted to accommodate the longer target?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a third primer to the reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lengthen the 72 degrees C elongation step

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower the annealing temperature to 37 degrees C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raise the denaturation temperature above 95 degrees C

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replace Taq with a polymerase from animal cells

explanation.summary: The duration of the 72 degrees C elongation step is set according to the length of the target.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the PCR cycle, denaturation (95 degrees C) and annealing (50-65 degrees C) have fixed short durations, whereas the elongation step at 72 degrees C has timing based on target length.
