A longer fragment requires more time for Taq polymerase to synthesize the complete strand, so the elongation step must be lengthened.

whyWrongByChoice.A: PCR uses exactly two primers, forward and reverse; a third primer would not extend the product.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Annealing occurs at 50-65 degrees C; dropping to 37 degrees C would reduce specificity and does not address product length.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 95 degrees C already denatures the template; raising it further does not help synthesize a longer product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polymerases from animal cells are not heat-stable and would be destroyed at 95 degrees C.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A PCR is started with a single copy of the target region and run for 10 cycles under ideal conditions, with each cycle doubling the amount of target. Approximately how many copies of the target are present at the end of the reaction?

explanation.summary: PCR amplification is exponential; the final amplification ratio is 2 to the power n, where n is the number of cycles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each PCR cycle doubles the amount of targeted regions, which is why amplification is exponential. The final amplification ratio can be calculated as 2^n, with n being the number of cycles, so 10 cycles yield 2^10 = 1,024 copies from a single starting copy. A typical PCR runs 20 to 40 cycles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ten would be the result of linear, one-copy-per-cycle amplification, but PCR doubles the product each cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Twenty corresponds to 2 times 10 rather than 2 raised to the 10th power.
whyWrongByChoice.C: One hundred is 10 squared and does not reflect the doubling per cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ten thousand is 10^4, not 2^10; the doubling base is 2, not 10.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A family is found to carry a newly described point mutation in the HBB gene. A laboratory proposes genotyping relatives by PCR followed by restriction enzyme digestion, but upon review, the mutation neither creates nor abolishes any restriction enzyme recognition sequence. Why is restriction digestion unsuitable for this family?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Digestion cannot distinguish heterozygotes from either homozygous genotype

choices.label: B
choices.text: Digestion requires fluorochrome-labeled ddNTPs for detection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restriction enzymes cut only single-stranded DNA templates

choices.label: D
choices.text: The HBB gene is too large to amplify reliably by PCR

choices.label: E
choices.text: The method only detects known mutations that alter a restriction site

explanation.summary: RFLP genotyping only works for mutations that are already known and that alter a restriction enzyme recognition site.
explanation.whyCorrect: Restriction enzyme digestion genotypes well-characterized diseases by exploiting mutations that alter a restriction enzyme recognition site, as with the DdeI site lost in sickle cell disease. This genotyping method is only applicable to mutations that are already known and that alter a restriction site; a mutation that leaves every recognition sequence intact produces the same digestion pattern as wild type and cannot be detected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Digestion patterns do distinguish genotypes: homozygous wild type is fully cut, homozygous mutant is uncut, and heterozygotes show both.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluorochrome-labeled ddNTPs are reagents of Sanger sequencing, not restriction digestion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Restriction enzymes are bacterial endonucleases that cut double-stranded DNA at specific sequences.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PCR readily amplifies the relevant HBB region, which is how the DdeI sickle cell assay is performed.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with anemia and recurrent episodes of severe limb pain is found to have a point mutation in the HBB gene. Which of the following best describes the molecular change responsible for sickle cell disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 3-base-pair deletion removing one phenylalanine

choices.label: B
choices.text: A balanced translocation disrupting the HBB locus

choices.label: C
choices.text: A trinucleotide repeat expansion within the gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: An A-to-T substitution replacing glutamate with valine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniparental disomy of the chromosome carrying HBB

explanation.summary: Sickle cell disease results from the c.20A>T point mutation in HBB, which substitutes valine for glutamate (p.Glu7Val).
explanation.whyCorrect: Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive disease due to a point mutation (c.20A>T, p.Glu7Val) in the HBB gene coding for beta globin, in which adenine is replaced by thymine. The abnormal hemoglobin makes red blood cells rigid, sticky, and sickle-shaped, causing anemia, vaso-occlusive pain crises, organ damage from low oxygen and avascular necrosis, and stroke.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deletion of a phenylalanine describes F508del in CFTR, the common cystic fibrosis mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The disease is caused by a point mutation, not a chromosomal rearrangement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sickle cell disease is a single-base substitution, not a repeat expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uniparental disomy is a copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity detected by SNP-arrays in cancer cells, not the cause of sickle cell disease.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: Before sending a PCR product for Sanger sequencing, a technician loads an aliquot of the undigested product on an agarose gel next to a DNA ladder with bands from 100 bp to 600 bp. The sample lane shows a single band at approximately 450 bp, the expected size. Which of the following conclusions is justified by this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amplification produced a single product of the predicted size

choices.label: B
choices.text: The DdeI recognition site is intact in both alleles

choices.label: C
choices.text: The exact nucleotide sequence of the product is known

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patient is heterozygous for a point mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The product contains a repeat expansion

explanation.summary: A single band at the expected size confirms successful amplification but reveals nothing about the DNA sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: The DNA ladder provides known fragment sizes for comparison, and a single band at about 450 bp indicates successful amplification of the target region. Electrophoresis is a fast, inexpensive preliminary check used before sequencing the PCR product; it confirms whether PCR amplified the target but does not reveal the exact DNA sequence.

whyWrongByChoice.B: No restriction digestion was performed, so nothing can be concluded about the DdeI site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Electrophoresis does not reveal the exact DNA sequence; that requires sequencing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single-base heterozygous change does not alter fragment size and cannot be seen on an agarose gel of undigested product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A band at the expected size argues against, not for, a size-altering repeat expansion.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A PCR amplifying a 600-bp region is run on three individuals, and the undigested products are loaded next to a DNA ladder. The wild-type lane shows a single band at about 600 bp, a second lane shows a single band at about 300 bp, and a third lane shows two bands at about 600 bp and 300 bp. No restriction enzyme was used. Which of the following best explains the single 300-bp band in the second lane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A heterozygous point mutation within the amplicon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deletion of about 300 bp at the homozygous state

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of PCR amplification in that sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insertion of about 300 bp at the homozygous state

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of a restriction enzyme cutting site at the homozygous state

explanation.summary: A single band smaller than wild type in an undigested PCR product indicates a homozygous deletion inside the amplified frame.
explanation.whyCorrect: If a deletion occurs inside the amplification frame defined by the primers, the PCR amplifies a smaller fragment. A single band at about 300 bp instead of 600 bp means both alleles carry a deletion of about 300 bp (homozygous state). The third lane, with both the 600-bp and 300-bp bands, represents the heterozygous carrier of the same deletion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A point mutation does not change fragment size and would look identical to wild type on an agarose gel.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failed amplification would show no band at all, not a discrete 300-bp band.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An insertion would make the homozygous band migrate higher (larger) than the wild-type band, not lower.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No restriction enzyme was used, so cutting sites are irrelevant; with a lost cutting site the wild-type band would be the one cut, appearing lower than the mutant.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with colorectal cancer and a family history of early-onset colorectal and endometrial cancers undergoes NGS with a targeted panel covering the exons and exon-intron boundaries of MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, and EPCAM. No pathogenic variant is identified, but Lynch syndrome is still strongly suspected. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Karyotyping of peripheral blood lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Repeat the same five-gene panel on a new sample

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restriction enzyme digestion of an MLH1 PCR product

choices.label: D
choices.text: SNP-microarray genotyping for common variants

choices.label: E
choices.text: Untargeted whole-exome sequencing

explanation.summary: When a targeted NGS panel is negative, an untargeted NGS approach such as exome or genome sequencing is used to find the causative mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: An NGS panel of mismatch repair genes sequences the exons and exon-intron boundaries of the five genes where the mutation is likely present. If no mutation is detected in this first screening, an untargeted NGS approach such as exome or genome sequencing can be performed to identify the causing mutation, because an unbiased approach identifies variants without a priori assumptions about the gene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Karyotyping detects chromosome-level abnormalities and cannot resolve point mutations or small indels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Repeating the same targeted panel re-examines the same five genes and cannot reveal a mutation elsewhere.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Restriction digestion only genotypes a single known mutation that alters a restriction site.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A SNP-array is another targeted approach limited to variants with probes on the chip and is less comprehensive than the panel already run.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A student sets up a Sanger sequencing reaction containing the PCR product, DNA polymerase, dNTPs, and fluorochrome-labeled ddNTPs, but forgets to add the sequencing primer. No labeled fragments are produced. Which of the following best explains why the primer is essential?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DNA polymerase needs a double-stranded region to initiate synthesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: The primer carries the fluorescent label detected by the laser

choices.label: C
choices.text: The primer separates the two template strands at 95 degrees C

choices.label: D
choices.text: The primer supplies the magnesium cofactor for the polymerase

choices.label: E
choices.text: The primer terminates chain elongation at each base position

explanation.summary: Sanger sequencing needs one primer because DNA polymerase can only initiate synthesis from a double-stranded region.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sequencing reaction requires the DNA sample (PCR product), a DNA polymerase, dNTPs, fluorochrome-labeled ddNTPs, and one primer to define the starting point of synthesis. DNA polymerase requires a double-stranded region to initiate synthesis, which is provided by the primer binding to the template. Unlike PCR, which needs two primers, Sanger sequencing uses a single primer.

whyWrongByChoice.B: In Sanger sequencing the fluorochrome label is on the ddNTPs, so each terminated fragment carries a label at its last base.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Strand separation is achieved by heat during denaturation, not by the primer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Magnesium is supplied by the buffer, not by the primer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chain termination is caused by ddNTPs lacking a 3' hydroxyl group, not by the primer.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A geneticist is asked to classify diagnostic methods as either targeted (requiring prior knowledge of the variant or locus) or unbiased (identifying variants without a priori). Which of the following is an unbiased approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization

choices.label: B
choices.text: PCR followed by restriction enzyme digestion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sanger sequencing of a single gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: SNP-microarray

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole-genome sequencing

explanation.summary: Genome and exome sequencing are unbiased approaches; SNP-arrays, FISH, restriction digestion, and single-gene Sanger sequencing are targeted.
explanation.whyCorrect: NGS-based whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing are unbiased approaches that identify variants without a priori assumptions. When a specific disorder is highly suspected, a targeted approach is used to confirm the exact mutation; when the phenotype is not well determined and no candidate gene or locus is in mind, an unbiased approach is used.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FISH probes a predetermined chromosomal sequence and is an approach with a priori, like the SNP-array.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Restriction digestion genotypes a single known mutation that alters a restriction site, a targeted method.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sanger sequencing reads only a selected region defined by the primer, so it is targeted to a chosen gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SNP-arrays are genotyping panels that can only detect variants with probes on the array; this is a targeted approach.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: An electropherogram from a Sanger sequencing run displays a series of clean, non-overlapping colored peaks. The technician begins reading base calls from the leftmost peak. Which of the following does the leftmost peak represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A heterozygous position in the sample

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 3' end of the sequenced DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 5' end of the sequenced DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: The binding site of the reverse PCR primer

choices.label: E
choices.text: The longest chain-terminated fragment

explanation.summary: An electropherogram is read left to right from the 5' end to the 3' end, with each peak representing one nucleotide.
explanation.whyCorrect: The electropherogram plots the results of electrophoresis, which separates the chain-terminated fragments by size and fluorescent label. The bases are read in order from left to right, corresponding to the 5' end of the sequenced DNA to the 3' end, and each peak represents a single nucleotide. Clear, non-overlapping peaks give reliable base calls.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A heterozygous position appears as two overlapping peaks at one position, not as the first peak of a clean trace.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 3' end is at the right side of the trace, read last.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sanger sequencing uses one primer to define the start point; the peaks represent bases synthesized beyond it, not a reverse PCR primer site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The leftmost peak comes from the shortest fragment, which migrates fastest and is detected first; the longest fragments appear at the right.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A Sanger electropherogram of a PCR-amplified exon shows clean single peaks for the first 120 bases. Beginning at base 121 and continuing to the end of the read, every position shows two superimposed sequences that are shifted relative to each other. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A heterozygous insertion or deletion starting at base 121

choices.label: B
choices.text: A heterozygous single-base substitution at base 121

choices.label: C
choices.text: A homozygous single-base substitution at base 121

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complete failure of the sequencing reaction in both directions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Successful restriction digestion of the amplicon before loading

explanation.summary: Overlapping sequences that begin at a specific point and persist downstream indicate an indel that shifts the alignment of one allele.
explanation.whyCorrect: On an electropherogram, overlapping sequences from a specific point onward typically indicate an insertion or deletion (indel), where the sequence alignment shows a shift starting at a particular position due to added or missing bases. Because one allele is shifted relative to the other, every position after the indel shows two superimposed sequences.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A heterozygous point mutation produces a single position with two overlapping peaks, after which the trace returns to clean single peaks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A homozygous substitution gives one clean peak of a different base at that position, with no overlap anywhere.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A failed reaction gives no readable peaks at all rather than 120 clean bases followed by a shifted overlap.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Restriction digestion is read as gel banding patterns and does not produce superimposed electropherogram sequences.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: Whole-exome sequencing of a child with an undiagnosed disorder identifies approximately 35,000 variants compared with the reference human genome. The bioinformatics team begins a multi-step filtering process to narrow this list to a few clinically relevant candidates. Which of the following is the initial filtering step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Exclude all missense variants

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exclude common variants found in population databases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exclude variants in genes associated with the phenotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retain only variants conserved across species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retain only variants inherited from the father

explanation.summary: Variant filtering starts by excluding common variants in population databases to focus on rare or novel ones.
explanation.whyCorrect: Typical exome sequencing identifies between 20,000 and 50,000 variants compared to a reference genome. Initially, common variants found in population databases are excluded to focus on rare or novel ones. Next, variants are filtered by predicted impact (missense, nonsense, frameshift), by location in genes known to be associated with the phenotype, and by additional criteria such as inheritance pattern and conservation across species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Missense variants are retained and assessed for predicted impact; they are among the changes of interest, not excluded wholesale.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Variants in genes associated with the phenotype are prioritized, not excluded.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conservation across species is an additional later filter, not the first step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inheritance pattern (dominant, recessive) is applied as a later filter, and restricting to paternal variants is not a described step.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man has a progressive neurologic disorder that has appeared at an earlier age in each successive generation of his family. Whole-exome sequencing by NGS is reported as negative. Which of the following best explains the negative result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deep coverage masks variants present in all cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exome sequencing does not cover protein-coding exons

choices.label: C
choices.text: NGS cannot detect single-nucleotide variants

choices.label: D
choices.text: NGS cannot detect small insertions or deletions

choices.label: E
choices.text: NGS has poor capability for detecting repeat expansions

explanation.summary: NGS detects SNVs and small indels well but performs poorly for repeat expansions, and does not directly detect epigenetic changes.
explanation.whyCorrect: NGS detection capability varies by mutation type: excellent for SNVs, good for small indels, variable for CNVs depending on size, moderate for structural variants, poor for repeat expansions, not direct for epigenetic changes, often missed for balanced translocations, and requiring high depth for low-level mosaicism. A repeat expansion disorder can therefore be missed by exome sequencing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deep coverage improves detection of rare variants; it does not hide variants present in every cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Exome sequencing specifically targets the exons and exon-intron boundaries.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NGS detection of single-nucleotide variants is rated excellent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NGS detection of small indels is rated good.

questions.topicName: Molecular Biology Techniques (2 of 3): DNA Analysis

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought in for evaluation of possible autism. His parents report delayed development and that he remains nonverbal, and he becomes overwhelmed and anxious with loud classroom noise. On examination he has large ears, a long narrow face, and a prominent forehead. Which of the following genes is most likely affected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DMPK

choices.label: B
choices.text: FMR1

choices.label: C
choices.text: FXN

choices.label: D
choices.text: HTT

choices.label: E
choices.text: TBP

explanation.summary: Developmental delay with a long face, large ears, and sensory hypersensitivity in a young boy points to Fragile X syndrome, caused by FMR1.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fragile X syndrome results from a CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. Classic features include intellectual disability, autism-like behavior and sensory hypersensitivity, and a long face with large ears and a prominent jaw, matching this child.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DMPK (CTG) causes myotonic dystrophy, presenting in the 20s-30s with myotonia and distal weakness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FXN (GAA) causes Friedreich ataxia, presenting at ages 5-15 with ataxic gait and areflexia, not this facial phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HTT (CAG) causes Huntington disease, an adult-onset chorea and dementia, not childhood developmental delay with these facies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TBP (CAG/CAA) is one of the spinocerebellar ataxia loci and causes autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia, not this childhood syndrome.

questions.stem: Molecular testing on the boy in the previous vignette reveals more than 200 CGG repeats in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1. Which of the following best explains how this expansion produces disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A frameshift mutation prematurely terminates translation of every transcript

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aberrant splicing produces a truncated, nonfunctional protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypermethylation of the promoter silences transcription and eliminates the FMRP protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: The expanded mRNA forms nuclear foci that trap RNA-binding proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: The expansion adds a long polyglutamine tract that makes the protein aggregate

explanation.summary: In Fragile X, a full CGG expansion (>200) triggers promoter hypermethylation, silencing FMR1 and abolishing FMRP.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the CGG repeat exceeds ~200, the FMR1 promoter becomes hypermethylated, transcription is silenced, and the FMRP protein—essential for synaptic function and neural development—is not produced. This loss-of-function mechanism drives the phenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The CGG expansion silences transcription by methylation rather than causing a frameshift in the coding sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aberrant splicing with reduced protein describes Friedreich ataxia (GAA in an intron), not the CGG expansion of Fragile X.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxic RNA nuclear foci that sequester splicing proteins are the mechanism of myotonic dystrophy type 1 (CTG).
whyWrongByChoice.E: A polyglutamine tract is the mechanism in Huntington disease (CAG in the coding region), not Fragile X.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man reports progressive muscle weakness and difficulty releasing his grip after shaking hands. He also notes fatigue, occasional trouble swallowing, and daytime sleepiness. On examination he has a thin elongated face with frontal balding and ptosis, and percussion of the thenar eminence produces a delayed relaxation response. His mother had similar symptoms and died of a cardiac arrhythmia in her 40s. Which gene is most likely mutated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: DMPK

choices.label: B
choices.text: FMR1

choices.label: C
choices.text: FshMD1A

choices.label: D
choices.text: FXN

choices.label: E
choices.text: HTT

explanation.summary: Grip and percussion myotonia with distal weakness, frontal balding, ptosis, and cardiac arrhythmia indicate myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DMPK).
explanation.whyCorrect: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (Steinert disease) is an autosomal dominant CTG expansion in the 3' UTR of DMPK. Hallmarks are myotonia (delayed muscle relaxation), distal weakness, a thin face with ptosis and frontal balding, cataracts, daytime sleepiness, and cardiac conduction defects, as seen here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FMR1 causes Fragile X syndrome, a childhood developmental disorder, not adult-onset myotonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is a distractor gene label; the presentation of myotonia points specifically to DMPK.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FXN causes Friedreich ataxia with childhood ataxia and areflexia, not grip myotonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTT causes Huntington disease with chorea and dementia, not myotonia and delayed muscle relaxation.

questions.stem: In myotonic dystrophy type 1, the CTG expansion lies in the 3' untranslated region of DMPK and does not alter the protein's amino acid sequence. Which mechanism best accounts for the disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gain-of-function point mutation that constitutively activates the kinase

choices.label: B
choices.text: An expanded polyglutamine tract makes the kinase aggregate in muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired iron-sulfur cluster assembly within mitochondria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of the DMPK protein due to promoter methylation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxic expanded RNA forms nuclear foci that sequester RNA-binding proteins

explanation.summary: The CTG expansion acts at the RNA level: toxic transcripts trap splicing factors and disrupt RNA processing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the repeat is in the noncoding 3' UTR, the protein sequence is unchanged. The expanded transcript accumulates as nuclear foci that sequester RNA-binding (splicing) proteins, disrupting normal RNA splicing and impairing muscle cell function, leading to cell death and progressive atrophy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The pathology arises from a toxic RNA gain of function, not an activating point mutation in the kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A polyglutamine aggregation mechanism belongs to Huntington disease (coding CAG expansion).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Impaired mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster assembly is the frataxin/Friedreich ataxia mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Promoter methylation and loss of protein is the Fragile X (FMR1) mechanism, not DMPK.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man develops jerky involuntary movements of his limbs and face, along with irritability, depression, and cognitive decline. His father developed similar symptoms at age 50. MRI shows atrophy of the caudate and putamen. Which of the following is the underlying molecular abnormality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of misfolded huntingtin protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased HTT gene transcription reducing huntingtin levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of FMRP due to gene silencing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nuclear accumulation of toxic CTG-containing RNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced frataxin causing mitochondrial dysfunction

explanation.summary: Adult-onset chorea with caudate/putamen atrophy and an affected parent is Huntington disease, caused by toxic polyglutamine huntingtin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Huntington disease results from a CAG expansion in the coding region of HTT, producing huntingtin with an abnormally long polyglutamine tract. The mutant protein misfolds and aggregates within neurons, causing selective neuronal loss and atrophy of the caudate and putamen, which manifests as chorea, dementia, and behavioral change.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Huntington disease is a toxic gain of function from an expanded protein, not simply decreased huntingtin production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of FMRP causes Fragile X syndrome, a childhood disorder, not adult chorea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxic CTG RNA is the mechanism of myotonic dystrophy type 1, not Huntington disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced frataxin causes Friedreich ataxia with ataxic gait, not chorea with basal ganglia atrophy.

questions.stem: A family history shows that a grandfather developed Huntington disease at age 60, his son at age 45, and a grandson at age 30, with each generation more severely affected. Repeat sizing shows progressively larger CAG expansions down the generations. Which phenomenon does this pattern illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic anticipation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genomic imprinting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable expressivity unrelated to genotype

explanation.summary: Earlier onset and increasing severity across generations, tracking with larger repeats, defines genetic anticipation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genetic anticipation is the phenomenon in which a disorder appears earlier and more severely in each successive generation because the number of trinucleotide repeats grows as the allele is transmitted. Longer expansions cause greater disruption, so the phenotype worsens over generations.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Genomic imprinting refers to parent-of-origin expression differences, not repeat expansion across generations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Incomplete penetrance describes carriers who never manifest disease, not a progressive change in onset age.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Locus heterogeneity means different genes cause the same phenotype; here a single gene expands over generations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The variability here is directly explained by repeat length, so it is not expressivity independent of genotype.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child has a 3-year history of a staggering, unsteady gait with frequent falls. Examination reveals absent deep tendon reflexes, diminished vibratory and position sense, and kyphoscoliosis. Echocardiography shows hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance pattern and repeat?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant, CAG repeat

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal dominant, CTG repeat

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autosomal recessive, GAA repeat

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitochondrial, GAA repeat

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked dominant, CGG repeat

explanation.summary: Childhood ataxia with areflexia, sensory loss, scoliosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is Friedreich ataxia—autosomal recessive, GAA repeat.
explanation.whyCorrect: Friedreich ataxia is caused by a GAA trinucleotide expansion in an intron of the FXN gene and is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. It presents at ages 5-15 with progressive ataxic gait, loss of deep tendon reflexes, diminished vibratory sensation, and kyphoscoliosis, and is commonly associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the leading cause of death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An autosomal dominant CAG repeat describes Huntington disease, which causes chorea, not childhood ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An autosomal dominant CTG repeat describes myotonic dystrophy type 1 with myotonia, not areflexic ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive; it is not mitochondrially inherited despite affecting mitochondrial function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An X-linked dominant CGG repeat describes Fragile X syndrome, not ataxia with cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: The gene mutated in Friedreich ataxia encodes frataxin, a mitochondrial protein. Deficiency of frataxin most directly impairs which of the following, driving neuronal and cardiac degeneration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron-sulfur cluster assembly and iron homeostasis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methylation of gene promoter CpG islands

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pre-mRNA splicing by nuclear spliceosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proteasomal degradation of misfolded cytoplasmic proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synaptic vesicle release of neurotransmitters

explanation.summary: Frataxin is essential for mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster assembly and iron homeostasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Frataxin is a mitochondrial protein needed for iron-sulfur cluster assembly and iron handling. Its deficiency causes free ionic iron accumulation, free radical formation, oxidative damage to DNA and proteins, and reduced ATP production, leading to cell death—especially in neurons, heart, and pancreatic cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Promoter methylation is the FMR1 silencing mechanism, unrelated to frataxin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disrupted splicing is characteristic of the toxic RNA in myotonic dystrophy, not frataxin deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective protein degradation is a downstream feature of huntingtin aggregation, not frataxin's primary function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Impaired synaptic transmission relates more to loss of FMRP or huntingtin dysfunction, not frataxin's defined role.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic 30-year-old woman is found to carry an FMR1 allele with 90 CGG repeats. She is concerned about her future children. Which of the following best describes her status and the risk to her offspring?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her allele will contract in offspring, eliminating disease risk

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her children can only be affected if the father also carries an expansion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her repeat count is within the normal range and poses no risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: She has a full mutation and will develop Fragile X syndrome herself

choices.label: E
choices.text: She is a premutation carrier whose allele may expand to a full mutation

explanation.summary: An FMR1 allele of 55-200 CGG repeats is a premutation—asymptomatic in the carrier but unstable and prone to full expansion in offspring.
explanation.whyCorrect: The premutation range (about 55-200 CGG for FMR1) does not cause classic Fragile X in the carrier because there are not enough repeats. However, loop structures and slippage make the allele unstable, so it can expand to a full mutation (>200) when transmitted, placing offspring at risk. Premutation carriers themselves may develop FXTAS or primary ovarian insufficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Premutation alleles tend to expand rather than contract across generations, increasing rather than removing risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Because FMR1 is X-linked, the mother's expanding allele alone confers risk; the father need not carry a mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The normal FMR1 range is below ~55 repeats, so 90 is above normal and unstable.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A full mutation is >200 repeats; 90 repeats is a premutation and she is asymptomatic for classic Fragile X.

questions.stem: Repetitive trinucleotide sequences are inherently unstable during DNA replication. Which of the following best describes the molecular event most responsible for adding extra repeat units in these regions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deamination of cytosine to uracil

choices.label: C
choices.text: DNA polymerase slippage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonhomologous end joining of double-strand breaks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleotide excision repair removing bulky adducts

explanation.summary: Repeat expansion arises from DNA polymerase slippage on repetitive sequences, inserting additional repeats.
explanation.whyCorrect: Slippage occurs when DNA polymerase detaches from the template strand in a repetitive region and reattaches incorrectly, often backtracking and inserting extra repeats. As repeat sequences grow, the likelihood of slippage increases, accelerating further expansion across generations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick attributes expansion to replication slippage rather than meiotic crossing over.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytosine deamination causes point mutations, not the length instability of trinucleotide repeats.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nonhomologous end joining repairs double-strand breaks and is not the source of repeat unit gain here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nucleotide excision repair addresses bulky helix-distorting lesions, not the addition of tandem repeats.

questions.stem: Fragile X syndrome is notable among the trinucleotide repeat disorders because it can be detected on a routine karyotype, whereas the others cannot. What is the characteristic karyotypic finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A balanced translocation between the X and chromosome 4

choices.label: B
choices.text: A non-staining gap at the long arm of the X chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: A ring chromosome formed from the X

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deletion of the short arm of the X chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trisomy of the X chromosome

explanation.summary: Fragile X shows a fragile site—a non-staining gap—near the tip of the long arm of the X chromosome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Karyotyping can diagnose Fragile X because the expansion produces a visible fragile site that appears as a non-staining gap at the terminal end of the long arm of the X chromosome. The other trinucleotide repeat disorders do not produce a cytogenetically visible lesion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fragile X is due to a repeat expansion, not a balanced translocation with chromosome 4.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A ring chromosome is not the described finding; Fragile X shows a terminal gap, not a ring.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lesion is a fragile gap on the long arm, not a deletion of the short arm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trisomy X is a numerical abnormality unrelated to the FMR1 repeat expansion.

questions.stem: A research team wants to develop a gene-directed therapy. They note that Huntington disease is caused by a toxic gain of function, whereas Fragile X syndrome results from loss of a protein. Which conclusion about therapeutic strategy is most consistent with the brick?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both disorders are best treated by silencing the mutated gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both disorders would benefit from increasing expression of the mutated gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither disorder can be targeted at the genetic level

choices.label: D
choices.text: siRNA gene silencing is rational for Fragile X but not for Huntington disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: siRNA gene silencing is rational for Huntington disease but not for Fragile X

explanation.summary: Silencing helps a toxic gain-of-function disease (Huntington) but is counterproductive when the problem is loss of a needed protein (Fragile X).
explanation.whyCorrect: In Huntington disease, siRNA-based strategies aim to silence or reduce the defective HTT gene, lowering production of the toxic mutant huntingtin. In Fragile X the disorder stems from absence of FMRP due to gene silencing, so reducing expression would not help; approaches such as CRISPR genome editing to correct the expansion are more promising.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Silencing is inappropriate for Fragile X because FMRP is needed, so both cannot be treated by silencing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increasing expression of mutant HTT would raise toxic protein levels, worsening Huntington disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick describes siRNA and CRISPR strategies, so genetic-level targeting is feasible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the logic: silencing worsens Fragile X, where the protein is already missing, and helps Huntington disease.

questions.stem: A forensic laboratory is asked to establish whether a man is the biological father of a child in a disputed paternity case. Which of the following classes of DNA markers is considered the gold standard for identifying individuals in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Copy number of ribosomal RNA gene clusters on acrocentric arms

choices.label: B
choices.text: Promoter methylation patterns of housekeeping genes in blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Short tandem repeats of 2-6 base pairs dispersed through the genome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Single-nucleotide substitutions scattered within protein-coding exons

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trinucleotide CAG repeat length within the HTT gene on 4p16.3

explanation.summary: STR (microsatellite) analysis is the gold standard for individual identification in forensics, paternity testing, and missing-person cases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microsatellites, or short tandem repeats (STRs), are repeating sequences of 2-6 base pairs found throughout the genome. Because DNA polymerase slips on repetitive sequences, these noncoding tracts are highly polymorphic among individuals, which makes them excellent markers for identity and inheritance tracking.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ribosomal gene copy number is not the marker class the brick describes as the forensic gold standard.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Promoter methylation is a regulatory mark (relevant to Fragile X silencing), not a tool for individual identification.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Single-nucleotide changes in exons are not the highly polymorphic length markers used for forensic identification.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The HTT CAG repeat is one disease locus; forensic identification relies on many polymorphic STR loci, not a single disease gene.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man undergoes resection of a colorectal adenocarcinoma. Molecular analysis of tumor DNA shows that many short tandem repeat loci have lengths that differ from those in his matched normal colonic tissue. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic anticipation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Germline repeat expansion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Microsatellite instability

choices.label: D
choices.text: Premutation carrier state

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat contraction

explanation.summary: Length changes in microsatellites between tumor and normal tissue define microsatellite instability, a hallmark of certain cancers such as colorectal cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Instability in microsatellites is a hallmark of certain cancers, including colorectal cancer, and is used clinically for diagnosis and prognosis. The variable microsatellite lengths in the tumor compared with normal tissue reflect this instability.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticipation describes earlier, more severe disease in successive generations of a family, not tumor-versus-normal differences within one patient.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Germline expansion refers to the repeat number inherited from a parent, which would be identical in tumor and normal tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A premutation is an intermediate repeat count at a specific disease gene, not widespread somatic instability in a tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeat contraction is a decrease in repeat length in a disease allele across transmission; it does not describe cancer-associated instability at many loci.

questions.stem: Genome analysis reveals that many trinucleotide repeat tracts located inside coding regions vary in length among healthy people without causing disease, whereas insertion of one or two nucleotides in the same regions is typically harmful. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adding a whole codon does not shift the reading frame of the gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mismatch repair removes triplet insertions before translation occurs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trinucleotide repeats are never transcribed into messenger RNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Triplet insertions are always converted to silent point mutations

choices.label: E
choices.text: Triplet repeats form hairpins that halt ribosome progression

explanation.summary: Small triplet insertions preserve the reading frame, which is why triplet repeats can 'safely' vary in length in both coding and noncoding DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because small-scale triplet insertions do not tend to cause harmful frameshift mutations, many locations throughout the genome contain triplet repeat segments that can safely vary in length. These tracts are found in both coding and noncoding portions of the genome, which is why trinucleotide repeats are common.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes tolerance to frame preservation, not to a repair pathway that excises triplets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coding-region triplet repeats are transcribed and translated; the HD CAG tract, for example, becomes a polyglutamine tract in huntingtin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Triplet insertions add an amino acid rather than being converted to silent substitutions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hairpin-mediated ribosome stalling is not the explanation given; the key point is that reading frame is maintained.

questions.stem: A medical student is reviewing the inheritance of the common triplet repeat expansion disorders. Which of the following statements is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most are autosomal dominant; Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive and Fragile X is X-linked

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most are autosomal dominant; Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive and myotonic dystrophy is X-linked

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most are autosomal dominant; myotonic dystrophy is autosomal recessive and Fragile X is X-linked

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most are autosomal recessive; Huntington disease is autosomal dominant and Fragile X is X-linked

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most are X-linked; Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive and Huntington disease is autosomal dominant

explanation.summary: Most triplet expansion disorders are autosomal dominant; the exceptions are Friedreich ataxia (recessive) and Fragile X (X-linked).
explanation.whyCorrect: More than 40 diseases, most affecting the nervous system, are caused by simple sequence repeat expansions. Most triplet expansion disorders are autosomal dominant, one is recessive (Friedreich ataxia), and one is X-linked (Fragile X).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is autosomal dominant on an autosome; Fragile X is the X-linked disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is autosomal dominant, not recessive; the recessive exception is Friedreich ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Most triplet disorders are dominant, not recessive; Huntington disease is one of the dominant majority, not an exception.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only Fragile X is X-linked; the majority are autosomal dominant.

questions.stem: A healthy 40-year-old man whose father died of Huntington disease requests predictive testing. Repeat sizing shows 37 CAG repeats in one HTT allele and 18 in the other. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling for this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He carries a pathogenic full mutation, and each of his children has a 50% chance of inheriting the same expanded allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is in the premutation range and unlikely to develop disease, but the allele may expand to a pathogenic size in his children

choices.label: C
choices.text: He will certainly develop Huntington disease, and motor onset is expected within the next decade regardless of transmission risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: The result lies entirely within the normal range, so neither he nor his children carry any risk of disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: The result reflects leukocyte somatic mosaicism and cannot be interpreted without sampling neuronal tissue

explanation.summary: For HTT, 36-39 CAG repeats is the premutation range: not enough repeats for disease, but unstable and at risk of expanding in the next generation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The population ranges for HTT are 5-35 CAG repeats (normal), 36-39 (premutation), and more than 40 (pathogenic). People in the premutation range do not develop the disease, but loop structures and slippage are more likely than in the normal range, so the next generation is at risk of inheriting more repeats and being affected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The pathogenic range for HTT is more than 40 repeats; 37 is an intermediate, premutation allele.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Individuals in the premutation range do not have enough repeats to cause clinical manifestations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The normal HTT range is 5-35 repeats; 37 is above normal and carries transmission risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeat sizing on blood DNA is the standard way to classify an allele; somatic expansion in neurons explains progression, not the interpretability of the inherited count.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with 8 months of amenorrhea and hot flashes; her serum FSH is markedly elevated. Her sister's son has Fragile X syndrome. FMR1 testing in the patient shows 95 CGG repeats. Which of the following best describes her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fragile X syndrome due to a fully methylated FMR1 allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency (FXPOI)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microsatellite instability at the FMR1 locus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatic contraction of the CGG repeat in ovarian tissue

explanation.summary: Female FMR1 premutation carriers are at risk of Fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency, which affects roughly 15-25% of them.
explanation.whyCorrect: An FMR1 allele of 55-200 CGG repeats is a premutation. Premutation carriers do not have Fragile X syndrome, but females with the premutation frequently develop ovarian insufficiency (FXPOI, in about 15-25% of female carriers), consistent with this patient's early menopausal picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fragile X syndrome requires a full mutation of more than 200 repeats with promoter hypermethylation; 95 repeats is a premutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FXTAS is the tremor/ataxia phenotype seen in about 10% of male premutation carriers, not an ovarian disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Microsatellite instability describes somatic length changes in tumors, not the germline premutation phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Repeat contraction reduces repeat length and tends to lessen or delay disease; it does not explain ovarian failure in a premutation carrier.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man develops intention tremor, gait ataxia, and cognitive decline. His grandson has Fragile X syndrome. FMR1 testing shows 105 CGG repeats. Which of the following best describes FMR1 expression expected in this man's cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both FMR1 mRNA and FMRP are at normal levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: FMR1 mRNA is absent while FMRP persists through prolonged stability

choices.label: C
choices.text: FMR1 mRNA is elevated while FMRP protein is reduced

choices.label: D
choices.text: FMR1 transcription is silenced by promoter hypermethylation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The FMR1 promoter region has been deleted along with the repeat

explanation.summary: In premutation carriers, FMR1 mRNA is transcribed (often at higher levels), yet FMRP protein is reduced, especially at larger CGG sizes; about 10% of male carriers develop FXTAS.
explanation.whyCorrect: This man is a premutation carrier (55-200 CGG) presenting with Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome, seen in about 10% of male carriers. Unlike the full mutation, the premutation allele is not silenced: FMR1 mRNA levels are higher, particularly in carriers with larger CGG repeats, while FMRP expression is reduced, especially in the higher repeat range.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Premutation carriers show altered expression: mRNA is increased and protein is decreased relative to controls.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The premutation transcript is present, not absent; it is the protein, not the mRNA, that is reduced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Promoter hypermethylation with transcriptional silencing occurs only when the repeat exceeds 200 (full mutation).
whyWrongByChoice.E: The premutation is an expansion of the repeat, not a deletion of the promoter.

questions.stem: A postmortem study is performed on a 60-year-old man who died of Huntington disease. Repeat sizing of his blood DNA years earlier showed 42 CAG repeats. Striatal neurons now show alleles with hundreds of CAG repeats, and repeat lengths differ widely between neighboring neurons. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic anticipation acting within this single individual's lifetime rather than across generations

choices.label: B
choices.text: Germline expansion that occurred during the formation of his own gametes in adolescence

choices.label: C
choices.text: Laboratory contamination of the neuronal DNA with a second patient's sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat contraction in the striatum that delayed his age of symptom onset by decades

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatic expansion within neurons over decades, producing mosaicism that drives progression

explanation.summary: The inherited (germline) repeat sets baseline risk, but somatic expansion in neurons drives progression and produces mosaicism of repeat length.
explanation.whyCorrect: The number of repeats inherited from a parent sets the baseline for disease risk and age of onset, but it is somatic expansion in neurons that drives disease progression. Over decades, neurons can accumulate hundreds of CAG repeats, far exceeding the inherited count; this expansion is uneven across tissues and even among neurons in the same brain region, producing mosaicism that influences severity and timing of onset.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticipation is a transgenerational phenomenon (earlier onset in successive generations), not intra-individual neuronal expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Germline expansion affects the allele transmitted to offspring, not the repeat length in the patient's own striatal neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Variable expansion among neurons is a described biological phenomenon, not an artifact requiring a contamination explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The neurons show larger, not smaller, repeats; contraction would reduce repeat length and tends to delay onset.

questions.stem: A woman with Huntington disease (45 CAG repeats) has two sons. The older son carries 48 CAG repeats and developed symptoms at age 38. The younger son carries 41 CAG repeats, developed milder symptoms at age 55, and has progressed slowly. Which of the following best accounts for the younger son's course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Contraction of the expanded allele during transmission

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genetic anticipation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Germline expansion during maternal transmission

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance of the maternal allele

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatic mosaicism confined to leukocytes

explanation.summary: Repeat contractions, though less common than expansions, can modify symptom severity and delay onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: The younger son inherited fewer repeats (41) than his mother carried (45), a repeat contraction during transmission. While repeat expansions are more commonly associated with disease, contractions also have significant clinical implications: they can modify the severity of symptoms or delay the onset, matching his later, milder course.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Anticipation would predict earlier and more severe disease than in the mother, which fits the older son, not the younger.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Germline expansion would produce a larger repeat than the mother's, as occurred in the older son (48), not a smaller one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: He is affected, so penetrance is not the issue; his milder phenotype tracks with a shorter repeat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leukocyte-restricted mosaicism is not described; his blood count of 41 reflects the inherited allele.

questions.stem: A geneticist explains to students that repeat expansion disorders violate one of the classical assumptions underlying Mendelian inheritance. Which of the following assumptions is being contradicted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dominant allele fully masks the phenotype of a recessive allele in heterozygotes

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mutation is fixed and static once it arises, remaining the same across generations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autosomal alleles are transmitted with equal probability by mothers and fathers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each parent contributes exactly one allele at every autosomal locus to each offspring

choices.label: E
choices.text: Genes located on different chromosomes assort independently during gamete formation

explanation.summary: Mendel assumed mutations were fixed and static; repeat expansions are unstable, dynamic mutations that change size across generations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once the critical threshold is crossed, repetitive sequences grow longer than normal and become dynamic mutations. Mendel stated that mutations were fixed and static, whereas repeat expansions are unstable and dynamic: the mutation often changes size in successive generations, so the phenotype is variable, with longer expansions causing more severe interference.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dominance relationships are not the assumption violated; most repeat disorders are in fact autosomal dominant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Equal transmission by either parent is not the principle the brick contrasts with dynamic mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Repeat disorders still involve one allele from each parent; what changes is the size of the allele, not the number transmitted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Independent assortment is unaffected; the instability is within a single locus.

questions.stem: A family with autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia is evaluated by PCR amplification of the TBP CAG/CAA repeat region followed by gel electrophoresis. An unaffected control shows a single band near 250 bp (alleles 39/40 repeats). Two affected members each show the same ~250 bp band plus an additional larger band (alleles 39/46 and 37/46). Which of the following best interprets the affected members' results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One allele carries an expanded repeat, yielding a longer amplification product

choices.label: B
choices.text: One TBP allele has been deleted, leaving a single amplifiable copy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promoter hypermethylation prevented amplification of the expanded allele

choices.label: D
choices.text: The larger band is a nonspecific primer-dimer artifact of the PCR

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are homozygous for a normal-length repeat allele

explanation.summary: PCR across a repeat region produces a longer product from an expanded allele; combined with sequencing it gives a precise repeat count.
explanation.whyCorrect: Southern blotting was traditionally used to detect repeat expansions, but PCR amplification of the region of interest is now more common and can be combined with sequencing for a precise repeat count. Affected heterozygotes show a normal-sized band plus a larger band from the expanded allele (46 repeats), as illustrated for the TBP CAG/CAA repeat in this family.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A deletion would remove a band, not add a larger one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The expanded allele was amplified (the larger band); methylation-based silencing is the Fragile X mechanism, not a feature of this analysis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The larger band is present only in affected individuals and corresponds to the sized 46-repeat allele, not an artifact.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two distinct bands indicate two different allele sizes, not homozygosity.

questions.stem: Sequencing in a family with autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia identifies a CAG/CAA repeat expansion in the TBP gene, one of 13 loci so far associated with this group of disorders. The normal product of this gene is which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A large protein of unclear function expressed mainly in brain

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mitochondrial protein required for iron-sulfur cluster assembly

choices.label: C
choices.text: A serine/threonine kinase involved in muscle development

choices.label: D
choices.text: An RNA-binding protein essential for synaptic function

choices.label: E
choices.text: The TATA-box binding protein

explanation.summary: TBP encodes the TATA-box binding protein and is one of the 13 loci identified for autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia (ADCA).
explanation.whyCorrect: The CAG repeat expansion illustrated in the brick's PCR example lies in the TBP gene, which encodes the TATA-box binding protein. TBP is one of the 13 loci associated with autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia (ADCA) identified so far.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brain-expressed protein of unclear function is huntingtin (HTT).
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster protein is frataxin (FXN), mutated in Friedreich ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The serine/threonine kinase is DMPK, mutated in myotonic dystrophy type 1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The RNA-binding synaptic protein is FMRP, lost in Fragile X syndrome.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with jerky involuntary movements, irritability, and progressive cognitive decline; her father had the same illness. Genetic testing confirms a heterozygous CAG expansion in the coding region of the responsible gene. On which chromosome is this gene located?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromosome 13

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chromosome 21

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chromosome 4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chromosome 9

choices.label: E
choices.text: X chromosome

explanation.summary: Huntington disease is caused by a heterozygous CAG expansion in the coding region of HTT on chromosome 4.
explanation.whyCorrect: Huntington disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by a heterozygous expansion of the CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene on chromosome 4. This autosomal dominant mutation lies in the coding region and produces an abnormally long polyglutamine tract in huntingtin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chromosome 13 is not the location of HTT.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chromosome 21 is not the location of HTT.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromosome 9 carries FXN, the gene for Friedreich ataxia (GAA repeat).
whyWrongByChoice.E: The X chromosome carries FMR1, the Fragile X gene (CGG repeat).

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with genetically confirmed Huntington disease is being counseled along with his family about long-term prognosis. Which of the following is among the leading causes of death in this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cerebrovascular events

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Respiratory muscle failure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suicide

explanation.summary: The leading causes of death in Huntington disease are suicide, aspiration pneumonia, and cardiac complications.
explanation.whyCorrect: Huntington disease produces aggression, depression, and dementia alongside chorea, and its leading causes of death are suicide, aspiration pneumonia, and cardiac complications. Other systemic findings include weight loss and sleep disturbances.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cerebrovascular events, along with cardiac issues, are listed as leading causes of death in Fragile X syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diabetes mellitus is associated with Friedreich ataxia, not a leading cause of death in Huntington disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with cardiac failure is the leading cause of death in Friedreich ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory failure from progressive respiratory muscle weakness is a leading cause of death in myotonic dystrophy type 1.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (Steinert disease) after presenting with grip myotonia and distal weakness. The gene that carries the CTG expansion in this disorder normally encodes which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mitochondrial protein required for iron-sulfur cluster assembly

choices.label: B
choices.text: A polyglutamine-tract protein expressed mainly in brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: A serine/threonine kinase involved in muscle development

choices.label: D
choices.text: A transcription factor that binds the TATA box

choices.label: E
choices.text: An RNA-binding protein required for synaptic function

explanation.summary: DMPK encodes a serine/threonine kinase involved in muscle development, cytoskeletal organization, and stress-responsive signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is caused by a CTG expansion in the 3' untranslated region of DMPK. DMPK encodes a serine/threonine kinase involved in muscle development, cytoskeletal organization, and stress-responsive signaling; because the repeat is in the 3' UTR, disease arises from toxic RNA rather than an altered kinase sequence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster protein is frataxin, encoded by FXN (Friedreich ataxia).
whyWrongByChoice.B: The polyglutamine-containing brain protein is huntingtin (HTT).
whyWrongByChoice.D: The TATA-box binding protein is encoded by TBP, an ADCA locus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The RNA-binding synaptic protein is FMRP, encoded by FMR1 (Fragile X).

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with myotonic dystrophy type 1 is found to have reduced fertility and an elevated fasting glucose attributed to insulin resistance. Which of the following additional findings is most consistent with the systemic manifestations of his disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrophy of the caudate and putamen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early-onset cataracts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kyphoscoliosis with cavovarus feet

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macro-orchidism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mitral valve prolapse

explanation.summary: DM1 is a multisystem disease: endocrine dysfunction (insulin resistance, gonadal insufficiency, reduced fertility), cardiac conduction defects, respiratory weakness, frontal balding, and early-onset cataracts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond myotonia and distal weakness, DM1 has systemic manifestations including endocrine dysfunction (insulin resistance, gonadal insufficiency, reduced fertility), cardiac conduction defects and arrhythmias, respiratory failure, and other signs such as frontal balding and early-onset cataracts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caudate and putamen atrophy is the hallmark of Huntington disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kyphoscoliosis and cavovarus foot are typical of Friedreich ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macro-orchidism (enlarged testicles after puberty) is a feature of Fragile X syndrome; DM1 causes testicular dysfunction, not enlargement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mitral valve prolapse is the cardiac association of Fragile X syndrome; DM1 causes conduction defects and arrhythmias.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with myotonic dystrophy type 1 develops chronic hypercapnic respiratory insufficiency and sleep apnea. Which of the following best explains her respiratory compromise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central hypoventilation from degeneration of the caudate nucleus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Progressive weakness of the diaphragm and chest wall muscles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pulmonary edema from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restrictive lung disease secondary to severe kyphoscoliosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upper airway obstruction from macroglossia

explanation.summary: Respiratory failure in DM1 results from progressive weakness of the respiratory muscles and is a major cause of mortality.
explanation.whyCorrect: DM1 primarily affects muscle tissue; the toxic CTG-repeat RNA disrupts splicing, impairing muscle cell function and causing cell death and progressive atrophy. Respiratory failure due to progressive weakness of respiratory muscles is one of the listed systemic complications and, with cardiac arrhythmias and aspiration pneumonia, a leading cause of death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caudate degeneration is the pathology of Huntington disease, not DM1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy belongs to Friedreich ataxia; DM1 cardiac involvement is conduction defects and arrhythmias.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Kyphoscoliosis is characteristic of Friedreich ataxia, not myotonic dystrophy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Macroglossia is not a described feature of DM1; the mechanism is muscle weakness.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy with moderate intellectual disability has a long face, large ears, and a prominent jaw. Testing confirms a full CGG expansion in FMR1. Which of the following additional physical findings is most likely on examination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chorea and sustained dystonic posturing of the limbs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enlarged testicles and hyperflexible finger joints

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grip myotonia and early frontal balding

choices.label: D
choices.text: Kyphoscoliosis with absent deep tendon reflexes in the legs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ptosis and early posterior subcapsular cataracts

explanation.summary: Fragile X features include macro-orchidism after puberty, hyperflexible joints (especially fingers), and hypotonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond intellectual disability and the facial features (long face, large ears, prominent jaw), Fragile X syndrome includes macro-orchidism (enlarged testicles after puberty), hyperflexible joints especially in the fingers, and hypotonia (reduced muscle tone), with developmental delays in speech and motor skills.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chorea and dystonia are the movement disorders of Huntington disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myotonia and frontal balding are features of myotonic dystrophy type 1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Kyphoscoliosis with loss of deep tendon reflexes characterizes Friedreich ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ptosis and early-onset cataracts are seen in myotonic dystrophy type 1.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy with Fragile X syndrome is found to have a mid-systolic click and murmur during a routine visit. Which of the following cardiac abnormalities is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrioventricular conduction block

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coarctation of the aorta

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mitral valve prolapse

explanation.summary: Cardiac involvement in Fragile X syndrome includes heart rhythm disorders and mitral valve prolapse, which may present as a heart murmur.
explanation.whyCorrect: The comparative summary of triplet repeat disorders lists heart rhythm disorders and mitral valve prolapse (which may present as a heart murmur) as the cardiac involvement of Fragile X syndrome, and cardiac issues together with cerebrovascular events as its leading causes of death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Conduction defects and arrhythmias are the cardiac complications of myotonic dystrophy type 1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aortic coarctation is not a feature of Fragile X syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dilated cardiomyopathy is not the cardiac association described for any of these disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the cardiac lesion of Friedreich ataxia, not Fragile X.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has moderate intellectual disability, autism spectrum behaviors, hypotonia, a long face, and large ears. CGG repeat sizing of FMR1 shows 30 repeats on his single X chromosome, and the promoter is unmethylated. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A nonsense, missense, or deletion mutation in FMR1 has eliminated FMRP function

choices.label: B
choices.text: A toxic RNA transcribed from the normal-length allele is forming nuclear foci

choices.label: C
choices.text: He carries a premutation allele that has not yet expanded past the threshold

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypermethylation of the HTT promoter is silencing an unrelated gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: The normal repeat count excludes Fragile X syndrome and another diagnosis must be sought

explanation.summary: Although most Fragile X is due to a methylated CGG full mutation, other FMR1 mutations (nonsense, missense, deletions) also cause the syndrome through loss of FMRP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Fragile X phenotype reflects absence of FMRP, which is essential for synaptic function and neural development. The usual cause is a CGG expansion beyond 200 with promoter hypermethylation, but other mutations in FMR1, including nonsense, missense, and deletions, have also been identified in individuals with Fragile X syndrome and would explain a classic phenotype with a normal repeat count.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxic RNA nuclear foci are the mechanism of myotonic dystrophy type 1; a normal-length CGG transcript does not form them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 30 repeats is in the normal range (below 55), not a premutation, and premutation carriers do not have classic Fragile X.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HTT is the Huntington disease gene and its promoter methylation is not a described mechanism of Fragile X.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A normal repeat count does not exclude Fragile X, because point mutations and deletions in FMR1 can also produce the syndrome.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl develops a progressively unsteady gait, absent ankle reflexes, and diminished vibratory sense. Genetic testing identifies a homozygous GAA trinucleotide expansion. Which of the following best describes the location of this expansion and its primary molecular consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 3' untranslated region of DMPK, producing toxic nuclear RNA foci

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5' untranslated region of FMR1, producing promoter hypermethylation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Coding region of HTT on chromosome 4, producing a polyglutamine tract

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intron of FXN on chromosome 9, producing aberrant splicing and reduced frataxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promoter of FXN on chromosome 9, producing overexpression of frataxin

explanation.summary: Friedreich ataxia is caused by a GAA expansion in an intron of FXN on chromosome 9, leading to aberrant splicing, drastically reduced frataxin, and truncated protein products.
explanation.whyCorrect: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the intronic region of the FXN gene on chromosome 9. The GAA expansion leads to aberrant splicing, drastically reduced frataxin expression, and truncated protein products, impairing mitochondrial function and causing degeneration of nervous tissue in the spinal cord.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 3' UTR CTG repeat producing toxic RNA foci is the myotonic dystrophy mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 5' UTR CGG repeat with promoter methylation is the Fragile X mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A coding CAG repeat in HTT is the Huntington disease lesion; the GAA repeat is not in a coding region.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The FXN expansion reduces rather than increases frataxin, and it lies in an intron, not the promoter.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy with genetically confirmed Friedreich ataxia undergoes brain and spine MRI. Which of the following imaging patterns is most consistent with his disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrophy of the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord with white matter abnormalities

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased posterior cerebellar vermis size with a normal brainstem and spinal cord

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diffuse cortical atrophy sparing the posterior fossa and the entire spinal cord

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isolated enlargement of the lateral ventricles with normal cerebellar volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Selective atrophy of the caudate and putamen with ex vacuo enlargement of the lateral ventricles

explanation.summary: MRI in Friedreich ataxia may reveal atrophy in the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord along with white matter abnormalities.
explanation.whyCorrect: Frataxin deficiency impairs mitochondrial function and ultimately causes degeneration of nervous tissue in the spinal cord. MRI findings in Friedreich ataxia may reveal atrophy in the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord, along with white matter abnormalities.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced posterior cerebellar vermis size is the finding illustrated for Fragile X syndrome, which does not involve spinal cord atrophy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Friedreich ataxia targets the cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord rather than sparing the posterior fossa.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isolated ventricular enlargement is not the described pattern for Friedreich ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Caudate and putamen atrophy is the characteristic imaging finding of Huntington disease.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with Friedreich ataxia develops polyuria, polydipsia, and persistent hyperglycemia. Which of the following best relates this new problem to her underlying disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Frataxin deficiency injures pancreatic cells, and diabetes mellitus is a recognized association

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kyphoscoliosis mechanically compresses the pancreatic duct and blocks insulin release

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of FMRP impairs endocrine signaling in both the ovaries and the pancreatic islets

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polyglutamine aggregates within the hypothalamus disrupt appetite and glucose regulation centrally

choices.label: E
