choices.text: Toxic RNA foci in skeletal muscle produce severe peripheral insulin resistance

explanation.summary: Friedreich ataxia is often associated with diabetes mellitus; neurons, heart cells, and pancreatic cells are the most affected by frataxin deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Absent frataxin impairs incorporation of iron with sulfur in mitochondria, causing free ionic iron accumulation, less ATP production, free radical formation, and oxidative damage leading to cell death. The most affected cells are neurons, heart cells, and pancreatic cells, and the condition is often associated with diabetes mellitus as well as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The diabetes reflects cellular frataxin deficiency, not mechanical compression by the spinal deformity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FMRP loss is the Fragile X mechanism; ovarian insufficiency relates to FMR1, not to Friedreich ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polyglutamine aggregation is the Huntington disease mechanism and is not the basis of diabetes here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxic RNA foci and insulin resistance describe myotonic dystrophy type 1, not Friedreich ataxia.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company is developing a small-molecule drug that stabilizes the structure of a mutant protein and disrupts its toxic interactions, thereby preventing its aggregation. Among the following repeat expansion disorders, which is the most rational target for this therapeutic approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fragile X syndrome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Friedreich ataxia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Huntington disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Myotonic dystrophy type 1

explanation.summary: Small molecules that prevent aggregation of mutant proteins target disorders driven by toxic misfolded protein, the mechanism of Huntington disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: There is currently no cure for trinucleotide repeat disorders, but new technologies include small-molecule treatments designed to prevent aggregation of mutant proteins by stabilizing protein structure or disrupting toxic interactions. Huntington disease is caused by toxic accumulation of misfolded, polyglutamine-expanded huntingtin that aggregates within neurons, so it is the logical target.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fragile X results from absence of FMRP due to transcriptional silencing; there is no aggregating mutant protein to stabilize.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FXPOI occurs in FMR1 premutation carriers and is not described as an aggregating-protein disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Friedreich ataxia results from reduced frataxin expression via aberrant splicing, a loss of protein rather than a toxic aggregate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myotonic dystrophy is driven by toxic RNA that forms nuclear foci, not by an aggregating mutant protein.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the emergency department for sudden, nontraumatic, painless bilateral loss of vision. He reports some initial blurring that progressed rapidly to loss of sight over a day, without pain or other symptoms. An ophthalmology consult confirms bilateral central scotomas with a normal-appearing retina. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Friedreich ataxia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON)

choices.label: C
choices.text: MELAS

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF)

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retinitis pigmentosa

explanation.summary: Sudden painless bilateral vision loss in a young man is the classic presentation of LHON.
explanation.whyCorrect: LHON is a mitochondrial disease characterized by sudden, painless vision loss in both eyes, typically presenting in the 2nd or 3rd decade of life, with about 90% of affected patients being male. Vision loss occurs because optic nerve cells die from mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired ATP production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Friedreich ataxia causes progressive gait ataxia and cardiomyopathy beginning in childhood, not sudden vision loss.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MELAS presents with mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes in the first decade, not isolated painless vision loss.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MERRF is defined by myoclonus, seizures, myopathy, and cerebellar ataxia, not acute bilateral optic neuropathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retinitis pigmentosa causes gradual, progressive peripheral and night-vision loss, not sudden bilateral central vision loss.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is evaluated for sudden, painless vision loss. His mother reports that both her older and younger brothers developed the same problem in their late teens, but none of the children of those uncles have been affected. Which of the following features best supports a mitochondrial (rather than another genetic) etiology?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance with anticipation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal pattern of inheritance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only males are ever affected

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paternal pattern of inheritance

choices.label: E
choices.text: The disease reliably skips generations

explanation.summary: Mitochondrial diseases follow a maternal inheritance pattern because only oocytes contribute mitochondria to offspring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitochondrial mutations are transmitted only through the mother, since only oocytes contribute mitochondria to the zygote. This explains why the patient's maternal uncles are affected (they inherited mutant mtDNA from the grandmother) but their own children are not (affected males cannot transmit the disease).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autosomal dominant inheritance would allow affected fathers to transmit disease to their children, which is not seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial diseases affect both sexes; in LHON males predominate, but males are not the only affected individuals and this alone does not define mitochondrial inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fathers do not transmit mitochondria, so a paternal pattern argues against mitochondrial inheritance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skipping generations is characteristic of recessive or reduced-penetrance nuclear traits, not the defining feature of maternal inheritance.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child has recurrent stroke-like episodes, migraine-like headaches, vomiting, muscle weakness, and seizures. Serum lactate is markedly elevated. A muscle biopsy stained microscopically shows ragged-red fibers from an accumulation of abnormal mitochondria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Friedreich ataxia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: MELAS

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pearson syndrome

explanation.summary: Encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes with ragged-red fibers define MELAS.
explanation.whyCorrect: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes) is a mitochondrial myopathy presenting within the first decade of life. It preferentially affects the brain and muscle, and muscle biopsy classically shows ragged-red fibers formed from accumulated diseased mitochondria; lactic acid buildup accounts for the vomiting, weakness, and dyspnea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked dystrophinopathy causing progressive proximal weakness, not lactic acidosis with stroke-like episodes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Friedreich ataxia produces gait ataxia and cardiomyopathy from a nuclear FXN defect, without lactic acidosis and ragged-red fibers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LHON causes sudden painless bilateral vision loss, not stroke-like episodes with lactic acidosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pearson syndrome is a mitochondrial disorder affecting the bone marrow and pancreas, not one defined by stroke-like episodes.

questions.stem: A young patient has myoclonus (involuntary muscle twitches), seizures, myopathy, and cerebellar ataxia. Muscle biopsy shows ragged-red fibers. Genetic testing reveals a point mutation in the mitochondrial tRNA-lysine gene MT-TK (A8344G). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Friedreich ataxia (FXN GAA expansion)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (complex I)

choices.label: C
choices.text: MELAS (ragged-red fibers, lactic acidosis, strokes)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wilson disease (copper accumulation)

explanation.summary: Myoclonus, seizures, ataxia, and ragged-red fibers with an MT-TK mutation define MERRF.
explanation.whyCorrect: MERRF is caused by mtDNA mutations, most commonly in the tRNA-lysine gene MT-TK (A8344G, T8356C, or G8363A). It is characterized mainly by myoclonus, seizures, myopathy, and cerebellar ataxia, and ragged-red fibers from mitochondrial accumulation in muscle are a hallmark seen microscopically after staining.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive nuclear FXN disorder without ragged-red fibers or an MT-TK mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LHON causes painless bilateral vision loss from complex I gene mutations, not a myoclonic epilepsy syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MELAS features stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis; although it also shows ragged-red fibers, myoclonus with an MT-TK tRNA-lysine mutation is specific for MERRF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Wilson disease is a disorder of copper accumulation, unrelated to mtDNA tRNA mutations or ragged-red fibers.

questions.stem: A child is referred for a suspected mitochondrial disorder. Mitochondrial DNA sequencing shows that some cells contain a mixture of both normal mitochondria and mutant mitochondria. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heterogeneity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heteroplasmy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homoplasmy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Threshold model of disease

explanation.summary: A cell containing both normal and mutant mtDNA is heteroplasmic.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heteroplasmy describes cells that contain both mitochondria with normal mtDNA and mitochondria with mutant mtDNA. Because mtDNA randomly assorts among mitochondria and daughter cells during division, the proportion of mutant mtDNA varies and is responsible for the variable expressivity of mitochondrial disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heterogeneity is a general term and does not specifically describe the mtDNA composition of a cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homogeneity is a general term implying uniformity, not a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Homoplasmy describes a uniform mtDNA population, either all normal or all mutant, which is the opposite of this finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The threshold model describes when symptoms appear once mutant load is high enough, not the coexistence of two mtDNA populations.

questions.stem: Two siblings carry the same mtDNA mutation, but one is severely affected while the other is asymptomatic. Studies show that a respiratory chain complex can be substantially inhibited up to a critical value before mitochondrial respiration and ATP synthesis decline and symptoms appear. Which of the following concepts best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anticipation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genomic imprinting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Locus heterogeneity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phenotypic threshold effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-inactivation (lyonization)

explanation.summary: Mitochondrial disease manifests only once mutant load and ATP loss exceed a tissue-specific threshold.
explanation.whyCorrect: The phenotypic threshold effect states that a genetic defect manifests only when a threshold level is exceeded. A respiratory chain complex can be considerably inhibited up to a critical value without affecting respiration or ATP synthesis; disease appears only after ATP production falls below the level required by that organ system, accounting for variable severity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticipation describes earlier or more severe disease across generations, typically with expanding repeats, not a mutant-load threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Genomic imprinting refers to parent-of-origin gene expression differences, not a threshold of mutant mitochondria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Locus heterogeneity means different genes cause a similar phenotype, which does not explain variable severity from the same mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: X-inactivation involves silencing one X chromosome and does not apply to mtDNA.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to describe the structure of a mitochondrion. Which of the following statements is accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contains its own circular, double-stranded DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: It divides by mitosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has only a single membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces only a small percentage of the cell's ATP

choices.label: E
choices.text: It relies solely on the nuclear genome to encode all of its proteins

explanation.summary: Mitochondria have their own circular, double-stranded mtDNA and their own machinery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitochondria contain their own circular, double-stranded mtDNA housed in the matrix, which encodes 13 OXPHOS proteins, 22 tRNAs, and 2 rRNAs. This reflects their bacterial endosymbiotic origin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitochondria divide by prokaryotic binary fission, not mitosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondria have two membranes, an outer membrane and an inner membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitochondria produce most of the cell's ATP via aerobic respiration, not a small percentage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although about 1100 mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded, mitochondria also use their own mtDNA to encode essential OXPHOS proteins.

questions.stem: Which of the following metabolic pathways does NOT take place within the mitochondria?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electron transport chain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fatty acid beta-oxidation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glycolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxidative phosphorylation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle

explanation.summary: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; the other listed pathways occur in mitochondria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Glycolysis takes place solely in the cell's cytoplasm. Pathways housed in the mitochondria include the electron transport chain, fatty acid beta-oxidation, oxidative phosphorylation, the TCA cycle, acetyl-CoA production, and ketogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The electron transport chain operates on the inner mitochondrial membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fatty acid beta-oxidation occurs within the mitochondria.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxidative phosphorylation is carried out in the mitochondria and is the cell's main site of ATP production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The TCA (Krebs) cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old child has had progressive difficulty walking, unsteady posture, and frequent falls since age 7, along with dysarthria. Echocardiography reveals cardiomyopathy. Genetic testing shows homozygous GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in intron 1 of the FXN gene. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ataxia-telangiectasia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Friedreich ataxia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: MELAS

choices.label: E
choices.text: MERRF

explanation.summary: Childhood-onset ataxia with cardiomyopathy and an FXN GAA repeat expansion defines Friedreich ataxia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is an autosomal recessive, progressive neurodegenerative disease typically presenting between ages 5 and 15 with unsteady posture, frequent falls, and progressive gait ataxia, and is associated with cardiomyopathy. It results from a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in intron 1 of the FXN gene, which disrupts transcription and leads to frataxin deficiency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ataxia-telangiectasia causes ataxia with oculocutaneous telangiectasias and immunodeficiency from ATM mutations, not an FXN GAA expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LHON causes painless vision loss from mtDNA complex I mutations, not gait ataxia with cardiomyopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MELAS is a maternally inherited mtDNA disorder with stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis, not an FXN repeat expansion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MERRF is a maternally inherited mtDNA disorder (MT-TK) with myoclonus and ragged-red fibers, not caused by an FXN mutation.

questions.stem: Friedreich ataxia results from deficiency of frataxin, a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial protein. Which of the following best describes the normal function of frataxin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acting as the electron carrier released to trigger apoptosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Charging the mitochondrial tRNA for lysine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial iron metabolism and iron homeostasis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repair of mitochondrial DNA damage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serving as a subunit of electron transport chain complex I

explanation.summary: Frataxin plays a crucial role in mitochondrial iron metabolism and iron homeostasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Frataxin is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial protein that plays a crucial role in mitochondrial iron metabolism and iron homeostasis. Deficient or non-functional frataxin, caused by FXN GAA repeat expansions, underlies Friedreich ataxia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytochrome C is the electron carrier released to trigger apoptosis, not frataxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The tRNA-lysine gene MT-TK relates to MERRF; frataxin does not charge tRNAs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: mtDNA repair is limited in mitochondria and is not the role of frataxin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Complex I subunits are encoded by genes such as MT-ND1/MT-ND4 (implicated in LHON), not by frataxin.

questions.stem: Mitochondria help determine whether a cell will undergo programmed cell death. Which of the following mitochondrial events triggers apoptosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accumulation of acetyl-CoA in the matrix

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fusion of two mitochondria into one

choices.label: C
choices.text: Import of nuclear-encoded proteins into the mitochondrion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of cytochrome C from the mitochondrion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replication of mitochondrial DNA

explanation.summary: Release of cytochrome C from mitochondria triggers apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: When a mitochondrion releases cytochrome C, normally an electron carrier of the electron transport chain, apoptosis (programmed cell death) is triggered and the cell dies. This makes mitochondria central regulators of whether a cell lives or dies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acetyl-CoA production is a normal metabolic function of mitochondria and does not by itself trigger apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitochondrial fusion adjusts to the cell's energy needs and is not the trigger for programmed cell death.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Import of nuclear-encoded proteins is required for normal mitochondrial function, not a death signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: mtDNA replication accompanies mitochondrial division and is unrelated to triggering apoptosis.

questions.stem: The mitochondrial genome contains only 37 genes, of which 13 are protein-encoding. All 13 protein-encoding genes encode subunits of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glycolytic enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Histone packaging proteins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oxidative phosphorylation complexes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ribosomal proteins of the cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urea cycle enzymes

explanation.summary: The 13 protein-coding mtDNA genes all encode oxidative phosphorylation subunits.
explanation.whyCorrect: mtDNA is a small circular genome of about 16,569 base pairs containing 37 genes: 13 protein-encoding (all oxidative phosphorylation subunits), 22 tRNA genes, and 2 rRNA genes. The remaining ~1100 mitochondrial proteins are nuclear-encoded and imported from the cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glycolytic enzymes function in the cytoplasm and are not encoded by mtDNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: mtDNA has no histones, and histone proteins are nuclear-encoded.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytoplasmic ribosomal proteins are nuclear-encoded; mtDNA encodes only 2 rRNAs and 22 tRNAs for its own translation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urea cycle enzymes are nuclear-encoded, not products of the 13 mtDNA protein-coding genes.

questions.stem: A first-year medical student is reviewing the endosymbiotic theory of mitochondrial origin, in which an anaerobic eukaryotic cell endocytosed an aerobic microorganism. According to this model, which of the following mitochondrial structures is thought to be derived from the engulfed microorganism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytoplasmic ribosomes of the host

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inner mitochondrial membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nuclear envelope of the host

choices.label: D
choices.text: Outer mitochondrial membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasma membrane of the host cell

explanation.summary: Under the endosymbiotic theory, the inner membrane comes from the original bacterial membrane and the outer membrane from the host cell membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitochondria are thought to have originated when an anaerobic eukaryotic cell endocytosed an aerobic microorganism that eventually evolved into the mitochondrion. This explains the two membranes: the inner membrane is thought to be derived from the original bacterial membrane, while the outer membrane, which surrounds the entire mitochondrion, is derived from the original host cell's membrane.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoplasmic ribosomes are host-cell machinery that translate nuclear-encoded proteins; they are not derived from the engulfed microorganism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The nuclear envelope belongs to the host eukaryotic cell and is not part of the mitochondrion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The outer membrane is thought to be derived from the host cell's membrane that wrapped around the engulfed organism, not from the bacterium itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The host plasma membrane is the proposed source of the outer mitochondrial membrane, not a structure derived from the microorganism.

questions.stem: A geneticist explains to a family that mutations in mitochondrial DNA tend to produce symptoms in a predictable set of organs. Which of the following groups of tissues is preferentially affected by mitochondrial diseases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adipose tissue and loose connective tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bladder urothelium and gut epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bone, cartilage, and tendon

choices.label: D
choices.text: Central nervous system, heart, and muscle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skin, hair, and nails

explanation.summary: Mitochondrial diseases preferentially affect tissues with high energy demands such as the CNS, heart, and muscle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because mitochondria are the cell's primary site of ATP production via aerobic respiration, mutations in mtDNA preferentially affect those tissues with high energy demands, such as the central nervous system (CNS), heart, and muscle. Cells that require a lot of energy can contain thousands of mitochondria per cell to meet their demands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adipose and loose connective tissue are not listed as the high-energy-demand targets of mitochondrial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bladder and gut epithelium are not the tissues singled out for high energy demand; the CNS, heart, and muscle are.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bone, cartilage, and tendon are not among the tissues the brick identifies as preferentially affected by mitochondrial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skin, hair, and nails are not described as high-energy-demand tissues that are preferentially injured by mtDNA mutations.

questions.stem: A biochemist fractionates hepatocytes and isolates a purified mitochondrial fraction. She finds that this fraction alone cannot complete one particular pathway because only some of that pathway's enzymes are located within the mitochondria. Which of the following pathways is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electron transport chain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fatty acid beta-oxidation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ketogenesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urea cycle

explanation.summary: Mitochondria contain only some of the enzymes for the urea cycle, heme synthesis, and gluconeogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitochondria house the complete enzyme sets for fatty acid beta-oxidation, acetyl-CoA production, ketogenesis, the TCA (Krebs) cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation. In contrast, they contain only some of the enzymes needed for heme synthesis, the urea cycle, and gluconeogenesis, so those pathways span mitochondrial and extramitochondrial compartments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The electron transport chain is housed in the mitochondria, where cytochrome C serves as one of its electron carriers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fatty acid beta-oxidation is carried out by enzymes contained within the mitochondria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ketogenesis is listed among the processes whose enzymes mitochondria contain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The TCA cycle is one of the pathways whose enzymes are contained within the mitochondria.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has progressive gait ataxia, frequent falls, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Laboratory studies confirm deficiency of frataxin, a mitochondrial protein. His parents are unaffected, and a paternal uncle had the same disease. Which of the following best explains why this mitochondrial-protein disorder does not follow maternal inheritance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Frataxin is encoded by the nuclear FXN gene, so the trait is transmitted in an autosomal recessive pattern

choices.label: B
choices.text: Frataxin is one of the 13 mtDNA-encoded proteins, but paternal mitochondria persisted in the zygote

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heteroplasmy within the father's sperm mitochondria allowed transmission of mutant mtDNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: The causative GAA expansion arose de novo within the mitochondrial genome of the boy

choices.label: E
choices.text: The disorder is X-linked recessive, so the unaffected mother is an obligate carrier

explanation.summary: Friedreich ataxia is autosomal recessive because frataxin is nuclear-encoded, not part of the mitochondrial genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Not all mitochondrial-related disorders arise from proteins made in the mitochondria. Frataxin is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial protein; it is among the ~1100 mitochondrial proteins that are translated in the cytoplasm and transported into the mitochondria. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is therefore an autosomal recessive genetic disease, so unaffected carrier parents can have an affected child and the trait can appear on the paternal side of the family.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The 13 mtDNA-encoded proteins are all oxidative phosphorylation subunits; frataxin is not among them, and mitochondria are contributed only by oocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only oocytes contribute mitochondria to offspring, so paternal sperm mitochondria do not transmit mtDNA regardless of heteroplasmy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The GAA repeat expansion lies in intron 1 of the nuclear FXN gene, not in the mitochondrial genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FRDA is autosomal recessive, not X-linked; an affected paternal uncle and unaffected parents fit recessive nuclear inheritance.

questions.stem: A researcher takes the sequence of a mitochondrially encoded oxidative phosphorylation subunit and translates it in a cell-free system that uses the standard nuclear genetic code. The product is prematurely truncated. Which of the following codons in the mitochondrial transcript most likely accounts for this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AGA

choices.label: B
choices.text: AGG

choices.label: C
choices.text: AUG

choices.label: D
choices.text: UAA

choices.label: E
choices.text: UGA

explanation.summary: In mtDNA the UGA triplet codes for tryptophan rather than acting as a stop codon as it does in nuclear DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitochondria use a slightly different genetic code from the nucleus. The UGA triplet codes for the amino acid tryptophan in mtDNA instead of serving as a stop codon, as it does in nuclear DNA. A nuclear-code translation system would therefore read an internal UGA as a stop signal and terminate the protein early.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AGA serves as a stop codon in mtDNA but codes for arginine in the nuclear code, so a nuclear system would read through it rather than truncate the protein.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AGG, like AGA, is a mitochondrial stop codon that the nuclear code reads as arginine; it would not cause premature truncation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AUG is not described as differing between the two codes and would not cause premature termination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: UAA is not one of the codons the brick identifies as differing between mtDNA and nuclear DNA.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes how the codons AGA and AGG are read in mitochondrial DNA compared with nuclear DNA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are entirely absent from the mitochondrial genome

choices.label: B
choices.text: They code for lysine in mtDNA instead of coding for arginine

choices.label: C
choices.text: They code for tryptophan in mtDNA instead of serving as stop codons

choices.label: D
choices.text: They serve as initiation codons in mtDNA instead of coding for methionine

choices.label: E
choices.text: They serve as stop codons in mtDNA instead of coding for arginine

explanation.summary: AGA and AGG act as stop codons in mtDNA rather than encoding arginine as in the nuclear code.
explanation.whyCorrect: One of the main differences between mtDNA and nuclear DNA is a slightly different genetic code. In mtDNA, the codons AGA and AGG serve as stop codons instead of coding for the amino acid arginine, which is their meaning in nuclear DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These codons are present in mtDNA, where they function as termination signals.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AGA and AGG do not switch to encoding lysine; they become stop codons in mtDNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: It is UGA, not AGA/AGG, that codes for tryptophan in mtDNA instead of serving as a stop codon.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AGA and AGG are not described as initiation codons; in mtDNA they terminate translation.

questions.stem: A study finds that mitochondrial DNA accumulates mutations at about 10 times the rate of the nuclear genome. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Histone packaging of mtDNA leaves it more accessible to mutagens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Limited DNA repair mechanisms combined with exposure to reactive oxygen species

choices.label: C
choices.text: Linear structure of mtDNA exposes unprotected chromosome ends

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replication of mtDNA is tightly coupled to each round of mitosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: The much larger size of the mitochondrial genome offers more targets

explanation.summary: mtDNA mutates faster because it lacks the nuclear DNA repair machinery and is damaged by ROS generated by mitochondrial reactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mtDNA mutation rate is 10 times higher than that of the nuclear genome because of the lack of DNA repair mechanisms compared with what is found within the nucleus, and because of damage by reactive oxygen species (ROS), which are common byproducts of mitochondrial reactions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: mtDNA does not use histones at all, so histone packaging cannot explain its mutation rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mitochondrial genome is circular, not linear, so exposed chromosome ends are not a factor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitochondrial division and mtDNA replication are somewhat independent of cell division; coupling to mitosis is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mitochondrial genome is tiny (16,569 base pairs versus 3.3 billion in the nuclear genome), so genome size does not account for a higher mutation rate.

questions.stem: A cell biologist observes that mitochondria within a cultured cardiomyocyte divide, and sometimes fuse, without the cell itself dividing. Which of the following best explains why mitochondrial division can be somewhat independent of cell division?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mitochondrion may hold multiple mtDNA copies, whereas the cell holds one copy of its genome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mitochondria divide by mitosis, borrowing the host cell's own spindle apparatus and centrosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mitochondrial division proceeds without any replication of the mtDNA it contains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitochondrial fusion is prohibited once a cell exits the cell cycle permanently

choices.label: E
choices.text: The number of mitochondria in each cell is fixed at birth and cannot change thereafter

explanation.summary: Multiple mtDNA copies per mitochondrion allow mitochondria to divide by binary fission independently of the cell cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: There may be multiple copies of mtDNA per mitochondrion, while a cell has only one copy of its genome. This is why mitochondrial division is somewhat independent of cell division. Mitochondria divide by prokaryotic binary fission, with division coordinated with mtDNA replication because mitochondria require mtDNA for proper function, and they can divide and fuse as needed depending on the cell's energy needs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitochondria divide by prokaryotic binary fission, not by mitosis, and do not use the cell's spindle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Because mitochondria require mtDNA for proper function, division is coordinated with mtDNA replication rather than occurring without it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitochondria can fuse as needed in response to energy demands; fusion is not restricted by cell-cycle status.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mitochondria divide and fuse as needed depending on the cell's energy needs, so their number is not fixed.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man is evaluated for a progressive neurodegenerative condition. His neurologist mentions that higher mitochondrial DNA mutation rates have been associated with the development of certain disorders. Which of the following pairs of diseases is associated with elevated mtDNA mutation rates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cystic fibrosis and sickle cell disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duchenne muscular dystrophy and myotonic dystrophy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease

explanation.summary: Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease have been associated with higher mtDNA mutation rates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond the classic mtDNA syndromes (MELAS, LHON, MERRF), the development of some diseases, such as Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease, has been associated with higher mtDNA mutation rates. This fits the preferential vulnerability of the high-energy-demand central nervous system to mitochondrial dysfunction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cystic fibrosis and sickle cell disease are single-gene nuclear disorders, not conditions associated with elevated mtDNA mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Duchenne and myotonic dystrophy are nuclear-gene muscle disorders not linked in the brick to mtDNA mutation rates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease are bleeding disorders unrelated to mtDNA mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos are connective tissue disorders with no described association with mtDNA mutation rates.

questions.stem: Mitochondrial disease refers to a broad range of disorders because impaired oxidative phosphorylation can affect nearly every organ. Which of the following organ-manifestation pairs is correctly matched?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood - Fanconi's syndrome (aminoaciduria)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Colon - diabetes mellitus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heart - Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Kidney - Pearson's marrow-pancreas syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pancreas - intestinal pseudo-obstruction

explanation.summary: Cardiac manifestations of mitochondrial disease include conduction disorders, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, and cardiomyopathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because ATP from oxidative phosphorylation supplies every organ, mitochondrial disease produces organ-specific manifestations: in the heart these are conduction disorder, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome, and cardiomyopathy. Other organ pairings include kidney (Fanconi's syndrome, glomerulopathy), blood (Pearson's syndrome), pancreas (diabetes mellitus), colon (pseudo-obstruction), inner ear (sensorineural hearing loss), liver (hepatopathy), and eye (optic neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, retinopathy).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fanconi's syndrome is a renal manifestation; the blood manifestation is Pearson's syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diabetes mellitus reflects pancreatic involvement; the colon manifests as pseudo-obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pearson's syndrome is the hematologic (blood) manifestation; the kidney manifestations are Fanconi's syndrome and glomerulopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pseudo-obstruction is the colonic manifestation; the pancreatic manifestation is diabetes mellitus.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with a known mtDNA mutation and stroke-like episodes develops polyuria with glycosuria, phosphaturia, and generalized aminoaciduria, reflecting proximal tubular dysfunction. Which of the following manifestations of mitochondrial disease does this represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diabetes mellitus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fanconi's syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glomerulopathy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatopathy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pearson's syndrome

explanation.summary: Renal Fanconi's syndrome is a recognized kidney manifestation of mitochondrial disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitochondrial disease can affect the kidney, producing Fanconi's syndrome or glomerulopathy. Proximal tubular wasting of glucose, phosphate, and amino acids in a child with an mtDNA mutation and stroke-like episodes represents the Fanconi's syndrome manifestation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diabetes mellitus is the pancreatic manifestation; glycosuria here occurs with phosphaturia and aminoaciduria from tubular dysfunction, not from hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glomerulopathy is the other renal manifestation but reflects glomerular rather than proximal tubular dysfunction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatopathy is the liver manifestation and would not present with tubular wasting of solutes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pearson's syndrome is the blood (hematologic) manifestation of mitochondrial disease, not a renal tubular disorder.

questions.stem: Genetic testing in a 9-year-old with progressive ataxia shows homozygous GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions of about 900 repeats in intron 1 of the FXN gene. Which of the following best describes the molecular consequence of this expansion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A frameshift producing a truncated, unstable frataxin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accelerated degradation of normally synthesized frataxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: An elongated frataxin protein with a toxic gain of function

choices.label: D
choices.text: Disrupted transcription of FXN leading to frataxin deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of frataxin import across the mitochondrial membranes

explanation.summary: The intronic GAA expansion disrupts FXN transcription, causing a deficiency of frataxin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The trinucleotide GAA repeat expansion in intron 1 disrupts transcription of FXN, leading to deficiency of the protein frataxin in those with FRDA. Because frataxin is crucial for mitochondrial iron metabolism and homeostasis, its deficiency underlies the ataxia and cardiomyopathy. Clinical severity correlates with the length of the expansion, as assessed by age of onset, rate of progression, or amount of residual frataxin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Frameshift deletions and point mutations are seen only in the ~4% of patients who are compound heterozygous, and the intronic expansion itself does not shift the reading frame.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FRDA reflects reduced synthesis from impaired transcription rather than accelerated breakdown of a normal protein.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The expansion sits in an intron and reduces transcription; it does not add residues to the protein or create a toxic gain of function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The defect is in the amount of frataxin produced, not in its transport into mitochondria.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with MELAS is brought to the emergency department with vomiting, abdominal pain, profound fatigue, muscle weakness, and difficulty breathing. Which of the following best accounts for this constellation of symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Buildup of lactic acid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expansion of GAA repeats in a nuclear gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homoplasmic mutant mtDNA in optic neurons

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron accumulation from frataxin deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of cytochrome C from mitochondria

explanation.summary: Lactic acid buildup in MELAS causes vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, muscle weakness, and dyspnea.
explanation.whyCorrect: MELAS is a mitochondrial myopathy that presents with myopathy, lactic acidosis, and CNS symptoms. The buildup of lactic acid in MELAS patients can lead to vomiting, abdominal pain, fatigue, muscle weakness, and difficulty breathing, which is exactly this boy's presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GAA repeat expansion in FXN causes Friedreich ataxia, a nuclear disorder unrelated to MELAS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A high mutant load in optic neurons is the requirement for vision loss in LHON, not the cause of these systemic symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Frataxin deficiency and disturbed iron homeostasis underlie Friedreich ataxia, not the acute symptoms of MELAS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytochrome C release triggers apoptosis of individual cells; it does not explain systemic vomiting, abdominal pain, and dyspnea.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated for dilated cardiomyopathy, progressive hearing loss, and new psychiatric symptoms. She has no myoclonus, seizures, myopathy, or ataxia. Several maternal relatives carry a diagnosis of MERRF. Which of the following mutations is most likely responsible for her presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A8344G in MT-TK

choices.label: B
choices.text: G8363A in MT-TK

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygous GAA expansion in FXN

choices.label: D
choices.text: MT-ND4 mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: MT-ND6 mutation

explanation.summary: The G8363A MT-TK mutation produces cardiomyopathy, hearing loss, and psychiatric symptoms without the other typical features of MERRF.
explanation.whyCorrect: Three mutations in the tRNA lysine gene MT-TK (A8344G, T8356C, G8363A) are associated with MERRF. The G8363A mutation specifically is associated with cardiomyopathy, hearing loss, and psychiatric symptoms with no other typical features of MERRF, matching this woman's presentation in a MERRF family.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A8344G is the mutation associated with the classic MERRF picture of myoclonus, seizures, myopathy, and cerebellar ataxia, which this patient lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A homozygous FXN GAA expansion causes Friedreich ataxia, an autosomal recessive disorder that would not track through maternal relatives with MERRF.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MT-ND4 mutations cause LHON, which presents with sudden painless bilateral vision loss, not cardiomyopathy with psychiatric symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MT-ND6 is another LHON gene affecting the optic nerve, not the MERRF-associated tRNA lysine gene.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with MERRF undergoes muscle biopsy, and quantitative analysis of the MT-TK A8344G mutation is performed on the muscle tissue. Which of the following best describes the relationship between the mutation level and the clinical picture in MERRF?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clinical severity is independent of the mutant load in any tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: High mutation levels of 80 to 90 percent in muscle correlate with symptom severity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mutation levels below 10 percent in muscle produce the most severe disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mutation levels in peripheral blood, not muscle, best predict severity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Symptoms appear only when the mutation reaches 100 percent in muscle

explanation.summary: In MERRF, mutant loads of 80 to 90 percent in muscle correlate with the severity of clinical symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: In most cases of MERRF, high mutation levels (80 to 90 percent) in the muscle correlate with severity of clinical symptoms. This is a concrete example of the threshold effect: the proportion of mutant mtDNA within a tissue determines the expressivity, or severity, of the disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The proportion of mutant mtDNA determines expressivity; severity is not independent of mutant load.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low mutant loads fall below the phenotypic threshold and are associated with milder or absent symptoms, not the most severe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick correlates severity with the mutation level in muscle, the tissue that shows ragged red fibers, not with blood levels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Symptoms correlate with high but not necessarily homoplasmic (100 percent) mutant loads; 80 to 90 percent is the level cited.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman develops sudden, painless loss of vision in both eyes. Testing confirms a pathogenic MT-ND4 mutation. Her brother lost his vision from the same mutation at age 20. Compared with affected males, females who develop LHON typically do which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Account for about 90 percent of affected patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: Are always homoplasmic whereas affected males are heteroplasmic

choices.label: C
choices.text: Are unable to transmit the mutation to their children

choices.label: D
choices.text: Present earlier in life with milder visual loss

choices.label: E
choices.text: Present later in life and are often more severely affected

explanation.summary: Women with LHON develop vision loss later in life and are often more severely affected than men.
explanation.whyCorrect: LHON typically presents in the 2nd or 3rd decade of life, with 90 percent of affected patients being male. Females can develop LHON later in life and are often more severely affected, as in this 47-year-old whose brother presented in his 20s.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 90 percent of affected patients are male, so females account for only a minority of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both sexes must be homoplasmic or carry a very high mutant load in optic neurons to be at risk; the brick describes no sex difference in plasmy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondrial mutations are transmitted only through the mother, so affected females can pass the mutation to their children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Females present later, not earlier, and tend to be more severely rather than more mildly affected.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old asymptomatic man learns that his maternal uncle and his mother's cousin lost their vision in early adulthood from Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. He carries the same MT-ND1 mutation. Which of the following best describes what is required for him to be at risk of developing vision loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mutant load of roughly 30 percent of the mtDNA within his optic neurons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any detectable level of heteroplasmy for the MT-ND1 mutation in his blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Co-inheritance of a nuclear FXN GAA repeat expansion on at least one allele of chromosome 9

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homoplasmy for the mutation or a very high proportion of mutant mtDNA within optic neurons

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inheritance of a second, paternally derived mtDNA mutation in the same gene

explanation.summary: Risk of LHON requires homoplasmy for the mutation or a very high percentage of mutant mtDNA in the optic neurons.
explanation.whyCorrect: To be at risk for developing LHON, one must be homoplasmic for the LHON mutation or have a very high percentage of mutant mtDNA within the optic neurons. Mutations in MT-ND1, MT-ND4, MT-ND4L, or MT-ND6 can cause the disease, and vision loss occurs when optic nerve cells die from mitochondrial dysfunction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 30 percent heteroplasmic load is depicted as a non-disease state; a very high mutant proportion is needed in optic neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low-level heteroplasmy falls below the phenotypic threshold; risk requires homoplasmy or a very high mutant proportion in the affected neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FXN expansions cause Friedreich ataxia, a nuclear autosomal recessive disorder, and play no role in LHON risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only oocytes contribute mitochondria, so no paternally derived mtDNA mutation can be inherited.

questions.stem: Mitochondrial diseases can arise from mutations in electron transport chain proteins or in mitochondrial tRNAs. Which of the following correctly contrasts the molecular lesions underlying Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: LHON: mutation in a mitochondrial rRNA gene; MERRF: nuclear gene mutation affecting iron homeostasis

choices.label: B
choices.text: LHON: mutation in nuclear-encoded OXPHOS subunits; MERRF: mutation in a mitochondrial rRNA gene

choices.label: C
choices.text: LHON: mutation in protein-encoding genes such as MT-ND1 or MT-ND4; MERRF: mutation in the tRNA lysine gene MT-TK

choices.label: D
choices.text: LHON: mutation in the tRNA lysine gene; MERRF: mutation in a complex I protein-encoding gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: LHON: nuclear FXN repeat expansion; MERRF: mtDNA protein-encoding gene mutation

explanation.summary: LHON results from mutations in mtDNA protein-encoding genes (MT-ND1, MT-ND4, MT-ND4L, MT-ND6), whereas MERRF results from mutations in the tRNA lysine gene MT-TK.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mitochondrial diseases can be caused by mutations in electron transport chain proteins or tRNAs. LHON is caused by mutations in the MT-ND1, MT-ND4, MT-ND4L, or MT-ND6 genes, which are among the 13 mtDNA protein-encoding OXPHOS subunit genes. MERRF, in contrast, is caused by three particular mutations (A8344G, T8356C, G8363A) in the tRNA lysine gene MT-TK, one of the 22 mtDNA tRNA genes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither disease involves an rRNA gene, and the nuclear iron-homeostasis defect describes frataxin deficiency in Friedreich ataxia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LHON genes are mtDNA-encoded, not nuclear, and MERRF involves a tRNA gene rather than an rRNA gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the pairing: the tRNA lysine gene mutations belong to MERRF and the protein-encoding MT-ND mutations to LHON.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The FXN repeat expansion causes Friedreich ataxia, not LHON; and MERRF involves a tRNA gene rather than a protein-encoding gene.

questions.stem: A woman whose blood cells carry roughly 50 percent mutant mtDNA has three children. Testing shows mutant loads of 10 percent, 45 percent, and 85 percent in the children, and only the child with 85 percent is symptomatic. Which of the following best explains the differing mutant loads among the siblings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Independent de novo GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions arising in each child

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parent-of-origin genomic imprinting of the mtDNA inherited from the mother

choices.label: C
choices.text: Random assortment of mtDNA among mitochondria and of mitochondria among daughter cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random X-inactivation in each embryo skewing the expression of mtDNA genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Variable paternal contribution of sperm mitochondria to each zygote at the time of fertilization

explanation.summary: Random segregation of mtDNA and mitochondria during cell division produces different mutant loads in different cells and offspring.
explanation.whyCorrect: A hallmark of mitochondrial disease is variable transmission and presentation. When cells divide, mtDNA replicates and randomly assorts among mitochondria, and these mitochondria then randomly assort among daughter cells. Some cells end up homoplasmic (all normal or all mutant) while others are heteroplasmic at varying proportions, and the proportion of mutant mtDNA determines the expressivity of the disease, so only the child above the threshold is symptomatic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GAA repeat expansions are the nuclear lesion of Friedreich ataxia and do not explain varying mtDNA heteroplasmy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Genomic imprinting refers to parent-of-origin expression of nuclear genes and does not govern mtDNA proportions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: X-inactivation involves silencing one X chromosome and has nothing to do with mtDNA distribution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only oocytes contribute mitochondria to offspring, so paternal contribution cannot vary the mutant load.

questions.stem: A patient with a single pathogenic mtDNA point mutation has an identical 60 percent mutant load in both cerebral neurons and dermal fibroblasts. The neurons show impaired ATP synthesis and the patient has seizures, yet the fibroblasts function normally. Which component of the phenotypic threshold model best explains this discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The number of mtDNA copies contained in each mitochondrion

choices.label: B
choices.text: The presence of protective histones on the mitochondrial genome itself

choices.label: C
choices.text: The relative abundance of the mutant mtDNA in each tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reliance of the organ system on mitochondrial ATP production

choices.label: E
choices.text: The severity of the pathogenic mtDNA point mutation

explanation.summary: The threshold model weighs mutation severity, mutation abundance, and how dependent an organ is on mitochondrial ATP; tissue dependence explains why identical loads produce different outcomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The phenotypic threshold effect model takes into account the severity of the mutation, the relative abundance of the mutation, and the reliance of an organ system on mitochondrial ATP production. Mitochondrial diseases manifest only after ATP production falls below the level, or threshold, required by the system. With the same mutation and the same 60 percent load in both tissues, only the third factor, the greater reliance of neurons on mitochondrial ATP, distinguishes the two.

whyWrongByChoice.A: mtDNA copy number per mitochondrion explains why mitochondrial division is independent of cell division; it is not a component of the threshold model.
whyWrongByChoice.B: mtDNA does not use histones, and histones play no role in the threshold model.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The relative abundance of the mutation is the same 60 percent in both tissues and therefore does not explain the discrepancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mutation is identical in both tissues, so mutation severity cannot account for the difference between them.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with longstanding insulin resistance is found to have an increased burden of mtDNA mutations and reduced mitochondrial function in skeletal muscle. Which of the following best describes the proposed mechanism linking his insulin resistance to mitochondrial damage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic hyperglycemia progressively expands GAA repeats within intron 1 of the FXN gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating insulin directly inhibits complex I of the mitochondrial electron transport chain in muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inefficient glucose metabolism increases production of reactive oxygen species that mutate mtDNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insulin resistance halts mtDNA replication so that mitochondria can no longer divide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin resistance triggers cytochrome C release and widespread myocyte apoptosis

explanation.summary: Insulin resistance causes inefficient glucose metabolism, raising ROS production and thereby increasing mtDNA mutations and mitochondrial dysfunction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recent studies have linked various mitochondrial defects with insulin resistance. Insulin resistance leads to inefficient glucose metabolism, which results in increased production of ROS; this increased ROS production leads to increased mtDNA mutations and mitochondrial dysfunction. It remains uncertain whether mitochondrial dysfunction is a cause or a result of insulin resistance, but the two are connected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GAA repeat expansion in FXN is the inherited nuclear lesion of Friedreich ataxia and is not induced by hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The described link runs through ROS from inefficient glucose metabolism, not through direct inhibition of complex I by insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin resistance is not described as arresting mtDNA replication or mitochondrial division.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytochrome C release is the mitochondrial trigger for apoptosis; it is not the proposed mechanism linking insulin resistance to mtDNA mutation.

questions.stem: Sequencing of muscle mtDNA from an 80-year-old woman without known mitochondrial disease reveals substantially more mutant mtDNA than sequencing from a 20-year-old. Which of the following best explains the age-related accumulation of mutant mtDNA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Age-related conversion of the mitochondrial genome from circular to linear

choices.label: B
choices.text: Age-related shift of UGA from a tryptophan codon to a stop codon

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing paternal mitochondrial contribution over the lifespan

choices.label: D
choices.text: Natural loss of protective mechanisms against reactive oxygen species with age

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progressive loss of histones from mtDNA with age

explanation.summary: We naturally lose ROS protective mechanisms and therefore accumulate mutant mtDNA as we age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reactive oxygen species are common byproducts of mitochondrial reactions and damage mtDNA, which already has limited repair mechanisms. We naturally lose ROS protective mechanisms, and therefore accumulate mutant mtDNA, as we age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The mitochondrial genome remains circular throughout life; no age-related linearization occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The mitochondrial genetic code is fixed; UGA codes for tryptophan in mtDNA regardless of age.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondria are contributed only by the oocyte; there is no paternal contribution at any point.
whyWrongByChoice.E: mtDNA does not use histones at any age, so their loss cannot explain mutation accumulation.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with unsteady posture, frequent falls, and progressive difficulty walking undergoes FXN testing. One allele carries an expansion of about 800 GAA repeats in intron 1; the other allele carries a nonsense point mutation with no expansion. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has Friedreich ataxia through the less common genotype seen in about 4 percent of patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is an unaffected carrier because only one of his alleles carries a GAA repeat expansion

choices.label: C
choices.text: The findings exclude Friedreich ataxia, which requires homozygous GAA expansions on both alleles

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nonsense mutation confers a toxic gain of function on the frataxin protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: The point mutation alone would cause disease even with a completely normal second allele

explanation.summary: About 4 percent of FRDA patients carry a point mutation or frameshift deletion on one FXN allele and an expanded GAA repeat on the other.
explanation.whyCorrect: FRDA most commonly (96 percent of patients) results from homozygous inheritance of FXN alleles containing GAA expansions of 66 to 1500 repeats; normal alleles have fewer than 36 repeats. The remaining 4 percent of patients carry a point mutation (nonsense, missense) or a frameshift deletion in one FXN allele and an expanded GAA repeat on the other. This boy, with typical onset between 5 and 15 years, has that compound genotype and therefore has FRDA. The disease affects about 1 in 50,000 to 100,000 individuals in the USA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: His second allele is not normal; it carries a nonsense mutation, so he has two abnormal alleles and is affected, not a carrier.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Homozygous expansion is the most common but not the only genotype; an expansion plus a point mutation also causes FRDA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FRDA results from deficient or non-functional frataxin, a loss of function, not a toxic gain of function.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FRDA is autosomal recessive, so a single mutant allele with a normal partner allele would not produce disease.

questions.stem: Two unrelated children are diagnosed with Friedreich ataxia. Patient 1 carries FXN alleles with 200 and 900 GAA repeats; Patient 2 carries alleles with 700 and 900 GAA repeats. Which of the following best predicts their relative clinical courses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neither can be predicted, because severity depends only on point mutation type

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patient 1 will have earlier onset, because a shorter allele yields more residual frataxin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patient 1 will have earlier onset, because the total number of repeats determines severity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patient 2 will have earlier onset, because severity tracks the length of the shorter allele

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their courses will be identical, because their longer alleles are the same length

explanation.summary: FRDA severity correlates with GAA expansion length, particularly on the shorter of the two alleles.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical severity of FRDA correlates with the length of the GAA expansion, particularly on the shorter of the two alleles, as assessed by age of onset, rate of progression, or amount of residual frataxin. Patient 2's shorter allele (700 repeats) is much longer than Patient 1's (200 repeats), so Patient 2 is expected to have earlier onset and faster progression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neither patient has a point mutation; both have the common homozygous-expansion genotype, and repeat length predicts severity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A shorter allele does allow more residual frataxin, but that predicts milder, later-onset disease for Patient 1, not earlier onset.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Severity is driven particularly by the shorter allele rather than by the sum of both alleles, and Patient 1 has the shorter of the short alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Matching longer alleles do not equalize severity; the shorter allele is the more informative determinant.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated for obesity and difficulty walking. At birth she had poor muscle tone and difficulty feeding. She now has a voracious appetite, and her family has locked the refrigerator to control her intake. Her BMI is 39, and she has mild intellectual impairment and hypogonadism. Which of the following best describes the underlying genetic abnormality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypomethylation of the paternal ICR1 at 11p15

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of maternally expressed UBE3A at the 15q11-q13 region

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of paternally expressed genes at the 15q11-q13 region

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trisomy 21

explanation.summary: Infantile hypotonia and feeding difficulty followed by childhood hyperphagia, obesity, and hypogonadism is the classic course of Prader-Willi syndrome, caused by loss of paternal gene expression at 15q11-q13.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of paternally expressed genes (including SNRPN) in the 15q11-q13 region, most often from paternal microdeletion or maternal uniparental disomy. Because the maternal copy of this region is normally imprinted (silenced), absence of the paternal contribution leaves the genes unexpressed, producing the characteristic biphasic feeding pattern and obesity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypomethylation of paternal ICR1 at 11p15 lowers IGF2 and causes Silver-Russell syndrome, a growth-restriction disorder, the opposite of this child's obesity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of maternal UBE3A at 15q11-q13 causes Angelman syndrome, which presents with severe developmental delay, ataxia, seizures, and a happy demeanor, not obesity and hyperphagia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 dysregulates PLAGL1 and causes transient neonatal diabetes, not Prader-Willi syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is an aneuploidy, not an imprinting disorder, and does not produce this hypotonia-then-hyperphagia course.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has severe intellectual disability with essentially absent speech. He is noted to be unusually happy, laughs and smiles frequently, and displays hand-flapping movements. He has microcephaly, ataxia, and a history of seizures. Which gene is most likely responsible for his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IGF2

choices.label: B
choices.text: PLAGL1

choices.label: C
choices.text: SNRPN

choices.label: D
choices.text: UBE3A

choices.label: E
choices.text: ZFP57

explanation.summary: Happy demeanor with frequent laughter, minimal speech, ataxia, microcephaly, and seizures is Angelman syndrome, caused by loss of maternally expressed UBE3A.
explanation.whyCorrect: Angelman syndrome is caused by loss of maternal expression of UBE3A in the 15q11-q13 region. UBE3A encodes a ubiquitin ligase responsible for protein degradation in neurons and is paternally imprinted, so only the maternal allele is expressed in the brain; loss of that allele produces the neurodevelopmental phenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IGF2 dysregulation at 11p15 causes Silver-Russell syndrome (growth restriction) or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (overgrowth), not this happy-puppet phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PLAGL1 at 6q24 is associated with transient neonatal diabetes mellitus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SNRPN loss of paternal expression causes Prader-Willi syndrome, characterized by hypotonia, hyperphagia, and obesity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ZFP57 is a methylation-sensitive transcription factor implicated in maintaining imprints and in cancer, not in Angelman syndrome.

questions.stem: A family has multiple members affected by Angelman syndrome. Pedigree analysis shows that unaffected fathers who carry a UBE3A mutation have affected children, whereas unaffected mothers who carry the same mutation do not have affected children. Which of the following best explains this inheritance pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The phenotype depends on mitochondrial inheritance from the mother

choices.label: B
choices.text: UBE3A follows classic autosomal dominant Mendelian inheritance

choices.label: C
choices.text: UBE3A is maternally imprinted, so only a paternally transmitted mutation causes disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: UBE3A is paternally imprinted, so only a maternally transmitted mutation causes disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: UBE3A is X-linked recessive

explanation.summary: For UBE3A the paternal allele is imprinted (silenced) and the maternal allele is expressed, so a UBE3A mutation causes Angelman syndrome only when inherited from the mother.
explanation.whyCorrect: Imprinting disorders do not follow typical Mendelian inheritance; the phenotype appears only when the deficient allele is transmitted by the parent whose allele is normally expressed. Because UBE3A is paternally imprinted (maternally expressed), a mutation causes disease only when inherited from the mother, so an unaffected carrier father can transmit disease to his children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mitochondrial inheritance would produce maternal transmission of disease, whereas here it is the carrier father who transmits the affected phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Classic autosomal dominant inheritance would produce disease regardless of the transmitting parent's sex, which is not observed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the imprint. If UBE3A were maternally imprinted, paternal transmission would cause disease, which contradicts the pedigree.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UBE3A is on chromosome 15, not the X chromosome, and the pattern is not X-linked recessive.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy has severe intrauterine and postnatal growth restriction with a relatively large-appearing head, a triangular face with prominent forehead, body asymmetry with one leg longer than the other, and clinodactyly of the fifth finger. Molecular testing points to an abnormality at chromosome 11p15. Which of the following is the most likely molecular defect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Duplication of 6q24

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypermethylation of the paternal 11p15 region, increasing IGF2 expression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypomethylation of the paternal ICR1, reducing IGF2 expression

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paternal deletion of 15q11-q13

explanation.summary: Severe growth restriction with a triangular face and body asymmetry is Silver-Russell syndrome, most often caused by hypomethylation of the paternal ICR1 at 11p15 that reduces IGF2.
explanation.whyCorrect: ICR1 is normally methylated only on the paternal allele near the paternally expressed IGF2 gene. Hypomethylation of the paternal ICR1 allows an insulator protein to bind and block enhancers from activating IGF2, reducing IGF2 (a growth factor) expression and producing the growth-restricted Silver-Russell phenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Duplication of 6q24 is associated with transient neonatal diabetes, not Silver-Russell syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypermethylation of paternal 11p15 increases IGF2 and causes Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, an overgrowth disorder, not growth restriction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 causes Prader-Willi syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome, not a growth-restriction disorder with triangular facies.

questions.stem: A newborn is noted to have a very large tongue, an umbilical hernia, and episodes of hypoglycemia, and he is large for gestational age. Genetic evaluation reveals an epigenetic abnormality of the 11p15 region. Which of the following molecular findings is most consistent with this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypermethylation of the paternal 11p15 region

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypomethylation of the paternal ICR1 at 11p15

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of maternal expression at 15q11-q13

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of paternal expression at 15q11-q13

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trinucleotide repeat expansion

explanation.summary: Macroglossia, umbilical hernia, hypoglycemia, and overgrowth describe Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, which in a subset of patients arises from hypermethylation of the paternal 11p15 region.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is an overgrowth syndrome; in about 5-10% of patients it is caused by hypermethylation of the 11p15 region on the paternal allele. This aberrant hypermethylation dysregulates the IGF2/H19 locus and drives excess growth, giving macroglossia, abdominal wall defects, and neonatal hypoglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypomethylation of paternal ICR1 reduces IGF2 and causes Silver-Russell syndrome, a growth-restriction disorder, not overgrowth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of maternal expression at 15q11-q13 causes Angelman syndrome, unrelated to macroglossia and overgrowth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of paternal expression at 15q11-q13 causes Prader-Willi syndrome, which features hypotonia and later obesity, not neonatal overgrowth with macroglossia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trinucleotide repeat expansion causes disorders such as fragile X or Huntington disease, not this imprinting-related overgrowth syndrome.

questions.stem: A full-term neonate is small for gestational age and develops hyperglycemia requiring insulin during the first weeks of life. The diabetes resolves spontaneously by 3 months of age. The child is at increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes later in life. Which of the following imprinted loci is most likely involved?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PLAGL1 at 6q24

choices.label: B
choices.text: IGF2 at 11p15

choices.label: C
choices.text: UBE3A at 15q11-q13

choices.label: D
choices.text: SNRPN at 15q11-q13

choices.label: E
choices.text: H19 at 11p15

explanation.summary: Low birth weight with neonatal diabetes that resolves by about 3 months is transient neonatal diabetes mellitus, linked to dysregulation of PLAGL1 at the 6q24 locus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transient neonatal diabetes is associated with paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6, duplication of 6q24, or hypomethylation of the 6q24 imprinting control region, all leading to dysregulation of PLAGL1. About 50% of cases resolve spontaneously after roughly 3 months, though these patients remain at higher risk of later type 2 diabetes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IGF2 at 11p15 is linked to Silver-Russell and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes, not transient neonatal diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: UBE3A at 15q11-q13 is the Angelman syndrome gene and is not associated with neonatal diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: SNRPN at 15q11-q13 is associated with Prader-Willi syndrome; the type 2 diabetes there appears with childhood obesity, not as transient neonatal diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: H19 at 11p15 is part of the IGF2/H19 imprinted domain related to 11p15 syndromes, not to the 6q24 transient neonatal diabetes locus.

questions.stem: A geneticist wants a single first-line test that can simultaneously detect an abnormal epigenetic mark, copy number variations, and uniparental disomy within known imprinted regions, and can indicate which parental allele is affected. Which of the following techniques is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) of patient genomic DNA alone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with locus-specific probes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Karyotyping of cultured peripheral blood lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methylation-sensitive multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole-genome sequencing at high read depth across the genome

explanation.summary: MS-MLPA is the most widely used first-line test for imprinting disorders because it detects abnormal methylation, CNVs, and UPD and, being probe-dependent, can indicate the affected parental allele.
explanation.whyCorrect: MS-MLPA detects abnormal DNA methylation patterns on selected regions, copy number variations, and uniparental disomy in known imprinted regions in a single assay. Because it is probe-dependent, it can distinguish which parental allele is affected, making it the preferred first-line diagnostic test.

whyWrongByChoice.A: aCGH identifies CNVs across the genome but does not provide information about parental origin or methylation status, so further analysis is required.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FISH can confirm a deletion but does not detect methylation abnormalities or uniparental disomy and does not distinguish parental origin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyotyping detects large structural or numerical chromosomal changes but cannot detect the methylation defects or UPD central to imprinting disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Whole-genome (and exome) sequencing is not well-suited for identifying imprinting disorders because it does not readily assess methylation or parental origin.

questions.stem: A researcher is studying how a specific cis-acting DNA sequence establishes parent-of-origin gene silencing at an imprinted locus. This sequence lies within a CpG island near a gene promoter. Which of the following molecular events at this region most directly leads to silencing of the associated gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A point mutation changing the coding sequence of the gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetylation of histones opening the chromatin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deletion of the entire chromosome arm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insertion of a trinucleotide repeat in the coding region

choices.label: E
choices.text: Methylation of cytosine residues

explanation.summary: Imprinting control regions lie within CpG islands, and methylation of their cytosine residues silences the associated gene without changing the DNA sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Correct imprinted expression depends on an imprinting control region (ICR), often located within a CpG island near a promoter. CpG islands are usually unmethylated to allow expression; when the ICR becomes methylated at cytosine residues, the gene is silenced. This is an epigenetic mark that alters chromatin compaction rather than the DNA sequence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A point mutation changes the DNA sequence and is not the epigenetic, parent-of-origin mechanism of imprinting-based silencing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Histone acetylation opens chromatin and promotes expression rather than silencing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deletion of a chromosome arm is a large structural change affecting many genes, not the specific methylation-based silencing of an ICR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Trinucleotide repeat insertion is the mechanism of repeat-expansion disorders, not of imprinting control region silencing.

questions.stem: During normal development, imprinting marks inherited by an embryo must be reset so that each new gamete carries sex-appropriate imprints. At which stage does the genome-wide erasure and re-establishment of imprinting marks primarily occur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During each round of mitosis in adult tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: During gametogenesis in primordial germ cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: During implantation of the blastocyst

choices.label: D
choices.text: In terminally differentiated somatic cells throughout life

choices.label: E
