choices.text: Only after birth during puberty

explanation.summary: Imprints are erased and rewritten during gametogenesis in primordial germ cells, when new sex-specific imprints are established.
explanation.whyCorrect: During gametogenesis, primordial germ cells undergo genome-wide demethylation that erases existing imprints, and new maternal or paternal imprints are then established in a sex-specific manner in developing gametes. These new marks are preserved through fertilization even during the waves of genome-wide demethylation that follow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Imprints are stably maintained through mitosis in adult tissues, not reset with each division.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imprints are already established in the gametes before fertilization; implantation is not when erasure and rewriting occur.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatic cells maintain the imprints inherited from the zygote; they do not erase and rewrite them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Imprint resetting occurs in germ cells during gametogenesis, not specifically at puberty.

questions.stem: A child with a clinical imprinting disorder is found to have inherited both copies of a chromosome from a single parent, with no deletion or point mutation identified. This abnormal gene dosage of imprinted genes explains the phenotype. Which of the following mechanisms best describes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Balanced reciprocal translocation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nondisjunction producing viable trisomy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Robertsonian fusion of acrocentric chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Somatic mosaicism for a coding mutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniparental disomy

explanation.summary: Inheriting both copies of a chromosome from one parent is uniparental disomy, a major cause of imprinting syndromes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Uniparental disomy (UPD) occurs when both copies of a chromosome come from one parent, often as a rescue event after abnormal chromosome segregation would otherwise cause a lethal aneuploidy. For imprinted genes, UPD directly alters gene dosage of the parent-of-origin-expressed allele and leads to disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A balanced reciprocal translocation exchanges segments between chromosomes without loss or gain of material and does not describe inheriting both copies from one parent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Viable trisomy involves three copies of a chromosome, not two copies from a single parent with normal total number.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A Robertsonian fusion joins two acrocentric chromosomes and is a structural rearrangement, not the parent-of-origin dosage abnormality described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatic mosaicism for a coding mutation involves a DNA sequence change in a subset of cells, not uniparental inheritance of a chromosome.

questions.stem: Two infants each have a documented 15q11-q13 microdeletion. One has Prader-Willi syndrome and the other has Angelman syndrome. Beyond identifying the deletion, which additional test is most useful to determine which parental allele is affected and thereby distinguish the two disorders?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete blood count

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microsatellite or SNP analysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repeat karyotyping

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequencing of an unrelated housekeeping gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum growth hormone level

explanation.summary: Because Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes involve the same 15q11-q13 region but opposite parental alleles, parental-origin testing such as microsatellite or SNP analysis (or DNA methylation analysis) is needed to distinguish them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microsatellite or SNP analysis compares the child's polymorphic markers to those of both parents, revealing the parental origin of the affected allele and detecting uniparental disomy. This distinguishes Prader-Willi (loss of paternal expression) from Angelman (loss of maternal expression), since the deletion alone does not indicate which parent's allele is involved.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A complete blood count is unrelated to identifying parental allele origin in an imprinting disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyotyping, like the initial detection, shows the deletion but cannot determine parental origin of the affected allele.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sequencing an unrelated housekeeping gene provides no information about the imprinted 15q11-q13 region or its parental origin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A growth hormone level assesses one clinical consequence and does not establish the parental origin of the genetic defect.

questions.stem: A cancer researcher observes that in many tumors the IGF2 gene loses its normal imprinting, resulting in increased IGF2 expression, and that this loss of imprinting can be detected in blood samples as a potential biomarker. Which of the following best explains the molecular basis of IGF2 loss of imprinting in these cancers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A frameshift mutation inactivating the entire IGF2 coding region

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete demethylation of all CpG islands genome-wide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deletion of the imprinted region at chromosome 6q24

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypermethylation of ICR1 leading to biallelic IGF2 expression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the maternal UBE3A allele on chromosome 15q11-13

explanation.summary: IGF2 loss of imprinting in cancer is associated with hypermethylation of ICR1, which leads to increased (effectively biallelic) IGF2 expression and can serve as a biomarker of cancer risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Loss of imprinting of IGF2 is associated with hypermethylation of ICR1 and leads to increased gene expression in the majority of cancers. Because the maternal allele normally uses unmethylated ICR1 as an insulator to keep IGF2 silent, hypermethylation abolishes this insulation and drives excess IGF2, contributing to tumorigenesis; because loss of imprinting is detectable in blood, it is a candidate biomarker.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A frameshift inactivating IGF2 would decrease IGF2 function, whereas loss of imprinting increases IGF2 expression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Genome-wide demethylation of all CpG islands is not the specific ICR1 mechanism described and would not selectively increase IGF2 through loss of imprinting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deletion of 6q24 relates to transient neonatal diabetes (PLAGL1), not IGF2 loss of imprinting in cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of the maternal UBE3A allele causes Angelman syndrome and is unrelated to IGF2 expression in tumors.

questions.stem: A genetics report describes a locus as a "maternally imprinted gene." Which of the following best describes the expression pattern of this gene in a normal somatic cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both copies are silenced until puberty

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both the maternal and paternal copies are actively expressed

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gene is expressed only in female offspring

choices.label: D
choices.text: The maternal copy is silenced and the paternal copy is expressed

choices.label: E
choices.text: The paternal copy is silenced and the maternal copy is expressed

explanation.summary: An imprinted gene is named for the parental copy that is silenced: a maternally imprinted gene has its maternal copy silenced and its paternal copy expressed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most genes are expressed from both inherited copies, but imprinted genes are expressed in a parent-of-origin-specific manner, meaning one allele is silent while the other is active. By convention, "maternally imprinted" means the maternal copy is silenced and the paternal copy is expressed; "paternally imprinted" means the paternal copy is silenced and the maternal copy is expressed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Imprints are established in the gametes and maintained throughout life; they are not a puberty-dependent silencing of both copies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Biallelic expression is the pattern of ordinary, non-imprinted genes, not of an imprinted gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imprinting is gene-specific and parent-of-origin-specific and occurs in both sexes; it does not restrict expression to female offspring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Silencing of the paternal copy with maternal expression describes a paternally imprinted gene, the opposite of the term used.

questions.stem: A student notes that both genomic imprinting and X chromosome inactivation (XCI) depend on DNA methylation and histone modifications to achieve long-term gene silencing. Which of the following features distinguishes genomic imprinting from XCI?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It occurs only in females

choices.label: B
choices.text: It relies on histone modification but not DNA methylation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It selects the silenced allele at random

choices.label: D
choices.text: It silences an entire chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: It silences specific genes according to parent of origin

explanation.summary: Imprinting is gene-specific, parent-of-origin-specific, and occurs in both sexes, whereas XCI is chromosome-wide, random, and confined to females.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both processes use DNA methylation and histone modifications for long-term silencing, but imprinting acts on individual genes and the silenced allele is determined by whether it came from the mother or the father. XCI instead inactivates one entire X chromosome chosen at random and takes place only in females.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Occurring only in females is a feature of XCI; imprinting occurs in both sexes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both DNA methylation and histone modifications contribute to silencing in both imprinting and XCI, so this does not distinguish them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Random choice of the silenced copy is characteristic of XCI; in imprinting the silenced allele is fixed by parental origin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromosome-wide silencing describes XCI; imprinting is gene-specific.

questions.stem: Advances in RNA sequencing and allele-specific expression analysis have steadily increased the number of imprinted genes identified in humans. Approximately what proportion of human protein-coding genes are currently known to be imprinted?

explanation.summary: About 228 human genes are known to be imprinted, roughly 1% of protein-coding genes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Next-generation sequencing technologies enabling RNA sequencing and allele-specific expression analysis have expanded the list of imprinted genes to approximately 228, representing about 1% of protein-coding genes in the human genome. To date, 13 imprinting disorders have been characterized, with more likely remaining uncharacterized.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.01% would correspond to only a couple of genes, far fewer than the roughly 228 known imprinted genes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 0.1% would be about 20 genes, an order of magnitude below the number identified.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 10% would be roughly 2,000 genes; while about 2,000 CpG islands are differentially methylated between oocytes and sperm, only a small subset retains allele-specific methylation and corresponds to imprinted genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A quarter of all protein-coding genes is far higher than the roughly 1% that are imprinted.

questions.stem: A research team reports the first generation of fertile mice through uniparental reproduction in mammals, using genetic material from two sperm cells. Which of the following interventions allowed the embryos to overcome this barrier?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deleting UBE3A and SNRPN from both sperm genomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Editing seven imprinting control regions in the sperm genomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypermethylating ICR1 on both sperm-derived alleles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overexpressing IGF2 throughout early embryogenesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Removing all DNA methylation from the zygote genome

explanation.summary: Fertile uniparental (two-sperm) mice were produced by genetically editing seven imprinting control regions to bypass imprinting blockages.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because both sperm genomes carry paternal imprints, an embryo made from two sperm normally cannot develop. Targeting seven imprinting control regions (ICRs) in the sperm allowed the researchers to bypass these imprinting blockages and obtain fertile mice, and the work highlighted that imprinted genes matter more in early development than in late gestation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deleting UBE3A and SNRPN would remove the Angelman and Prader-Willi genes rather than reconfigure the imprinting marks that block two-sperm development.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypermethylating ICR1 on paternal alleles would not address the multiple ICRs whose paternal-only imprints prevent two-sperm embryos from developing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IGF2 overexpression is associated with overgrowth and cancer-related loss of imprinting, not with enabling uniparental reproduction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genome-wide removal of methylation would erase all imprints rather than correct the specific ICRs that block uniparental development; imprints normally survive the waves of genome-wide demethylation after fertilization.

questions.stem: A healthy woman inherited one of her chromosome 15 homologs from her father; in her somatic cells that chromosome carries a paternal imprint at the 15q11-q13 region. When this same chromosome 15 is packaged into one of her oocytes, which of the following best describes its imprint at 15q11-q13?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It carries a maternal imprint, rewritten during her gametogenesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: It carries a random mixture of maternal and paternal marks

choices.label: C
choices.text: It carries no imprint; marks are added by the zygote after fertilization

choices.label: D
choices.text: It keeps the paternal imprint in half of her oocytes and gains a maternal one in the rest

choices.label: E
choices.text: It retains the paternal imprint because the chromosome came from her father

explanation.summary: In the egg, all imprints are rewritten as maternal imprints, even on genes that originally came from the father.
explanation.whyCorrect: During gametogenesis, primordial germ cells undergo genome-wide demethylation that erases existing imprints, and new imprints are then established in a sex-specific manner. In a woman's oocytes every chromosome, regardless of whether it was inherited from her mother or her father, receives maternal imprints; the opposite occurs in sperm, where paternal imprints are established.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Imprint establishment is sex-specific and uniform for the gamete type, not a random mix of marks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imprints are written in the developing gamete before fertilization and are then preserved; the zygote does not create them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: All of a woman's oocytes receive maternal imprints; there is no split between oocytes retaining paternal marks and those gaining maternal ones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The original parental imprint is erased in primordial germ cells; it is not carried forward according to the chromosome's ancestry.

questions.stem: A couple undergoing in vitro fertilization asks about the risk of imprinting disorders in children conceived through assisted reproductive technology (ART). Which of the following is the most accurate counseling statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The risk is about 1 in 150, roughly 100 times the general-population rate

choices.label: B
choices.text: The risk is estimated at about 2 to 5 in 15,000, and the reason remains unclear

choices.label: C
choices.text: The risk is increased and has been proven to result from embryo culture conditions

choices.label: D
choices.text: The risk is increased and has been proven to result from the parents' fertility problems

choices.label: E
choices.text: The risk is unchanged from the general-population rate of about 1 in 15,000

explanation.summary: Children conceived through ART have an estimated imprinting-disorder risk of 2 to 5 in 15,000 versus 1 in 15,000 in the general population, and the underlying cause is not established.
explanation.whyCorrect: The estimated risk of imprinting disorders after ART is between 2 and 5 in 15,000, compared with 1 in 15,000 in the general population. The reason is unclear: some researchers propose that components of ART such as ovarian stimulation, embryo culture conditions, and timing of embryo transfer disrupt epigenetic reprogramming, while other studies suggest the risk is linked to the underlying fertility issues rather than the in vitro procedures themselves.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A risk of 1 in 150 greatly overstates the estimate of 2 to 5 in 15,000.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Embryo culture conditions are one proposed contributor, but a causal role has not been proven; the reasons for the increased risk remain unclear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Underlying fertility issues are an alternative hypothesis, but they have not been proven to be the cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The estimated ART-associated risk is several-fold higher than the general-population rate, not identical to it.

questions.stem: Approximately 2,000 CpG islands are differentially methylated between oocytes and sperm, yet only a small subset retains allele-specific methylation after fertilization, and these correspond to imprinted genes. Which of the following features of imprinting control regions best explains why this subset is preserved?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are confined to the X chromosome, where dosage compensation machinery maintains them

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are located within the coding exons of imprinted genes, where transcription shields them

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are transcribed into long non-coding RNAs in every tissue, which coat and protect them

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contain a higher density of CpG dinucleotides than other islands, resisting demethylation

choices.label: E
choices.text: They contain specific DNA motifs that bind regulatory proteins maintaining the marks

explanation.summary: Unlike other CpG islands, ICRs contain specific DNA motifs that recruit regulatory proteins which maintain imprinting marks and regulate allele-specific expression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most differentially methylated CpG islands lose their gamete-specific methylation during the genome-wide demethylation that follows fertilization. ICRs within imprinted loci are different because they contain specific DNA motifs that facilitate binding of regulatory proteins (such as the methylation-sensitive transcription factor ZFP57), which play a crucial role in maintaining the imprinting marks and controlling gene expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Imprinted loci are autosomal (for example 15q11-q13, 11p15, 6q24); confinement to the X chromosome describes X inactivation, not imprinting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ICRs are typically located within CpG islands near gene promoters, not within coding exons.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Some imprinted loci include non-coding RNAs such as H19, but ubiquitous lncRNA transcription is not the feature that preserves ICR methylation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CpG richness is a property of all CpG islands; it does not explain why only a subset retains allele-specific methylation.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with infantile hypotonia and feeding difficulty followed by hyperphagia is evaluated. Methylation analysis at 15q11-q13 shows a maternal-only methylation pattern. Array CGH shows no deletion, and microsatellite analysis confirms that he inherited one chromosome 15 from each parent. Which of the following best describes the cause of his disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A balanced translocation involving chromosome 15 that disrupts the SNRPN promoter

choices.label: B
choices.text: A de novo point mutation in the paternal SNRPN gene that abolishes its transcription

choices.label: C
choices.text: A microdeletion of the paternal 15q11-q13 region spanning about 5 to 7 megabases

choices.label: D
choices.text: An epimutation that made both alleles carry the maternal imprint

choices.label: E
choices.text: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 arising through trisomy rescue

explanation.summary: A maternal-only methylation pattern with biparental inheritance and no deletion indicates an imprinting defect (epimutation), an epigenetic change with no alteration of the DNA sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Imprinting defects, known as epimutations, are epigenetic changes that switch the parental expression pattern, for example from a paternal to a maternal-only DNA methylation pattern, despite the presence of both parental alleles (biparental). Here the child has one chromosome 15 from each parent and no deletion, yet the paternal allele carries a maternal methylation pattern, producing loss of paternal expression and the Prader-Willi phenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A balanced translocation does not produce a maternal-only methylation pattern and is not the mechanism of an imprinting defect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A point mutation changes the DNA sequence but would not convert the paternal allele's methylation pattern to a maternal one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A paternal microdeletion would have been detected by array CGH, which showed no deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Maternal UPD would be excluded by microsatellite analysis showing that one chromosome 15 came from each parent.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with a history of neonatal hypotonia and poor suck now has a rapidly increasing appetite. SNRPN methylation analysis is performed. An unaffected individual shows both a methylated and an unmethylated allele at this locus. Which of the following results is expected in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both a methylated and an unmethylated allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methylation of both alleles restricted to neurons

choices.label: C
choices.text: No detectable SNRPN signal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only a methylated allele

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only an unmethylated allele

explanation.summary: In Prader-Willi syndrome, methylation analysis shows only the methylated (maternal) allele because the paternal, unmethylated contribution is absent.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA methylation analysis is one of the most reliable tests for imprinting disorders. Members of the general population have both a methylated and an unmethylated allele at an imprinted locus, whereas individuals with an imprinting disorder have only the methylated allele. In Prader-Willi syndrome, loss of paternal gene expression at 15q11-q13 (by paternal microdeletion, maternal UPD, or imprinting defect) leaves only the methylated maternal pattern at SNRPN, which is why SNRPN methylation is commonly used to diagnose the syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The presence of both a methylated and an unmethylated allele is the normal biparental pattern seen in unaffected individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methylation analysis is performed on blood, and the imprint is present in all somatic cells derived from the zygote, not restricted to neurons.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The locus is present; in maternal UPD or an imprinting defect both copies are present, and even with a paternal deletion the maternal SNRPN copy remains detectable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only an unmethylated allele would reflect loss of the methylated maternal contribution, not the loss of paternal expression seen in this patient.

questions.stem: A pediatrician suspects an imprinting disorder in an infant and considers ordering whole-exome sequencing. A geneticist advises a different approach. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation and its rationale?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A targeted NGS panel, because it assesses methylation across multiple DMRs

choices.label: B
choices.text: FISH, because it identifies the parental origin of the affected allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: Karyotyping, because it visualizes methylation on metaphase chromosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whole-exome sequencing, because imprinting defects lie in coding sequence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole-genome sequencing, because it covers all imprinted regions

explanation.summary: Targeted next-generation sequencing panels detect CNVs, UPDs, and methylation changes across multiple differentially methylated regions, unlike whole-genome or exome sequencing, which are not well-suited to imprinting disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: Whole-genome and exome sequencing are not well-suited for identifying imprinting disorders, but targeted NGS panels are valuable tools. They can detect CNVs, UPDs, and methylation changes across multiple differentially methylated regions (DMRs) that are commonly impacted in imprinting disorders.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FISH can confirm a deletion but does not indicate the parental origin of the affected allele; that requires microsatellite or SNP analysis or methylation testing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyotyping detects large structural chromosomal changes; it does not assess DNA methylation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Imprinting defects are epigenetic changes (epimutations) with no change in DNA sequence, so exome sequencing of coding regions is not the right tool.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Whole-genome sequencing is explicitly not well-suited for imprinting disorders because it does not readily capture methylation status or parental origin.

questions.stem: To determine whether a child's two copies of chromosome 15 came from one parent or from both, a laboratory compares the child's microsatellite patterns with those of the parents. Which property of microsatellites makes them useful for this purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are methylated only on the paternal allele and unmethylated on the maternal copy in every cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are short repetitive sequences whose length is highly polymorphic between individuals

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are single base-pair substitutions that always cause a disease phenotype

choices.label: D
choices.text: They have an identical repeat sequence in every individual in the population

choices.label: E
choices.text: They lie within the coding exons of imprinted genes and change the protein sequence

explanation.summary: Microsatellites are short, repetitive, highly polymorphic DNA sequences whose length differs between individuals, allowing inheritance to be traced from parents to child.
explanation.whyCorrect: Microsatellites are short, repetitive DNA sequences that vary in length between individuals and are typically found in non-coding regions. Because they are highly polymorphic, comparing the proband's microsatellite patterns to those of the parents traces inheritance, allowing detection of uniparental disomy or of the parental origin of CNVs and methylation abnormalities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Microsatellites are used as inheritance markers; their utility depends on length polymorphism, not on parent-specific methylation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Single base-pair variations describe SNPs, which are common and mostly do not cause disease; microsatellites are length-variable repeats.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sequences identical in everyone would be uninformative; microsatellites are useful precisely because they are highly polymorphic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microsatellites are typically found in non-coding regions, not within coding exons.

questions.stem: Array CGH in a 4-year-old reveals a 15q11-q13 microdeletion; parental-origin studies are pending. Which of the following childhood findings would most strongly favor the deletion being on the maternally inherited chromosome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hyperphagia and central obesity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypogonadism and type 2 diabetes mellitus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypotonia and failure to thrive

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seizures and widely spaced teeth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Short stature and small hands

explanation.summary: A maternal 15q11-q13 deletion causes Angelman syndrome, whose childhood features include developmental delay, seizures, widely spaced teeth, and an abnormally flat back of the head.
explanation.whyCorrect: The same 15q11-q13 deletion produces Angelman syndrome when maternal and Prader-Willi syndrome when paternal. In childhood, Angelman syndrome is characterized by developmental delay, seizures, widely spaced teeth, and an abnormally flat back of the head, with minimal speech, ataxia, and inappropriate laughter later. Prader-Willi childhood features are instead hypotonia, failure to thrive, short stature, and small hands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyperphagia and obesity are the adulthood features of Prader-Willi syndrome and point to a paternal deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypogonadism and type 2 diabetes mellitus are adult features of Prader-Willi syndrome, which results from a paternal deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypotonia and failure to thrive are the childhood features of Prader-Willi syndrome, indicating a paternal deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Short stature and small hands are childhood features of Prader-Willi syndrome, not Angelman syndrome.

questions.stem: Four children have been diagnosed with Angelman syndrome, each with a different genetic cause: paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15, an imprinting defect, a mutation in the maternal UBE3A allele, and a maternal 15q11-q13 deletion. Which of these genetic causes is associated with the mildest phenotype?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An imprinting defect at 15q11-q13 that silences the maternal allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal deletion of 15q11-q13 removing UBE3A and neighboring genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mutation in the maternal UBE3A allele that truncates the protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paternal deletion of 15q11-q13 with an intact maternal UBE3A allele

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15

explanation.summary: Angelman syndrome causes ranked from mildest to most severe are paternal UPD, imprinting defects, maternal UBE3A mutations, and maternal deletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Angelman syndrome results from loss of maternal expression of UBE3A at 15q11-q13. In order of increasing phenotypic severity, the genetic causes identified in patients are paternal uniparental disomy, imprinting defects, mutations in the maternal allele of UBE3A, and maternal deletion, so paternal UPD carries the mildest phenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Imprinting defects are intermediate in severity, between paternal UPD and UBE3A mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Maternal deletion is at the most severe end of the spectrum, since it removes UBE3A together with neighboring genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A maternal UBE3A mutation ranks more severe than paternal UPD and imprinting defects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome, not Angelman syndrome.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with Angelman syndrome is found to have a loss-of-function mutation in his maternal UBE3A allele. The protein normally encoded by this gene has which of the following functions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Growth factor that promotes fetal and postnatal growth

choices.label: B
choices.text: Long non-coding RNA expressed from the maternal allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methylation-sensitive transcription factor that maintains imprints

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small nuclear ribonucleoprotein involved in pre-mRNA processing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ubiquitin ligase responsible for protein degradation in neurons

explanation.summary: UBE3A codes for a ubiquitin ligase responsible for protein degradation in neurons.
explanation.whyCorrect: UBE3A is the main gene in the 15q11-q13 region with a paternal imprint (maternal expression). It codes for a ubiquitin ligase responsible for protein degradation in neurons, which is why loss of the expressed maternal allele produces the neurodevelopmental phenotype of Angelman syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A growth factor describes IGF2 at 11p15, involved in Silver-Russell and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A maternally expressed long non-coding RNA describes H19, located near IGF2 at 11p15.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A methylation-sensitive transcription factor that maintains ICR methylation describes ZFP57.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A small nuclear ribonucleoprotein polypeptide with a role in pre-mRNA processing is the product of SNRPN, the Prader-Willi region gene.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old girl with Prader-Willi syndrome has low serum insulin-like growth factor I. Human growth hormone therapy is started. Beyond supporting linear growth, which of the following benefits is expected from this treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Correction of hypogonadism at the time of puberty

choices.label: B
choices.text: Improved muscle tone and reduced body fat

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prevention of seizures and epileptiform EEG changes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resolution of hyperphagia and constant food seeking

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restoration of paternal gene expression at 15q11-q13

explanation.summary: Growth hormone therapy in Prader-Willi syndrome improves muscle tone and reduces body fat, thereby lowering the risk of developing diabetes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Between 40% and 100% of patients with Prader-Willi syndrome have growth hormone deficiency, specifically low levels of insulin-like growth factor I, so human GH treatment is standard for infants and children with the syndrome. In addition to supporting growth, GH therapy improves muscle tone and reduces body fat, which lowers the risk of developing diabetes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypogonadism is addressed with testosterone or estrogen/progesterone during puberty, not with growth hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seizures are a feature of Angelman syndrome, not a target of growth hormone therapy in Prader-Willi syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Growth hormone reduces body fat but does not resolve the hyperphagia; dietary management and support programs address intake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Growth hormone treats a hormonal consequence of the syndrome; it does not restore the lost paternal expression at 15q11-q13.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy with Prader-Willi syndrome has not entered puberty. His endocrinologist recommends testosterone therapy. Which of the following is a goal of this treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Improve intellectual development and expressive language skills

choices.label: B
choices.text: Improve lean muscle tone and reduce total body fat mass

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promote secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raise serum insulin-like growth factor I to normal levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppress hyperphagia and lower constant food-seeking behavior

explanation.summary: Sex steroid therapy at puberty in Prader-Willi syndrome addresses hypogonadism, promotes secondary sexual characteristics, and reduces the risk of osteoporosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypogonadism is a major feature of Prader-Willi syndrome. Testosterone (or estrogen/progesterone in girls) is indicated during puberty to address hypogonadism, promote secondary sexual characteristics, and help reduce the risk of osteoporosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Intellectual impairment in Prader-Willi syndrome is not corrected by testosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Improved muscle tone and reduced body fat are benefits of growth hormone therapy, not of sex steroid replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Low IGF-I reflects growth hormone deficiency, which is treated with growth hormone rather than sex steroids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperphagia is managed with dietary programs and supervision; sex steroids do not suppress appetite.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with Prader-Willi syndrome confirmed by SNRPN methylation analysis is seen for a routine visit. His examination shows almond-shaped eyes, a narrow bifrontal diameter, a thin upper lip, and skin-picking lesions. Which of the following additional findings is most consistent with his diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypopigmentation and strabismus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low birth weight and neonatal hyperglycemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macroglossia and umbilical hernia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Triangular face and clinodactyly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Widely spaced teeth and prognathia

explanation.summary: Less frequent features of Prader-Willi syndrome include hypopigmentation, small hands and feet, strabismus, and scoliosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Prader-Willi syndrome shows highly variable expressivity across multiple body systems. Beyond the major features (hypotonia, poor suck, hyperphagia, obesity, mild intellectual impairment, hypogonadism, growth hormone insufficiency), less frequent characteristics include hypopigmentation, small hands and feet, strabismus, and scoliosis; the characteristic facial appearance includes a narrow bifrontal diameter, almond-shaped up-slanting eyes, a narrow nasal bridge, and a thin upper lip.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Low birth weight with diabetes at birth describes transient neonatal diabetes mellitus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macroglossia and umbilical hernia are features of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, the 11p15 overgrowth disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A triangular face and clinodactyly of the fifth finger are features of Silver-Russell syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Widely spaced teeth and prognathia are physical features of Angelman syndrome.

questions.stem: A laboratory uses the methylation status of a single gene in the 15q11-q13 region to detect uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 and to diagnose Prader-Willi syndrome. Which of the following correctly identifies this gene and its product?

choices.label: A
choices.text: H19, encoding a maternally expressed long non-coding RNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: IGF2, encoding an insulin-like fetal growth factor

choices.label: C
choices.text: PLAGL1, encoding a zinc-finger transcriptional regulator

choices.label: D
choices.text: SNRPN, encoding a small nuclear ribonucleoprotein

choices.label: E
choices.text: UBE3A, encoding a ubiquitin protein ligase E3A

explanation.summary: SNRPN methylation is commonly used to detect chromosome 15 UPD and diagnose Prader-Willi syndrome; the gene encodes small nuclear ribonucleoprotein polypeptide N, which functions in pre-mRNA processing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The paternally expressed region associated with Prader-Willi syndrome contains several coding genes including SNRPN, whose methylation is commonly used to detect uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 or, more generally, to diagnose PWS. SNRPN encodes the small nuclear ribonucleoprotein polypeptide N, which plays a role in pre-mRNA processing; a recently reported de novo SNRPN mutation in a PWS patient reinforces the importance of losing paternal expression of this gene within the typical deletion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H19 is a maternally expressed long non-coding RNA at 11p15, not a chromosome 15 marker.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IGF2 is at 11p15 and is involved in Silver-Russell and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PLAGL1 is at 6q24 and is dysregulated in transient neonatal diabetes mellitus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: UBE3A is in the same region but is the maternally expressed Angelman syndrome gene, not the marker used to diagnose Prader-Willi syndrome.

questions.stem: For most genes, both inherited copies are expressed, and loss of a single copy typically causes no disease or only a recessive disease. Yet a child who loses only the paternal copy of the SNRPN region at 15q11-q13 develops Prader-Willi syndrome. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single functional copy is insufficient for every human gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genes at 15q11-q13 are hemizygous because they lie on the X chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of the paternal copy triggers methylation of the maternal copy

choices.label: D
choices.text: The maternal copy is already silenced by imprinting

choices.label: E
choices.text: The maternal copy is deleted at the same time in most patients

explanation.summary: Because the maternal copy of the Prader-Willi region is normally imprinted (silenced), losing the paternal copy leaves no expressed allele, unlike a typical gene where the remaining copy compensates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two copies of each gene are inherited, and in most cases both are expressed, so impairment of one copy typically leads only to a recessive disease. Imprinted genes are expressed in a parent-of-origin-specific manner: the Prader-Willi region is maternally imprinted, so the maternal copy is silenced and only the paternal copy is expressed. Loss of paternal expression, whether by paternal microdeletion, maternal UPD, or an imprinting defect, therefore leaves the child with no active copy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Most genes tolerate a single functional copy, which is why loss of one copy usually produces at most a recessive disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The 15q11-q13 region is on an autosome, chromosome 15, not on the X chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The maternal allele is methylated because of the imprint set during oogenesis, not as a response to loss of the paternal copy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The maternal copy is usually present; the disorder arises because it is silenced, not because it is also deleted.

questions.stem: Two unrelated infants with transient neonatal diabetes mellitus both have hypomethylation of the 6q24 imprinting control region. One has dysmorphic features and a prolonged course, while the other has a mild course without dysmorphism. Which of the following best explains the variable expressivity of this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anticipation from a trinucleotide repeat expansion that lengthens each generation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incomplete penetrance of a PLAGL1 coding mutation inherited from the father

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 in the milder case, sparing PLAGL1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mosaicism for the epigenetic defect, present in about half of patients

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skewed X chromosome inactivation favoring the paternal X in the milder case

explanation.summary: Half of patients with transient neonatal diabetes are mosaic for the 6q24 defect, which partly accounts for the variable expressivity of the disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: Transient neonatal diabetes shows variable expressivity, with some patients exhibiting dysmorphic features. Paternal UPD of chromosome 6, duplication of 6q24, and hypomethylation of the 6q24 ICR all dysregulate PLAGL1, and half of patients present with mosaicism, which is partially responsible for the variability observed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticipation from repeat expansion is a feature of trinucleotide repeat disorders, not of this imprinting disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TND is attributed to dysregulation of PLAGL1 by UPD, duplication, or ICR hypomethylation, not to a coding mutation with incomplete penetrance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paternal, not maternal, UPD of chromosome 6 is associated with TND, and UPD would not explain the difference between two patients who both have ICR hypomethylation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 6q24 is autosomal; skewed X inactivation does not modulate expression of PLAGL1.

questions.stem: A tumor sample shows aberrant methylation at several unrelated imprinted loci simultaneously, a pattern described as multi-locus imprinting disturbance. Sequencing reveals loss of a methylation-sensitive transcription factor that normally binds methylated alleles at imprinting control regions and recruits a co-repressor complex. Which of the following genes is most likely affected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IGF2

choices.label: B
choices.text: PLAGL1

choices.label: C
choices.text: SNRPN

choices.label: D
choices.text: UBE3A

choices.label: E
choices.text: ZFP57

explanation.summary: ZFP57 maintains DNA methylation at ICRs by binding methylated alleles and recruiting a co-repressor complex; its loss in cancer causes multi-locus imprinting disturbances.
explanation.whyCorrect: ZFP57 is a methylation-sensitive transcription factor that maintains DNA methylation at imprinting control regions by binding methylated alleles and recruiting a co-repressor complex, preserving parent-of-origin-specific expression during early development. In cancer, loss or mutation of ZFP57 disrupts this maintenance, leading to multi-locus imprinting disturbances (MLID) and aberrant methylation patterns that enhance imprinting errors in tumor cells and contribute to pathogenicity and tumor progression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IGF2 is an imprinted growth factor gene whose loss of imprinting is common in cancer, but it is a target of imprinting rather than the factor that maintains it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PLAGL1 is the imprinted gene dysregulated at 6q24 in transient neonatal diabetes, not a trans-acting maintenance factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SNRPN is a paternally expressed gene in the Prader-Willi region encoding a ribonucleoprotein involved in pre-mRNA processing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: UBE3A encodes a neuronal ubiquitin ligase and is the Angelman syndrome gene; it does not maintain methylation across multiple ICRs.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with Silver-Russell syndrome has a head that appears disproportionately large. His parents ask whether he has a brain abnormality. Which of the following best explains the appearance of his head?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enlarged ventricles from obstructive hydrocephalus expand the skull and widen the sutures

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess IGF2 expression drives true overgrowth of the skull and the underlying brain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Growth hormone excess enlarges the cranial vault and the facial bones together

choices.label: D
choices.text: Head growth is normal while growth of the rest of the body is severely restricted

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypermethylation of paternal 11p15 causes cranial overgrowth out of proportion to the body

explanation.summary: In Silver-Russell syndrome head growth is typically normal, but because of failure to thrive the head appears disproportionately large relative to the growth-restricted body.
explanation.whyCorrect: Silver-Russell syndrome is characterized by severe intrauterine and postnatal growth retardation and is considered a form of dwarfism. Head growth is typically normal; however, due to failure to thrive, the head may appear disproportionately large compared to the rest of the body. Feeding difficulties, gastrointestinal problems, and recurrent hypoglycemia are common, and facial features and body asymmetry usually become more subtle with age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The relatively large head reflects normal head growth against a small body, not hydrocephalus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Silver-Russell syndrome results from reduced IGF2 expression (hypomethylation of paternal ICR1 or IGF2 mutation), not from IGF2 excess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Growth hormone excess is not part of Silver-Russell syndrome; the child's body growth is severely restricted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypermethylation of paternal 11p15 is found in a subset of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome patients, an overgrowth disorder, not in Silver-Russell syndrome.

questions.stem: A heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in IGF2 is identified in a family. Every child who inherited the mutation from an affected or carrier father shows Silver-Russell syndrome, whereas children who inherited the same mutation from a carrier mother are unaffected. Which of the following best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IGF2 is inherited through mitochondrial DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: IGF2 is maternally imprinted, so only the paternal allele is expressed

choices.label: C
choices.text: IGF2 is paternally imprinted, so only the maternal allele is expressed

choices.label: D
choices.text: IGF2 is X-linked dominant with male-limited expression

choices.label: E
choices.text: IGF2 mutations are autosomal dominant with complete penetrance

explanation.summary: Silver-Russell features from IGF2 mutations occur only through paternal transmission, consistent with maternal imprinting of IGF2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Silver-Russell syndrome can be caused by heterozygous mutations in IGF2 at 11p15. Clinical features occurred only through paternal transmission, consistent with maternal imprinting of IGF2: the maternal allele is normally silenced, so only a paternally inherited mutant allele removes the sole expressed copy of this growth factor. A maternally inherited mutation lies on the allele that is silenced anyway and produces no phenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mitochondrial inheritance is exclusively maternal, the opposite of the paternal-only transmission seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Paternal imprinting with maternal expression is the pattern of UBE3A in Angelman syndrome; it would make maternal, not paternal, transmission pathogenic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IGF2 lies on chromosome 11p15, an autosome, and both sons and daughters are affected through paternal transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Classic autosomal dominant inheritance would cause disease regardless of which parent transmitted the mutation.

questions.stem: In a normal cell, the maternal IGF2 allele at 11p15 is silent even though the gene itself is structurally intact. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this silencing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A protein binds the unmethylated maternal ICR1 and insulates IGF2 from enhancers

choices.label: B
choices.text: H19 long non-coding RNA base-pairs with and degrades maternal IGF2 transcripts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methylation of the maternal ICR1 blocks the IGF2 promoter directly and prevents initiation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The maternal IGF2 allele is deleted during oogenesis by programmed recombination

choices.label: E
choices.text: ZFP57 binds the methylated maternal ICR1 and represses IGF2 transcription

explanation.summary: ICR1 is methylated only on the paternal allele; on the unmethylated maternal allele an insulator protein binds ICR1 and blocks enhancers from activating IGF2.
explanation.whyCorrect: ICR1 lies upstream of H19, a maternally expressed long non-coding RNA, near the paternally expressed gene IGF2. ICR1 is methylated exclusively on the paternal allele. A protein binds the unmethylated maternal ICR1 and acts as an insulator that blocks enhancers from activating the nearby IGF2 gene, so maternal IGF2 is silent while the methylated paternal ICR1 cannot bind the insulator and paternal IGF2 is expressed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: H19 is a maternally expressed lncRNA neighboring ICR1, but the brick attributes maternal IGF2 silencing to the insulator mechanism, not to transcript degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The maternal ICR1 is unmethylated; it is the paternal ICR1 that is methylated, and that methylation permits rather than blocks IGF2 expression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both IGF2 alleles are present; the maternal allele is epigenetically silenced, not deleted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ZFP57 binds methylated ICR alleles, and the maternal ICR1 is unmethylated; moreover, methylated ICR1 is associated with IGF2 expression, not repression.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to classify the factors that contribute to a multifactorial (complex) disorder such as hypertension. Which of the following is LEAST characteristic of the way multifactorial disorders arise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Environmental exposures such as diet and toxins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epigenetic modifications such as DNA methylation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genetic predisposition from multiple variants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lifestyle factors such as physical activity and stress

choices.label: E
choices.text: Single-gene (monogenic) Mendelian inheritance

explanation.summary: Multifactorial disorders arise from many interacting factors rather than a single gene.
explanation.whyCorrect: By definition, multifactorial diseases do not follow a clear-cut, single-gene inheritance pattern; they result from the combined action of many genetic variants together with epigenetic, environmental, and lifestyle influences. Classic monogenic Mendelian inheritance is the exception, not the rule, for these conditions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Environmental exposures including diet, stress, and toxins shape disease risk and progression.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epigenetic modifications such as CpG methylation play a crucial role in these disorders.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genetic predispositions from multiple variants increase susceptibility and are a core component of multifactorial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lifestyle factors are among the environmental influences that contribute significantly.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman whose father developed early-onset Alzheimer disease asks her physician about her own chance of developing the condition given this family history. The likelihood the physician estimates for her, because an affected relative is already known, is best described by which of the following terms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Concordance rate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Occurrence risk

choices.label: C
choices.text: Penetrance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Population prevalence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrence risk

explanation.summary: Recurrence risk is the likelihood of disease when a family member is already affected.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick distinguishes occurrence risk (chance of disease with NO family history) from recurrence risk (chance of disease when someone in the family already has it). Because this woman has an affected father, the estimate applies specifically to recurrence risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Concordance rate compares affected status between twin pairs, not an individual's familial risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Occurrence risk applies when there is no family history, which is not the case here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penetrance describes the proportion of genotype carriers who express a phenotype, not familial risk estimation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Population prevalence is the overall frequency in a population, independent of a specific family history.

questions.stem: Neural tube defects occur in approximately 1 in 1,500 live births, reflecting a relatively low population prevalence. A couple whose first child was born with a neural tube defect is told their recurrence risk in a future pregnancy is roughly 2-5%, about 37.5 times higher than the baseline. Using the liability-threshold model, which statement best explains this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A high liability threshold produces low prevalence but higher recurrence risk

choices.label: B
choices.text: A high threshold lowers recurrence risk because fewer relatives are susceptible

choices.label: C
choices.text: A low liability threshold produces both low prevalence and low recurrence risk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recurrence risk is independent of how many genetic risk factors a family carries

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defect follows autosomal dominant inheritance with 50% recurrence

explanation.summary: A higher liability threshold lowers population prevalence yet raises recurrence risk in affected families.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the threshold model, a higher threshold means more genetic and environmental risk factors are required to cross into the affected range, so the disease is rare in the general population. But an affected individual must carry a heavy load of risk factors, and their relatives share more of those factors, giving a higher recurrence risk, as with the ~2-5% recurrence for neural tube defects.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A high threshold increases recurrence risk in affected families because affected members carry more risk factors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A high (not low) threshold underlies the low prevalence, and recurrence risk within families is elevated, not low.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recurrence risk rises with the genetic risk-factor load shared among relatives.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neural tube defects are multifactorial, not simple autosomal dominant traits with 50% recurrence.

questions.stem: Pyloric stenosis is about four times more common in male infants than in female infants. A pediatric geneticist counsels the family of an affected female infant that the relatives of an affected girl carry a notably higher recurrence risk than the relatives of an affected boy. Which concept best accounts for this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An affected female indicates the trait is purely environmental in her family and not heritable

choices.label: B
choices.text: Females have a higher threshold, so an affected girl must carry a greater genetic load

choices.label: C
choices.text: Males have a higher threshold and therefore transmit more risk alleles to their relatives

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sex has no effect on the liability threshold for multifactorial traits such as this one

choices.label: E
choices.text: The condition is X-linked recessive, sparing most females who carry a single copy

explanation.summary: When the less-susceptible sex is affected, it signals a heavier genetic load and higher recurrence risk in relatives.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that females have a higher threshold for pyloric stenosis, requiring more genetic and environmental risk factors. An affected female therefore carries a greater genetic load despite the higher threshold, and her relatives are more likely to inherit those risk factors, producing a higher familial recurrence risk (the Carter effect).

whyWrongByChoice.A: An affected female implies a heavier genetic contribution, not a purely environmental cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Males have the LOWER threshold; the male predominance reflects easier crossing into the affected range.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The incidence of many multifactorial diseases differs by sex precisely because thresholds differ.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyloric stenosis is a multifactorial trait, not an X-linked recessive single-gene disorder.

questions.stem: A study of oral clefts found a concordance rate of 50% in monozygotic twins compared with 8% in dizygotic twins. Which conclusion about oral clefts is best supported by these data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Environment plays no role because concordance is higher in monozygotic twins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genes play no role because monozygotic twins are not 100% concordant

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a multifactorial condition with a substantial genetic component

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a purely environmental condition with no genetic basis

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a single-gene autosomal recessive disorder

explanation.summary: Higher MZ than DZ concordance, but well below 100%, indicates a multifactorial trait with a strong genetic component.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because monozygotic twins share nearly identical genotypes, concordance far above the dizygotic rate (50% vs 8%) points to a strong genetic contribution. Yet the fact that 50% of MZ twins are discordant shows non-genetic factors also matter, so oral cleft is multifactorial with a substantial genetic component.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Incomplete MZ concordance (50% discordant) shows environmental factors do contribute.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Higher MZ than DZ concordance directly implicates genes; incomplete concordance does not erase that.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The much higher MZ concordance demonstrates a clear genetic contribution, not a purely environmental cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Single-gene autosomal recessive inheritance would predict very different, more predictable concordance, not this multifactorial pattern.

questions.stem: Investigators note that a pair of monozygotic twins is discordant for a particular disease, meaning only one twin is affected despite the twins being genetically nearly identical. What does discordance in monozygotic twins most strongly suggest about the disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Non-genetic factors contribute to the disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: The disease cannot be studied using twin methods

choices.label: C
choices.text: The disease has complete genetic determination

choices.label: D
choices.text: The disease is caused solely by a single dominant gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: The twins are actually dizygotic

explanation.summary: Discordance in genetically identical twins points to non-genetic contributions and a multifactorial origin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monozygotic twins have nearly identical genotypes, so if only one twin is affected, genetics alone cannot explain the difference. The brick states this discordance indicates that non-genetic factors contribute, supporting a multifactorial origin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Twin studies are in fact a powerful method for exactly this kind of gene-versus-environment analysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complete genetic determination would predict concordance in identical twins, the opposite of what is seen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single fully penetrant dominant gene would tend to make identical twins concordant, not discordant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The premise specifies monozygotic (identical) twins; discordance does not reclassify their zygosity.

questions.stem: A research team wants to identify common genetic variants that occur more frequently in patients with type 2 diabetes than in unaffected controls, testing millions of variants across tens of thousands of individuals. Which study design is being described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genome-wide association study (GWAS)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotype analysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Linkage analysis in a single large family

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monozygotic twin concordance study

choices.label: E
choices.text: Randomized controlled trial

explanation.summary: GWAS scan many genomes to find SNPs more common in cases than controls.
explanation.whyCorrect: A genome-wide association study scans the genomes of thousands to millions of individuals to find single-nucleotide polymorphisms that occur more frequently in people with a disease than in those without it. The brick notes GWAS have identified about 75 susceptibility loci for type 2 diabetes and related metabolic traits.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotype analysis detects large chromosomal abnormalities, not common single-nucleotide risk variants.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Linkage analysis tracks co-inheritance within families and is suited to higher-penetrance, familial loci rather than common risk SNPs across populations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A twin concordance study estimates heritability, but it does not localize specific SNPs across the genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A randomized controlled trial tests interventions or treatments, not naturally occurring genetic associations.

questions.stem: A geneticist explains that a typical human genome carries roughly 5 to 10 million single-nucleotide variants, most of which are benign and present in more than 1% of the population. Which term best describes this class of common, benign sequence variants?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromosomal aneuploidies

choices.label: B
choices.text: De novo Mendelian mutations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deleterious mutations

choices.label: D
choices.text: Frameshift mutations

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polymorphisms

explanation.summary: Polymorphisms are benign variants with a population frequency above 1%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines polymorphisms as benign mutations with a frequency greater than 1%, and notes a human genome typically carries 5 to 10 million SNPs. Some of these common variants are now recognized as risk factors for multifactorial disease through GWAS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aneuploidies are gains or losses of whole chromosomes, not single-nucleotide variants.
whyWrongByChoice.B: De novo Mendelian mutations are rare, newly arising, disease-causing changes rather than common polymorphisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Deleterious mutations are rare variants with a direct disease-causing effect, especially in Mendelian disorders, not common benign variants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Frameshift mutations are a specific disruptive mutation type, not a description of common benign SNPs.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man is started on warfarin. Genotyping shows a CYP2C9 variant associated with reduced enzyme activity. Based on the pharmacogenomics discussed for warfarin, what is the most likely consequence of this variant, and how should dosing be adjusted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faster drug breakdown lowers warfarin levels, so a higher dose is needed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Slower drug breakdown raises blood warfarin levels, so a lower dose is needed

choices.label: C
choices.text: The variant has no effect on warfarin metabolism or dosing

choices.label: D
choices.text: The variant increases vitamin K synthesis, requiring more warfarin

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variant makes warfarin ineffective, so it should be discontinued entirely

explanation.summary: Reduced-activity CYP2C9 variants slow warfarin breakdown, raising drug levels and requiring lower doses.
explanation.whyCorrect: CYP2C9 encodes the liver enzyme that breaks down warfarin. Certain variants slow this process, increasing warfarin levels in the blood. The brick states patients with such variants may require lower doses to avoid bleeding, and this information is used clinically to personalize dosing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A reduced-activity variant slows metabolism and raises levels; it does not speed breakdown or lower levels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The variant meaningfully alters metabolism and is used to guide dosing, so it is not inconsequential.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CYP2C9 affects warfarin breakdown, not vitamin K synthesis; VKORC1 is the gene linked to the vitamin K epoxide reductase target.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin remains effective; dosing is simply reduced to prevent excessive anticoagulation.

questions.stem: GWAS have identified variants in VKORC1 that influence a patient's response to warfarin. According to the brick, VKORC1 affects warfarin response primarily through which mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Altering expression of vitamin K epoxide reductase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Directly binding warfarin in the plasma to inactivate it

choices.label: C
choices.text: Encoding a serotonin receptor targeted by the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Encoding the hepatic enzyme that metabolizes and clears warfarin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increasing intestinal absorption of warfarin

explanation.summary: VKORC1 alters expression of warfarin's target enzyme, vitamin K epoxide reductase, changing drug sensitivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states VKORC1 affects the drug's target enzyme by altering the expression of vitamin K epoxide reductase, which influences the body's sensitivity to warfarin. This is distinct from CYP2C9, which affects metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.B: VKORC1 does not act by directly binding and inactivating warfarin in plasma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serotonin receptors (for example HTR1F) relate to migraine drug targets, not warfarin's mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metabolism and clearance of warfarin are governed by CYP2C9, not VKORC1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes VKORC1's effect to the target enzyme, not to intestinal absorption.

questions.stem: A recent migraine GWAS discovered new risk loci, some containing genes that encode existing migraine-specific drug targets. Monoclonal antibodies and gepants used for migraine act on the product of which of these genes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CALCA/CALCB, encoding calcitonin gene-related peptide

choices.label: B
choices.text: CYP2C9, encoding a warfarin-metabolizing enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIST1H2BD, encoding a histone protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: IL10RA, encoding an interleukin-10 receptor subunit

choices.label: E
choices.text: VKORC1, encoding vitamin K epoxide reductase

explanation.summary: Gepants and anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies target CGRP, encoded by CALCA/CALCB.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that migraine GWAS identified loci with genes encoding migraine-specific drug targets, namely the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CALCA/CALCB). CGRP is the target of preventive and acute migraine therapies delivered via monoclonal antibodies and gepants.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CYP2C9 relates to warfarin metabolism, not migraine therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIST1H2BD is associated with cocaine dependence, not migraine treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL10RA is implicated in inflammatory bowel disease, not migraine drug targeting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VKORC1 is a warfarin-response gene, unrelated to CGRP-targeting migraine drugs.

questions.stem: Studies suggest that a grandmother's smoking during pregnancy may alter DNA methylation patterns in her daughter and potentially in her grandchildren, influencing health outcomes beyond the immediate generation. This phenomenon is best described by which term?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anticipation in a trinucleotide repeat disorder

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genomic imprinting reversal in the germline

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mendelian codominance at a single locus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Somatic mosaicism arising after fertilization

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance

explanation.summary: Environmental exposures altering methylation across generations reflect transgenerational epigenetic inheritance.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes how prenatal environmental exposures, such as grandmaternal smoking, can alter DNA methylation and affect biological outcomes in later generations, a phenomenon called transgenerational epigenetic inheritance. Watkins et al. reported sex-specific methylation associations linked to grandmaternal smoking.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anticipation describes worsening or earlier onset over generations in repeat-expansion disorders, not methylation transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The example involves inherited methylation changes across generations, not a reversal of genomic imprinting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Codominance is a Mendelian allelic expression pattern, unrelated to environmentally induced epigenetic changes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatic mosaicism refers to genetically distinct cell populations within one individual, not inherited epigenetic marks.

questions.stem: A researcher is sorting the contributors to a complex phenotype into three categories: genetic, epigenetic, and environmental. Which of the following contributors is correctly classified as epigenetic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dietary nutrient intake

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exposure to environmental toxins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histone modification

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infection with pathogens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Single-nucleotide polymorphisms

explanation.summary: Histone modification and CpG methylation are the epigenetic contributors in the gene-environment model.
explanation.whyCorrect: The gene-environment Venn diagram places CpG methylation and histone modification within the epigenetics circle. SNPs and mutations belong to genetics, while nutrition, toxins, drugs, and pathogens are environmental factors. Non-coding RNAs sit at the overlap of genetics and epigenetics, and the phenotype emerges where all three interact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nutrition is an environmental factor in the model.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Toxins are classified as environmental exposures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pathogens, like drugs and toxins, fall in the environmental circle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SNPs and mutations are genetic factors, not epigenetic modifications.

questions.stem: Investigators examined DNA methylation in the peripheral blood of teenage grandchildren whose grandmothers had smoked during pregnancy. Which of the following best describes the pattern of methylation that was reported?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Identical methylation changes in both sexes at a single autosomal promoter

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of methylation confined to mitochondrial DNA in female grandchildren only

choices.label: C
choices.text: No methylation differences at any site, refuting transgenerational effects

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sex-specific associations at two X-chromosome sites and one imprinting control region

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniform hypermethylation across all autosomes in grandchildren of both sexes

explanation.summary: Grandmaternal smoking was linked to sex-specific methylation changes at two X-chromosome sites and one imprinting control region.
explanation.whyCorrect: Watkins and colleagues reported an association between grandmaternal smoking and DNA methylation in the peripheral blood of teenage grandchildren, identifying sex-specific associations at two sites on the X chromosome and one in an imprinting control region located within transcription factor binding sites. Studies on this question have nevertheless produced contradictory findings overall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The associations were sex-specific and involved multiple sites, including the X chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The reported sites were on the X chromosome and in an imprinting control region, not mitochondrial DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An association was found; the field's contradictions reflect inconsistent results across studies, not a null finding in this one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The associations were localized and sex-specific, not uniform across all autosomes.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with alcohol use disorder asks whether his genes played a role. He is told that variants in MAOA, SLC6A4, and COMT are among those associated with addiction and with protection against it. Through which mechanism are different alleles of these genes thought to influence addiction risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acting as the single gene for alcoholism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Altering an individual's stress responses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Blocking hepatic breakdown of alcohol

choices.label: D
choices.text: Encoding the histone linked to cocaine dependence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increasing intestinal absorption of alcohol

explanation.summary: MAOA, SLC6A4, and COMT are stress-resilience genes whose alleles shape stress responses that, combined with other influences, affect addiction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick groups MAOA, SLC6A4, and COMT with other genes associated with stress resilience. Different alleles of these genes impact stress responses, which, when combined with other influences, could impact addiction. There is no single addiction or alcoholism gene, and the environment plays a crucial role.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick states explicitly that there is not just one addiction or alcoholism gene.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These genes are described in terms of stress resilience, not hepatic alcohol metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIST1H2BD is the histone gene associated with cocaine dependence, not these three genes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Their effect is on stress responses, not on absorption of alcohol.

questions.stem: A large study of an international database identified more than 400 locations in the human genome and at least 566 variants related to smoking or alcohol use. Which of the following sets of genes was specifically identified as playing a significant role in that study?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CALCA, CALCB, and HTR1F

choices.label: B
choices.text: CUL3, PDE4B, and PTGER3

choices.label: C
choices.text: IL10RA, XIAP, and CYBB

choices.label: D
choices.text: MAOA, SLC6A4, and COMT

choices.label: E
choices.text: VKORC1 and CYP2C9

explanation.summary: CUL3, PDE4B, and PTGER3 were singled out among the hundreds of loci tied to smoking or alcohol use.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick reports that a large international database study found more than 400 genomic locations and at least 566 variants related to smoking or alcohol use, and that CUL3, PDE4B, and PTGER3 were specifically identified as playing a significant role. Most such genes are not yet clinically relevant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CALCA, CALCB, and HTR1F encode migraine drug targets found in migraine GWAS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL10RA, XIAP, and CYBB are genes directly implicated in inflammatory bowel disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MAOA, SLC6A4, and COMT are stress-resilience genes linked to addiction generally, not the genes singled out in the smoking and alcohol database study.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VKORC1 and CYP2C9 influence warfarin response, not substance use.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old infant develops severe, treatment-refractory inflammatory bowel disease. Genetic testing identifies a highly penetrant mutation in a single gene, one of the few genes directly implicated in monogenic forms of the disease. A mutation in which of the following genes is most consistent with this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: COMT

choices.label: B
choices.text: CUL3

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIST1H2BD

choices.label: D
choices.text: HTR1F

choices.label: E
choices.text: IL10RA

explanation.summary: IL10RA, XIAP, and CYBB are the genes directly implicated in the uncommon monogenic forms of inflammatory bowel disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although monogenic cases of inflammatory bowel disease are not frequently observed, a few genes have been directly implicated, namely IL10RA, XIAP, and CYBB. Highly penetrant mutations in these genes cause monogenic IBD at the familial end of the disease spectrum, whereas most cases result from a combination of genetic factors and environmental pressures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: COMT is a stress-resilience gene associated with addiction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CUL3 was identified in relation to smoking or alcohol use, not IBD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIST1H2BD is associated with cocaine dependence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HTR1F encodes a serotonin receptor implicated in migraine, not IBD.

questions.stem: A geneticist studies a large multigenerational family in which inflammatory bowel disease segregates in a pattern consistent with a single highly penetrant mutation. Considering the spectrum of complex-disease etiology from familial monogenic to sporadic polygenic forms, which approach is best suited to localize the causative gene in this family?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genome-wide association study

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linkage analysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Manhattan plot of common risk variants

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monozygotic-dizygotic concordance comparison

choices.label: E
choices.text: Population-wide common SNP frequency survey

explanation.summary: Linkage maps the familial, monogenic end of the complex-disease spectrum; GWAS covers the oligogenic-to-polygenic, sporadic end.
