explanation.whyCorrect: The IBD etiology figure aligns study methods with the spectrum of disease: linkage sits beneath the familial, monogenic end where highly penetrant mutations (such as IL10 or XIAP) cause disease, while GWAS spans the oligogenic and polygenic range where environment increasingly dominates. A family with Mendelian-like segregation of a highly penetrant mutation is therefore the setting for linkage analysis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GWAS scans large populations for common SNPs of small effect, which is suited to polygenic and sporadic disease rather than a single high-penetrance familial mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A Manhattan plot is a way of displaying GWAS results, which target common variants rather than a family's private mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Twin concordance estimates the relative genetic versus environmental contribution but does not localize a gene.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Common-variant frequency surveys address the polygenic end of the spectrum, not a rare highly penetrant familial mutation.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man who smokes develops inflammatory bowel disease. No relative has ever been affected. According to the model of complex inflammatory disease etiology, which of the following best explains the development of disease in most patients like him?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A highly penetrant monogenic mutation in IL10 or XIAP inherited from a parent

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single oligogenic locus that would be detected by family linkage analysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Environmental factors such as the gut microbiome acting on a genetically predisposed host

choices.label: D
choices.text: Purely environmental injury from smoking with no underlying genetic contribution

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance of methylation marks from a grandparent

explanation.summary: Most IBD develops when mostly unknown environmental factors act on a genetically predisposed host.
explanation.whyCorrect: The IBD figure shows that in most patients (the population-prevalence curve peaking in the polygenic range) disease develops through mostly unknown environmental factors, including the gut microbiome, acting on a genetically predisposed host. Sporadic cases at the environmental end are influenced by exposures such as infections and smoking, with gene-environment interactions central to etiology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Highly penetrant monogenic IBD is described but is uncommon and sits at the familial end of the spectrum, not the typical sporadic case.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oligogenic familial disease is a different, less common region of the spectrum; typical sporadic cases are polygenic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Even sporadic disease occurs on a genetically predisposed background; the model never removes genetics entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transgenerational methylation effects are discussed for grandmaternal smoking, not as the usual mechanism of IBD.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman whose mother and brother have type 2 diabetes asks her physician to tell her exactly whether she will develop the disease. The physician explains that a precise prediction is not possible. Which of the following best explains why the likelihood that a particular family member will develop type 2 diabetes is difficult to estimate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least 150 DNA variants interact with lifestyle factors such as diet and physical activity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Family clustering does not occur, so relatives share no risk with one another

choices.label: C
choices.text: The condition arises only from environmental exposures that cannot be measured in clinic

choices.label: D
choices.text: The disease is caused by a single dominant gene with highly variable expressivity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 2 diabetes follows a strict autosomal recessive pattern with 25% recurrence

explanation.summary: Type 2 diabetes involves at least 150 DNA variants interacting with lifestyle, making individual prediction difficult.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complex diseases cluster within families but do not follow a simple pattern of inheritance, so it is difficult to estimate the likelihood that a particular member will develop the condition. Type 2 diabetes has been associated with at least 150 DNA variants that are likely to interact with lifestyle factors such as diet and physical activity to influence how the condition presents.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Complex diseases do cluster in families, with more cases than in the general population.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genetic variants are central; the condition is not purely environmental.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 2 diabetes is polygenic and multifactorial, not a single dominant gene disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no strict Mendelian pattern for type 2 diabetes.

questions.stem: In the multifactorial (threshold) model, disease occurrence is drawn as a bell-shaped curve with a vertical threshold line; individuals beyond the threshold are affected. The horizontal axis of this curve represents which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allele frequency of a single risk polymorphism in the population

choices.label: B
choices.text: Liability from combined genetic and environmental factors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Penetrance of a single dominant disease allele among carriers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Population frequency of affected individuals in the sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrence risk among first-degree relatives of a proband

explanation.summary: The threshold curve plots population frequency against liability, the combined load of genetic and environmental risk factors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The disease occurrence and risk factor threshold figure places population frequency on the vertical axis and liability, from low to high, on the horizontal axis. Liability reflects the accumulated combination of genetic and environmental risk factors; individuals whose liability exceeds the threshold fall into the affected portion of the curve.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The model integrates many risk factors, not the frequency of a single polymorphism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penetrance applies to single-gene disorders and is not the axis of the liability curve.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Population frequency is the vertical axis, not the horizontal axis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recurrence risk is a concept derived from the threshold model, not the quantity plotted on the axis.

questions.stem: Two multifactorial conditions show opposite sex ratios: autism is about four times more common in males, whereas migraine occurs two to three times more often in women than in men. Applying the threshold model, in which of the following conditions is the threshold for manifestation likely higher in males than in females?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Migraine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neural tube defect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral cleft

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pyloric stenosis

explanation.summary: The less commonly affected sex has the higher threshold; for migraine that is males.
explanation.whyCorrect: The incidence of multifactorial diseases may differ between sexes. Because women experience migraines at a rate two to three times higher than men, the threshold for manifestation is likely higher in males than in females. By contrast, autism is about four times more common in males, suggesting a higher threshold in females.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autism is more common in males, so the threshold is likely higher in females.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick describes neural tube defects in terms of prevalence and recurrence risk, not a male-predominant threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral cleft is used to illustrate twin concordance, and no higher male threshold is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pyloric stenosis has a strong male predominance, and females have the higher threshold.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old boy is brought to the clinic with several days of forceful, projectile vomiting after feeds, signs of dehydration, and poor weight gain. Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic inflammation of the colonic mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of neural tube closure in early gestation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertrophy of the lower esophageal sphincter

choices.label: D
choices.text: Incomplete fusion of the palatal shelves in utero

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thickened pyloric muscle narrowing the stomach outlet

explanation.summary: Pyloric stenosis is abnormal thickening of the pyloric muscle that obstructs food passage, causing projectile vomiting in infants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pyloric stenosis is a condition in infants in which the muscles of the pylorus, the passage between the stomach and small intestine, become abnormally thickened, causing a narrowing that obstructs the flow of food. This leads to projectile vomiting, dehydration, and poor weight gain, typically diagnosed within the first few months of life. It affects about 2 to 5 per 1,000 live births with a male-to-female ratio of about 4:1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic colonic inflammation characterizes inflammatory bowel disease, not the gastric outlet obstruction described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neural tube defects are structural malformations present at birth, not a cause of projectile vomiting in a feeding infant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The obstruction in pyloric stenosis is at the pylorus, distal to the stomach, not at the esophageal sphincter.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral clefts involve the palate and lip; they do not obstruct gastric outflow.

questions.stem: An infant is diagnosed with pyloric stenosis. Which of the following is the standard, effective treatment for this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Feeding through a gastrostomy tube

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous antibiotics for fourteen days

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term proton pump inhibitor therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Observation until spontaneous resolution

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surgical pyloromyotomy

explanation.summary: Surgical correction by pyloromyotomy is the standard, effective treatment for pyloric stenosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that surgical correction (pyloromyotomy) is the standard and effective treatment for pyloric stenosis, a relatively common infant condition caused by abnormal thickening of the pyloric muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bypassing feeds does not correct the obstruction; the definitive treatment is surgical.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pyloric stenosis is a muscular obstruction, not an infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acid suppression does not relieve the mechanical narrowing of a thickened pylorus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The obstruction causes dehydration and poor weight gain and is treated surgically rather than observed.

questions.stem: Both members of a monozygotic twin pair develop schizophrenia. Which term describes this twin pair with respect to the disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Concordant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Discordant

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterozygous

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penetrant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sporadic

explanation.summary: Twins who both have the same disease are concordant.
explanation.whyCorrect: When monozygotic twins both have the same disease, they are considered concordant. Twin studies compare concordance in monozygotic versus dizygotic twins to evaluate the influence of genetic versus environmental factors.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Discordant twins are those in which only one twin is affected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heterozygous describes a genotype at one locus, not shared disease status.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penetrance refers to whether a genotype is expressed, not to the status of a twin pair.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sporadic refers to a case without family history, which does not apply to two affected twins.

questions.stem: Genetic testing in a child with a classic Mendelian disorder reveals a variant present in far fewer than 1% of the population that directly causes the disease. Which term best classifies this variant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Benign polymorphism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Common risk-factor SNP

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deleterious mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epigenetic modification

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatic copy-number variant

explanation.summary: Deleterious mutations are rare variants with a direct disease-causing effect, classically in Mendelian disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA sequence variants are classified by their population frequency. Polymorphisms are benign and occur at a frequency greater than 1%, whereas deleterious mutations are rare variants with a direct disease-causing effect, especially in the context of Mendelian disorders. A rare, directly causal variant in a Mendelian disease is therefore a deleterious mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Polymorphisms are benign and occur at greater than 1% frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Common SNPs recognized as risk factors are frequent and confer susceptibility, not direct Mendelian causation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An epigenetic modification such as methylation is not a DNA sequence variant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The variant described is an inherited sequence change causing Mendelian disease, not a somatic copy-number change.

questions.stem: A figure from a GWAS meta-analysis shows, for each chromosome, thousands of points plotted by -log10(P), with a horizontal dashed line and several highlighted peaks rising above it. What does this Manhattan plot primarily display?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The concordance of monozygotic versus dizygotic twin pairs for the studied trait

choices.label: B
choices.text: The liability distribution of a population relative to its disease threshold

choices.label: C
choices.text: The methylation status of CpG islands across tissues and developmental stages

choices.label: D
choices.text: The recombination rate at each position along the genome in centimorgans

choices.label: E
choices.text: The statistical significance of variant-trait associations across the genome

explanation.summary: A Manhattan plot displays the genome-wide statistical significance of associations between variants and a trait.
explanation.whyCorrect: To visualize GWAS results, a Manhattan plot is commonly used. It displays the statistical significance of associations between genetic variants and a trait across the genome, highlighting regions that may harbor risk loci for the condition under investigation. Peaks above the significance line mark genome-wide significant loci, such as the 12 loci found for ADHD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Twin concordance is a separate method for gauging genetic versus environmental contribution.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The liability distribution is the bell-shaped curve of the threshold model, not a GWAS plot.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methylation is an epigenetic measure, not the association statistics a Manhattan plot shows.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recombination rate appears as a secondary axis in LocusZoom plots, not as the main content of a Manhattan plot.

questions.stem: A GWAS meta-analysis of attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder included 20,183 affected individuals and 35,191 controls. Which of the following best describes its key result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single causative gene was found, confirming monogenic inheritance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eighty-six new loci were discovered, several encoding drug targets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nearly 75 susceptibility loci were replicated for the disorder

choices.label: D
choices.text: No locus reached genome-wide significance in the combined sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: Twelve genome-wide significant risk loci were identified for the first time

explanation.summary: The ADHD GWAS meta-analysis discovered the first 12 genome-wide significant risk loci for the disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Manhattan plot from the GWAS meta-analysis of ADHD, based on 20,183 individuals with ADHD and 35,191 controls, identified 12 genome-wide significant loci, marked as orange diamonds above the significance line. This represented the discovery of the first genome-wide significant risk loci for ADHD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADHD is a multifactorial condition influenced by many genes of small effect; no single causative gene was found.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eighty-six new loci describes the recent migraine GWAS, not the ADHD study.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nearly 75 replicated susceptibility loci refers to type 2 diabetes and related metabolic traits.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Twelve loci exceeded the genome-wide significance threshold.

questions.stem: A recent GWAS discovered 86 new loci associated with migraine. Beyond identifying loci that encode drug targets, which additional observation from this study offers clues to the underlying mechanisms of the disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All risk variants were located within the CYP2C9 gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Distinct SNPs marked migraine with versus without aura

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every locus was shared with type 2 diabetes and ADHD

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migraine loci were confined to the X chromosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Risk loci appeared only in monozygotic twin pairs

explanation.summary: The migraine GWAS found subtype-specific SNPs distinguishing migraine with aura from migraine without aura.
explanation.whyCorrect: The recent migraine study discovered 86 new loci, and the researchers observed specific SNPs characteristic of migraine types (with or without aura), offering clues to help decipher the underlying mechanisms of the disease. The newly identified loci also include genes encoding migraine-specific drug targets, CALCA/CALCB and HTR1F.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYP2C9 relates to warfarin metabolism, not migraine loci.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The study characterized migraine subtypes; sharing every locus with other disorders is not described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The two highlighted loci were on chromosomes 11 and 3, not confined to the X chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GWAS scans unrelated individuals; the finding was not about twins.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with acute migraine attacks is prescribed a ditan. GWAS of migraine identified a risk locus containing the gene that encodes this drug's target. Which of the following is that gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CALCA

choices.label: B
choices.text: CALCB

choices.label: C
choices.text: HTR1F

choices.label: D
choices.text: PTGER3

choices.label: E
choices.text: VKORC1

explanation.summary: Ditans act on the serotonin 5-HT1F receptor encoded by HTR1F, a migraine GWAS locus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The LocusZoom plots show two previously unknown migraine loci containing genes that are targets of recent migraine-specific drugs. The chromosome 3 locus contains HTR1F, which encodes a serotonin 5-HT1F receptor that is the target of acute therapies via ditans. The chromosome 11 locus contains CALCA and CALCB, encoding CGRP, the target of monoclonal antibodies and gepants.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CALCA encodes calcitonin gene-related peptide, the target of monoclonal antibodies and gepants, not ditans.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CALCB, like CALCA, encodes CGRP targeted by antibodies and gepants.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PTGER3 was identified in relation to smoking or alcohol use.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VKORC1 encodes vitamin K epoxide reductase and governs warfarin sensitivity.

questions.stem: A hospital implements genotype-guided dosing of warfarin based on VKORC1 and CYP2C9 variants. Which property of warfarin makes such personalized dosing especially important for safety and effectiveness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has a narrow therapeutic window

choices.label: B
choices.text: It has no identifiable target enzyme

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is absorbed unpredictably from the gut

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is eliminated exclusively by the kidney

choices.label: E
choices.text: It works only in patients with a family history of clots

explanation.summary: Warfarin's narrow therapeutic window is why genotype-guided dosing improves safety and effectiveness.
explanation.whyCorrect: Warfarin is a blood thinner with a narrow therapeutic window. Because SNPs in VKORC1 and CYP2C9 change sensitivity to and metabolism of the drug, patients with specific variants may require lower doses to avoid bleeding risks. This information is now used in clinical settings to personalize dosing, improving both safety and effectiveness.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Warfarin's target enzyme is vitamin K epoxide reductase, whose expression is altered by VKORC1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes variability to metabolism and target sensitivity, not to absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Warfarin is broken down by a liver enzyme encoded by CYP2C9, not eliminated exclusively by the kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warfarin's efficacy does not depend on family history; genotype guides dose, not eligibility.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with normal fasting glucose reports that both of his parents have type 2 diabetes. Based on the familial risk figures cited from health resources, his risk of developing type 2 diabetes is closest to which of the following?

explanation.summary: With both parents affected, offspring risk of type 2 diabetes is approximately 70%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The case explains that if one parent has type 2 diabetes, the offspring's risk is around 40%, and if both parents have type 2 diabetes the risk jumps to approximately 70%. This increased risk is largely due to a combination of genetic predisposition and shared lifestyle factors within families.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 2-5% is the recurrence risk of a neural tube defect after an affected pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 8% is the dizygotic twin concordance for oral clefts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 40% is the risk when only one parent is affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 50% is the monozygotic twin concordance for oral clefts, not the parental-risk figure.

questions.stem: A healthy 26-year-old man with normal laboratory results asks why his physician kept asking whether his parents have type 2 diabetes. Which of the following best explains why a family history raises his risk even though his current labs are normal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Family history is relevant only for monogenic forms of diabetes caused by single deleterious mutations

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genetic predisposition combines with lifestyle habits such as diet and exercise shared within the family

choices.label: C
choices.text: His parents' diagnoses prove that he inherited a highly penetrant mutation in one gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal laboratory results exclude any genetic contribution, making the family history irrelevant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 2 diabetes is transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait with complete penetrance in offspring

explanation.summary: Family history signals both inherited genetic risk and shared lifestyle factors, so risk is elevated even before disease appears.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type 2 diabetes is multifactorial, influenced by both genes and lifestyle. Individuals with a family history face a significantly higher risk because of a combination of genetic predisposition and shared lifestyle factors within families, such as diet and exercise habits. Knowing the family history lets the doctor watch early and guide prevention, even when the patient is currently healthy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The family history matters precisely because common type 2 diabetes is multifactorial, not only monogenic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multifactorial disease reflects many variants of small effect plus environment, not one highly penetrant mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Normal current labs do not remove an inherited predisposition to a disease that develops later.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 2 diabetes does not follow an autosomal dominant pattern with complete penetrance.

questions.stem: A student claims that allelic variation in humans matters only for disease and occurs only in non-coding DNA. Which of the following statements correctly describes the role of allelic variation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It affects only pathogenic traits and is restricted to protein-coding regions of the genome

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is irrelevant to normal human traits such as body size and affects only Mendelian disorders

choices.label: C
choices.text: It occurs only in non-coding regions and influences only susceptibility to disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces phenotypic variation only through single-gene effects with Mendelian inheritance

choices.label: E
choices.text: It shapes normal traits such as size and eye color as well as disease, in coding and non-coding regions

explanation.summary: Allelic variation contributes to normal traits, disease susceptibility, and disease, and occurs in both coding and non-coding DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Allelic variation contributes to normal traits, disease susceptibility, and disease. It affects normal human traits such as our size (multifactorial) and the color of our eyes (multigenic), and these variants occur in both coding and non-coding regions of the genome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic variation underlies normal traits too, and it is not restricted to coding regions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Body size is given as a multifactorial normal trait shaped by allelic variation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Variants occur in coding as well as non-coding regions and affect normal traits, not only disease susceptibility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Normal traits such as size are multifactorial and eye color is multigenic, not single-gene Mendelian effects.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor tells a couple whose first child had a neural tube defect that the recurrence risk in a future pregnancy is approximately 2-5%. On what basis is a recurrence risk figure like this derived for a multifactorial disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Empirical data observed in families with an affected child

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hardy-Weinberg calculation from the population carrier frequency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mendelian segregation ratios of 25% or 50% for each pregnancy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penetrance of the single causative allele among carriers

choices.label: E
choices.text: The concordance rate observed in dizygotic twin pairs

explanation.summary: Recurrence risks for multifactorial disorders come from empirical observation, not Mendelian calculation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complex diseases do not follow a simple pattern of inheritance, so the likelihood that a family member will develop the condition cannot be derived from segregation ratios. Instead, empirical data are used to evaluate recurrence risk, such as the observed 2-5% recurrence among women who have previously had a child with a neural tube defect, roughly 37.5 times the 1 in 1,500 baseline.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hardy-Weinberg carrier-frequency calculations are for single-locus recessive traits, not multifactorial liability.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mendelian ratios apply to single-gene disorders, whereas neural tube defects are multifactorial.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no single causative allele in a multifactorial disorder to which penetrance could be assigned.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Twin concordance helps gauge genetic versus environmental contribution but is not how a family recurrence figure is derived.

questions.stem: A genetic association study of individuals with cocaine dependence identifies a gene that encodes a histone protein. Which of the following is that gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CYBB

choices.label: B
choices.text: HIST1H2BD

choices.label: C
choices.text: MAOA

choices.label: D
choices.text: PDE4B

choices.label: E
choices.text: XIAP

explanation.summary: HIST1H2BD, a histone gene, has been associated with cocaine dependence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the genes associated with addiction to specific substances, the brick lists HIST1H2BD, which has been associated with cocaine dependence. It sits alongside stress-resilience genes (MAOA, SLC6A4, COMT) and the smoking and alcohol loci (CUL3, PDE4B, PTGER3) as examples of the polygenic basis of addiction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CYBB is one of the genes directly implicated in inflammatory bowel disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MAOA is a stress-resilience gene associated with addiction in general, not a histone gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PDE4B was identified in relation to smoking or alcohol use.
whyWrongByChoice.E: XIAP is implicated in monogenic inflammatory bowel disease.

questions.stem: A group of 500 people leaves an island by raft to settle a new island. Before departure, 400 have curly hair (dominant) and 100 have straight hair (recessive). During the voyage several rafts sink, and the group that arrives contains 375 with curly hair and 25 with straight hair. The change in allele proportions in the arriving group was caused by the random sinking of rafts rather than any survival advantage of a trait. Which phenomenon best explains this change in allele frequency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gene flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mendelian inheritance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural selection

explanation.summary: A random disaster that sharply cuts population size and shifts allele frequencies by chance is the bottleneck effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bottleneck effect is a sharp reduction in population size (and therefore alleles) caused by a random event such as a disaster. The sinking rafts randomly eliminated individuals, changing allele frequencies through genetic drift rather than through any fitness advantage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assortative mating is a preference for mating with similar individuals, which does not apply to a disaster that randomly removes people.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gene flow is the transfer of alleles between populations by migration and would increase variation, not the random loss seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mendelian inheritance describes random reassortment of parental alleles into offspring genotypes, not a population-level frequency shift from a disaster.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Natural selection favors alleles that confer a reproductive advantage; here the loss was random, with no trait providing an advantage.

questions.stem: In a stable, randomly mating population of 10,000 people, 5 individuals are affected by an autosomal recessive condition. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, which of the following best approximates the frequency of the recessive allele (q)?

explanation.summary: The recessive allele frequency q is the square root of the homozygous recessive frequency q-squared.
explanation.whyCorrect: The affected homozygous recessive genotype frequency is q-squared = 5/10,000 = 0.0005. Taking the square root gives q = the square root of 0.0005, which is approximately 0.022.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.0005 is q-squared (the frequency of affected individuals), not the allele frequency q itself; you must take its square root.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 0.043 corresponds to the heterozygote frequency 2pq, not the recessive allele frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 0.5 would only occur if both alleles were equally common, which is not the case for a rare disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 0.978 is the frequency of the dominant allele p (equal to 1 minus q), not the recessive allele frequency.

questions.stem: In a randomly mating population of 1,000 people at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, 20 people are affected by an autosomal recessive disease. Approximately how many people in this population are unaffected heterozygous carriers?

explanation.summary: Carrier count equals the heterozygote frequency 2pq multiplied by the total population.
explanation.whyCorrect: q-squared = 20/1000 = 0.02, so q = approximately 0.14 and p = 1 minus 0.14 = 0.86. The carrier frequency is 2pq = 2 x 0.86 x 0.14 = approximately 0.24, and 0.24 x 1000 = 240 carriers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 24 results from multiplying the carrier frequency of 0.24 by 100 instead of by the true population of 1,000.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 140 confuses the allele frequency q (0.14) scaled to the population with the number of carriers, which requires 2pq.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 320 is not obtained by any correct step of the Hardy-Weinberg calculation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 860 corresponds to p x 1000, the scaled dominant allele frequency, not the heterozygote count.

questions.stem: A woman with curly hair reports that she is only romantically attracted to men who also have curly hair. If this preference were widespread, it would reduce random pairing in the population. This behavior is an example of which genetic phenomenon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Founder effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gene flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Genetic drift

explanation.summary: Preferring mates with similar traits, decreasing random mating, is assortative mating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Assortative mating refers to the tendency of individuals to mate with others who are similar to them, which decreases random mating within a population. Attraction to a partner who shares the same phenotype (curly hair) is phenotypic assortative mating, a violation of the Hardy-Weinberg random-mating assumption.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The bottleneck effect is a disaster-driven reduction in population size, not a mate-choice pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The founder effect involves a small group separating from a larger population, not a mating preference.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gene flow is the transfer of alleles between populations by migration, unrelated to choosing similar mates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency by chance and does not involve mate preference.

questions.stem: The Afrikaner population of South Africa descends largely from a small number of Dutch colonists and today has an unusually high frequency of the gene that causes Huntington disease. This elevated frequency is best explained by which mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A high spontaneous mutation rate at the Huntington locus

choices.label: B
choices.text: A recent environmental disaster reducing the population

choices.label: C
choices.text: Founder effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gene flow from neighboring populations

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural selection favoring the Huntington allele

explanation.summary: A disease that is common because a few original settlers happened to carry the allele reflects the founder effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The founder effect occurs when a small group separates from a larger population; the new subpopulation resembles that small founding group. Because the founding Dutch colonists carried the Huntington allele by chance, it spread to their descendants within the isolated community, raising its frequency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The high frequency reflects inheritance from founders who already carried the allele, not an elevated mutation rate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A sudden disaster describes the bottleneck effect; the Afrikaner example is driven by a small founding group, not a catastrophe.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gene flow mixes alleles between populations and increases diversity; here an isolated community concentrated a founder allele.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Huntington disease confers no reproductive advantage, so selection does not explain its high frequency; the spread was by chance.

questions.stem: A physician in a small town notes that residents were historically descendants of southern European immigrants, among whom thalassemia minor was common. Over recent generations, young people left for university, married partners from elsewhere, and returned to raise families, so many current residents no longer share the southern European ancestry. The physician now observes that the incidence of thalassemia minor has decreased. Which mechanism best explains this decline?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Founder effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gene flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural selection against the thalassemia allele

explanation.summary: New alleles entering a population through migration and mating is gene flow, which increases variation and dilutes a previously common allele.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gene flow is genetic variation caused by migration of individuals from other populations into a given population. As residents married outsiders and introduced new alleles, the shared inherited thalassemia allele became diluted, lowering the disease incidence. This may make broad screening less cost-effective than before.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assortative mating is preference for similar partners; the scenario describes mixing with dissimilar outsiders.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The bottleneck effect reduces population size via disaster and decreases diversity; here diversity is increasing through migration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The founder effect concentrates alleles in a small isolated group, the opposite of what mixing produces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no described selective pressure acting against the thalassemia allele; the change is due to incoming alleles.

questions.stem: In regions of the world where malaria is endemic, the recessive HbS allele of the beta-globin chain is maintained at a relatively high frequency in the population, whereas in non-malarial regions it is selected against. Which of the following best explains why HbS persists where malaria is common?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gene flow continually imports HbS from non-malarial regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: HbS/HbA heterozygotes have a survival advantage against severe malaria

choices.label: C
choices.text: HbS/HbS homozygotes are protected from malaria and reproduce more

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random genetic drift fixes HbS in large malarial populations

choices.label: E
choices.text: The HbS allele mutates back to HbA more slowly in malarial regions

explanation.summary: Heterozygote advantage: carriers with sickle cell trait resist the worst complications of malaria and reproduce, keeping HbS frequent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carriers of HbS (genotype HbA/HbS) have sickle cell trait and are more likely to survive severe malaria, giving them a reproductive advantage where malaria is common. This natural selection for heterozygotes maintains the HbS allele in the population, even though homozygotes (HbS/HbS) have sickle cell disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Non-malarial regions select against HbS and have lower frequencies, so they are not a source of imported HbS.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HbS/HbS homozygotes have sickle cell disease and historically suffered early mortality, so they do not drive the allele's persistence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Genetic drift is random and strongest in small populations; the pattern here is driven by consistent selection tied to malaria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Persistence is explained by selection favoring heterozygotes, not by differences in reverse-mutation rates.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant of Ashkenazi Jewish descent presents with seizures, progressive neurologic deterioration, and a cherry-red macula on fundoscopic examination. This disorder results from deficiency of which of the following enzymes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha-galactosidase A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Glucocerebrosidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hexosaminidase A

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phenylalanine hydroxylase

choices.label: E
choices.text: The CFTR chloride transporter

explanation.summary: Tay-Sachs disease results from hexosaminidase A deficiency and is more common in Ashkenazi Jews.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tay-Sachs disease results from a deficiency of the hexosaminidase A enzyme, causing seizures, a cherry-red macula, and other neurologic deficits. It is found at higher rates in Ashkenazi Jews, prompting ACOG to recommend screening for Ashkenazi Jews or those of mixed Jewish ancestry considering children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease, which is not associated with this presentation in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes Gaucher disease, another founder-effect disorder in Jewish populations, but it does not produce the cherry-red macula of Tay-Sachs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes phenylketonuria, which is not the disorder described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The CFTR chloride transporter is defective in cystic fibrosis, not in this neurodegenerative presentation.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor explains to a couple that a cystic fibrosis carrier screening panel has an estimated sensitivity of 71.9% in white-American couples but only 23.4% in Asian-American couples. What is the best interpretation of this difference for counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A negative screen more reliably rules out carrier status in white-American than in Asian-American couples

choices.label: B
choices.text: A positive screen is a false positive more often in white-American than in Asian-American couples

choices.label: C
choices.text: Asian-American couples have a higher absolute risk of having an affected child regardless of screening results

choices.label: D
choices.text: Screening sensitivity is identical across ancestries once the number of mutations tested is equalized

choices.label: E
choices.text: The CFTR gene is present only in white-American populations and is absent in Asian-American ones

explanation.summary: Because causative CFTR mutations differ by ancestry, panel sensitivity varies, so a negative result is more trustworthy where sensitivity is higher.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carrier rates and the specific CFTR mutations causing cystic fibrosis are highly dependent on ancestry. Because the panel detects more of the relevant mutations in white-American couples (71.9% sensitivity) than in Asian-American couples (23.4%), a negative test is more likely to be truly negative for a white-American couple.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The figures describe sensitivity (detection of true carriers), not the false-positive rate of a positive result.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lower sensitivity means residual risk is harder to exclude after a negative test; it does not by itself establish a higher baseline disease risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The point of the example is that sensitivity genuinely differs by ancestry because causative mutations differ.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The CFTR gene is present in all populations; only the frequency and type of mutations differ.

questions.stem: A textbook describes the differences in DNA sequence for a specific gene at the same position on a chromosome, noting that these differences can lead to diverse traits, disease risks, and medication responses within a population. This description best defines which term?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic variation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Assortative mating

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bottleneck effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Founder effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Genetic drift

explanation.summary: Different alleles of a gene at the same locus contributing to varied phenotypes is allelic variation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Allelic variation describes differences in DNA sequence (alleles) for a specific gene at the same position on a chromosome. This variation contributes to observable phenotypes in both normal and pathogenic ways and increases overall genetic diversity, influencing traits, disease risk, and drug response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Assortative mating is a mate-choice pattern, unrelated to defining DNA sequence differences at a locus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The bottleneck effect is a type of genetic drift that decreases diversity, not the definition of sequence differences at a locus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The founder effect is also a form of genetic drift and concentrates alleles in a small group; it is not the definition of allelic differences.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency and decreases diversity, rather than defining the differences themselves.

questions.stem: A student lists conditions under which a population would remain in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Which of the following, if present in a population, would violate a Hardy-Weinberg assumption and shift gene frequencies over generations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A very large population size

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absence of any immigration or emigration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Completely random mating

choices.label: D
choices.text: Natural selection favoring one allele

choices.label: E
choices.text: No mutation between generations

explanation.summary: Selection favoring an allele violates the no-selection assumption of Hardy-Weinberg and changes allele frequencies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumes no selective forces favor one allele over another. If natural selection gives one allele a reproductive advantage, its frequency will change across generations, breaking equilibrium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A large population is one of the required assumptions; it helps maintain, not violate, equilibrium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No immigration or emigration is a required assumption; its presence supports equilibrium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Random mating is an assumption of the model and supports equilibrium rather than disrupting it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absence of mutation is a required assumption; it preserves stable allele frequencies.

questions.stem: A population geneticist explains that a certain deleterious recessive allele persists in a population at a stable low frequency because new copies arise from errors in DNA replication at the same rate that affected homozygotes are removed from the breeding population. This steady state is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating for a similar phenotype

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect after a natural disaster

choices.label: C
choices.text: Founder effect in a small separated group

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gene flow from a neighboring population

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mutation-selection equilibrium

explanation.summary: A balance between mutation creating deleterious alleles and selection removing them is mutation-selection equilibrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mutation-selection equilibrium is a state where the rate of creation of deleterious alleles (usually recessive) by mutation is balanced by the rate of their elimination by selection. This balance helps maintain genetic variation within populations at a stable low frequency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assortative mating is a preference for similar mates and does not describe this equilibrium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The bottleneck effect is a disaster-driven reduction in population size, unrelated to a steady mutation-selection balance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The founder effect concentrates alleles in a small separated group and is a form of genetic drift, not a mutation-selection balance.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gene flow is the migration-driven transfer of alleles between populations, not a within-population balance of mutation and selection.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to distinguish population genetics from classical Mendelian genetics. Which of the following best describes the focus of population genetics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How a single gene's DNA sequence is transcribed and translated in a cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: How dominant and recessive alleles are written with capital and lowercase letters

choices.label: C
choices.text: How gene frequencies affect a population and vary over time within it

choices.label: D
choices.text: How homologous chromosomes segregate during a single meiotic division

choices.label: E
choices.text: How one copy of each autosomal gene passes randomly from parent to child

explanation.summary: Population genetics studies inheritance and variation of genes across an entire population rather than from specific parents to children.
explanation.whyCorrect: In genetics, a population is a collection of individuals, and population genetics refers to the genetic inheritance and variation of certain genes throughout an entire population. Rather than thinking about how genes flow from specific parents to their children, it studies how the frequency of genes both affects a population and varies over time within that population. Clinicians use this knowledge to rapidly consider the most likely condition affecting a patient given his or her background.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transcription and translation of a gene describe molecular gene expression, not the frequency of genes across a population.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Capital and lowercase letters are simply the nomenclature for dominant and recessive alleles in Mendel's model.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromosome segregation during meiosis is a cellular mechanism of Mendelian inheritance, not the study of allele frequencies in populations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Random transmission of one copy of each autosomal gene from each parent is the Mendelian model of inheritance within a family, not the population-level focus.

questions.stem: In the early 1900s, some geneticists proposed that if Mendel was correct, the quantity of dominant alleles should increase throughout a population while recessive alleles decrease. Which of the following best describes the response that created the groundwork for population genetics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 2011 study of facial attraction refuted the proposal experimentally

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hardy and Weinberg independently refuted the proposal in 1908

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hardy and Weinberg jointly confirmed the proposal mathematically in 1908

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mendel confirmed the proposal by expanding his pea-plant crosses

choices.label: E
choices.text: The discovery of single nucleotide polymorphisms confirmed the proposal

explanation.summary: G. H. Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg independently refuted in 1908 the idea that dominant alleles must increase over time, founding population genetics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Population genetics arose to reconcile Mendelian and biostatistical models of inheritance. When geneticists argued that Mendel's model implied dominant alleles should take over a population, scientists G. H. Hardy and Wilhelm Weinberg independently refuted this notion in 1908, which created the groundwork for population genetics and later their equation predicting stable allele frequencies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 2011 facial-attraction study relates to phenotypic assortative mating, not to the origin of population genetics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hardy and Weinberg refuted, not confirmed, the notion, and they did so independently rather than jointly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mendel described inheritance within crosses; he did not address or confirm the population-level claim about dominant allele frequencies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Single nucleotide polymorphisms are a source of allelic variation; their discovery did not confirm the dominant-allele proposal.

questions.stem: A laboratory report describes a patient's allele at a particular locus as wildtype. Which of the following best describes the meaning of this term?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The allele arose recently by a new mutation in this patient

choices.label: B
choices.text: The allele correlates with a nondiseased, healthy individual

choices.label: C
choices.text: The allele encodes a diseased trait in homozygotes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The allele is dominant over every other allele at that locus

choices.label: E
choices.text: The allele is expressed only when two copies are present

explanation.summary: A wildtype allele is one that correlates to a nondiseased, healthy individual; alleles encoding diseased traits are mutant alleles.
explanation.whyCorrect: If an allele correlates to a nondiseased and healthy individual, that allele is called wildtype. Other alleles are considered to be mutant alleles if they encode for diseased traits. For example, HbA is described as the wildtype hemoglobin allele, in contrast to the HbS allele.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A newly arisen variant is a mutation; wildtype is the allele associated with the healthy, nondiseased state.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Alleles that encode diseased traits are mutant alleles, the opposite of wildtype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Wildtype refers to association with health, not to dominance; dominance describes whether one or two copies are needed for expression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Expression only with two copies describes a recessive allele, which is a separate concept from wildtype versus mutant.

questions.stem: A researcher studying why individuals in a population differ in their response to a medication identifies many single-base differences in the DNA sequence of a drug-metabolizing gene. Which of the following best describes this source of allelic variation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Directional natural selection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Founder effect after migration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonrandom assortative mating

choices.label: D
choices.text: Population bottleneck effect

choices.label: E
choices.text: Single nucleotide polymorphism

explanation.summary: Single nucleotide polymorphisms are one of the sources from which allelic variation arises.
explanation.whyCorrect: Allelic variation contributes to phenotypes in both normal and pathogenic ways, including differences in medication responses. This variation is essential for species adaptation and arises from sources such as mutations, genetic recombination, single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP), and the random shuffling of genes during reproduction. Single-base sequence differences among individuals are SNPs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Natural selection favors alleles that already exist because they confer an advantage; it does not create single-base differences.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The founder effect concentrates existing alleles in a small separated group; it is not a source of new sequence variation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Assortative mating is a mate-choice pattern that decreases random mating; it does not create sequence differences.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The bottleneck effect is a form of genetic drift that reduces population size and decreases diversity; it does not generate new sequence variants.

questions.stem: A geneticist wants to use a single Hardy-Weinberg calculation to simultaneously predict genotype frequencies for two different genes, CFTR and hexosaminidase A, in the same population. Which of the following best describes the limitation of this approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The equation applies only to dominant alleles and not recessive alleles

choices.label: B
choices.text: The equation applies only to genes located on the X chromosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The equation cannot be applied to autosomal recessive diseases

choices.label: D
choices.text: The equation requires a family pedigree rather than population data

choices.label: E
choices.text: The equation studies only one specific gene and its alleles at a time

explanation.summary: The Hardy-Weinberg equation can only be used to study one specific gene at a time with its associated alleles.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Hardy-Weinberg equation allows quantitative determination of both genotypes and the proportion of alleles in a population, with some exceptions. It should be noted that the equation can only be used to study one specific gene at a time with its associated alleles, so two genes must be analyzed with separate calculations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The equation includes both p (dominant allele frequency) and q (recessive allele frequency).
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick derives the equation for an autosomal gene with alleles A and a; it is not restricted to the X chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The equation is explicitly derived for an autosomal recessive disease such as Laron syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The equation predicts genotypes and allele frequencies of an entire population, not just a family.

questions.stem: A student derives the Hardy-Weinberg equation by squaring both sides of p + q = 1 and asks why the heterozygote term is 2pq rather than simply pq. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A heterozygote arises two ways: A is the paternal allele or A is the maternal allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each heterozygote carries two copies of the recessive allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterozygotes are counted once as carriers and once as affected individuals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heterozygotes have twice the reproductive fitness of either homozygote

choices.label: E
choices.text: The recessive allele mutates at twice the rate of the dominant allele

explanation.summary: The factor of 2 accounts for the two parental combinations that yield a heterozygote.
explanation.whyCorrect: The middle term of p-squared + 2pq + q-squared = 1 equals two times the probability of having one dominant allele and one recessive allele, representing the probability of being a heterozygote. The 2 is involved because there are two combinations that allow one to be a heterozygote: in one combination A is the paternal allele, and in the other A is the maternal allele.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A heterozygote (Aa) carries one dominant and one recessive allele, not two recessive alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heterozygotes for a recessive condition are unaffected carriers; they are not counted as affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The equation assumes no selective forces favoring any genotype; fitness plays no role in the derivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The equation assumes alleles do not mutate from generation to generation; mutation rates are not part of the term.

questions.stem: In a large, randomly mating population at Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of the recessive allele (q) for an autosomal recessive condition is 0.1. What is the expected frequency of heterozygous carriers in this population?

explanation.summary: Heterozygote frequency is 2pq; with q = 0.1 and p = 0.9, 2pq = 0.18.
explanation.whyCorrect: From p + q = 1, p = 1 minus 0.1 = 0.9. The heterozygote frequency is the middle term of the Hardy-Weinberg equation, 2pq = 2 x 0.9 x 0.1 = 0.18. The genotype frequencies check: 0.81 + 0.18 + 0.01 = 1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.01 is q-squared, the frequency of homozygous recessive (affected) individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 0.09 is pq, which omits the factor of 2 that accounts for both parental combinations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 0.81 is p-squared, the frequency of homozygous dominant individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 0.90 is p, the frequency of the dominant allele, not a genotype frequency.

questions.stem: In a randomly mating population of 10,000 people, 5 individuals express the autosomal recessive disease Laron syndrome. Using the Hardy-Weinberg equation, approximately how many individuals in this population are homozygous dominant?

explanation.summary: Homozygous dominant count = p-squared x total population = 0.956 x 10,000 = 9,560.
explanation.whyCorrect: q-squared = 5/10,000, so q = 0.022 and p = 1 minus 0.022 = 0.978. The frequency of homozygous dominant individuals is p-squared = 0.978 squared = 0.956. Multiplying the frequency as a decimal by the total population gives 0.956 x 10,000 = 9,560 homozygous dominant individuals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5 is the given number of homozygous recessive (affected) individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 430 is the number of heterozygotes (2pq = 0.043 x 10,000), not homozygous dominant individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 9,780 is p x 10,000, the scaled dominant allele frequency rather than the p-squared genotype frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 9,995 is the sum of all three genotype counts (9,560 + 430 + 5), not the homozygous dominant count alone.

questions.stem: A student applying the Hardy-Weinberg equation to a population of 10,000 calculates 9,560 homozygous dominant individuals, 430 heterozygotes, and 5 homozygous recessive individuals, for a total of 9,995. Which of the following best explains why the subpopulations do not sum exactly to 10,000?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Five individuals carry a newly mutated third allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rounding in the earlier calculations of p and q

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 5 missing individuals emigrated from the population

choices.label: D
choices.text: The heterozygote term was calculated without the factor of 2

choices.label: E
choices.text: The population is not actually in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium

explanation.summary: Genotype counts that sum to approximately, not exactly, the total population reflect rounding of p and q.
explanation.whyCorrect: Checking work by confirming that subpopulations summate to approximately the total population is expected: 9,560 + 430 + 5 = 9,995. The missing 5 result from rounding in the previous calculations (q was rounded to 0.022 and p to 0.978), just as p-squared + 2pq + q-squared = 0.9995, which approximately equals 1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The model assumes only two alleles (A and a) and no mutation; a third allele is not part of the calculation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The calculation assumes no immigration or emigration; the discrepancy is arithmetic, not demographic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The heterozygote count of 430 already reflects 2pq (2 x 0.978 x 0.022 = 0.043); omitting the 2 would give about 215.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A shortfall of 5 out of 10,000 after rounding does not indicate a departure from equilibrium; the check is meant to be approximate.

questions.stem: A geneticist studies a remote village of 30 people that has been completely isolated for generations. There is no selection at the locus of interest, alleles have not mutated, mating is random, and no one has moved in or out. Which Hardy-Weinberg assumption is most likely violated, making genetic drift a powerful force in this village?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alleles do not mutate from one generation to the next at the locus of interest

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mating occurs randomly within the population with respect to this genotype

choices.label: C
choices.text: No selective forces favor one allele over another at the locus of interest

choices.label: D
choices.text: The population is large enough that one birth does not alter allele proportions

choices.label: E
choices.text: There is no immigration into or emigration from the population in either direction

explanation.summary: Hardy-Weinberg requires a population large enough that a single new individual does not significantly alter allele proportions; small populations are subject to powerful drift.
explanation.whyCorrect: One assumption for a stable allele frequency is that the population is large enough so that one new individual born into it does not significantly alter the proportion of alleles. In a village of 30 people this assumption fails. Genetic drift, random fluctuation of allele frequencies driven by chance rather than fitness, can be a powerful force in small populations where changes in genetic frequencies can have big impacts on the phenotype of future generations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stem states alleles have not mutated, so this assumption holds.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stem states mating is random, so this assumption is not violated.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stem states there is no selection at the locus, so this assumption is satisfied.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No one has moved in or out, so the no-migration assumption is satisfied.

questions.stem: A patient with a family history of an autosomal recessive disease visits a genetic counselor. Which of the following questions can be answered using data derived from the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: How many generations ago the allele entered the family

choices.label: B
choices.text: The likelihood that the patient is a carrier of the disease allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether the disease allele confers a reproductive advantage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether the disease allele will mutate in the patient's children

choices.label: E
choices.text: Which environmental exposures raised the patient's disease risk

explanation.summary: Hardy-Weinberg data answer questions about allele frequency, genotype frequency, and who is a carrier of a genetic disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Calculating allele frequencies, predicting genotype frequencies, and determining carriers of genetic diseases are three ways Hardy-Weinberg can be applied medically. When a patient goes to a genetic counselor, Hardy-Weinberg data can answer questions about the frequency of an allele in the population, the frequency of certain genotypes, and who is a genetic disease carrier. Screening programs for at-risk groups and genetic counseling both benefit from this information.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hardy-Weinberg describes current population frequencies, not the generational history of an allele within a family.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The model assumes no selective forces; it does not evaluate reproductive advantage of an allele.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The Hardy-Weinberg model assumes alleles do not mutate between generations, so it cannot predict new mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Environmental risk factors are outside the scope of an equation that describes allele and genotype frequencies.

questions.stem: In a population where malaria is common, individuals with sickle cell trait survive and reproduce more successfully than those without it. A geneticist describes the contribution of the HbS/HbA genotype to overall reproductive success in this population. Which of the following terms best describes this concept?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allelic variation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fitness

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gene flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genetic drift

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mutation-selection equilibrium

explanation.summary: Fitness is the contribution of a given genotype or phenotype to overall reproductive success.
explanation.whyCorrect: Populations with a higher risk of malaria have selected for the sickle cell trait because heterozygotes are more likely to survive. These concepts refer to the fitness of a population, specifically the contribution of a given genotype or phenotype to overall reproductive success.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic variation describes differences in DNA sequence at a locus, not the reproductive contribution of a genotype.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gene flow is the transfer of alleles between populations by migration, unrelated to reproductive success of a genotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Genetic drift is random fluctuation of allele frequencies driven by chance, explicitly not by genetic fitness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mutation-selection equilibrium is the balance between creation of deleterious alleles and their elimination, not a measure of a genotype's reproductive success.

questions.stem: A physician in a region with little to no malaria notes that sickle cell disease is essentially absent from the local, geographically isolated population. Which of the following best explains why this population selected against the HbS allele?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gene flow from malarial regions diluted the HbS allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heterozygotes had a reproductive advantage that eliminated the allele

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygous recessive individuals historically died before reproducing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random genetic drift fixed the HbA allele in the population

choices.label: E
choices.text: The HbS allele reverted to HbA in the absence of malaria

explanation.summary: Without malaria there is no advantage to sickle cell trait, and early mortality of HbS/HbS homozygotes removed HbS alleles from the population.
explanation.whyCorrect: Populations in regions with little to no prevalence of malaria select against the sickle cell gene (HbS) because homozygous recessive individuals historically suffered from early mortality. Because they passed away before reproducing, the number of HbS alleles in the population was decreased. These populations typically do not have sickle cell disease, as there was no evolutionary advantage to having the trait.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gene flow from malarial regions would introduce HbS alleles, not remove them, and the population is described as isolated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heterozygote advantage operates where malaria is common and maintains HbS; it is not the mechanism removing HbS in non-malarial regions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The loss of HbS is described as selection driven by early mortality of homozygotes, not a random drift event.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick describes selection against HbS through mortality, not reverse mutation of the allele.

questions.stem: A physician in a small town historically screened residents with a complete blood count because thalassemia minor was common among the town's southern European descendants. Over several decades, residents have increasingly married people from outside the community, and the incidence of thalassemia minor has fallen. Which of the following is the most appropriate response in clinical practice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue universal screening because the allele frequency is unchanged

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expand screening to include partners who marry into the community

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reassess whether universal screening is still indicated or cost-effective

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replace the complete blood count with CFTR mutation panel testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Restrict screening to residents with no southern European ancestry

explanation.summary: As gene flow reduces disease incidence, screening that was once reasonable may no longer be indicated or cost-effective.
explanation.whyCorrect: If many people in a stable community share the same inherited gene associated with a disease such as thalassemia minor, screening with a complete blood count may be implemented. However, as gene flow introduces more genetic variation and the incidence of the disease decreases, screening may not be indicated or cost-effective. Population genetics guides clinical decision making: what was reasonable to do before might not be now.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The allele frequency has not remained unchanged; gene flow has decreased it, which is exactly why the incidence fell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Incoming partners are the source of new alleles that diluted the thalassemia allele; expanding screening to them is not supported by the falling incidence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The disease in question is thalassemia minor, detected with a complete blood count; CFTR testing is for cystic fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Residents without southern European ancestry are the group least likely to carry the allele, so targeting them makes no sense.

questions.stem: A small population has been completely isolated for many generations. No allele at a particular locus confers any reproductive advantage, and no selective pressure acts on the locus. Over a very long period of time, which of the following is the expected fate of a given allele at this locus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It will be held at a stable low frequency by selection

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will be replaced by alleles introduced through gene flow

choices.label: C
choices.text: It will either be lost or become fixed through drift

choices.label: D
choices.text: It will stabilize at a frequency of exactly 0.5

choices.label: E
choices.text: It will steadily increase because it is dominant

explanation.summary: Without selective pressure, genetic drift eventually causes every allele to be either lost or fixed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genetic drift describes random fluctuations of genetic frequencies driven by chance rather than fitness, and it is a powerful force in small populations. Over the course of time, without selective pressure, all alleles will either be lost or become fixed through drift.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A stable low frequency maintained by selection describes mutation-selection equilibrium, but the stem specifies no selective pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The population is completely isolated, so there is no gene flow to introduce new alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Drift is random and does not converge on any particular intermediate frequency; it drives alleles toward loss or fixation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hardy and Weinberg refuted the notion that dominant alleles steadily increase simply because they are dominant.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor is asked how common the carrier state for Gaucher disease, an autosomal recessive condition, is among Jewish people compared with non-Jews. Which of the following is the best approximation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1 in 1,000 Jewish people versus about 1 in 100 non-Jews

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1 in 10 Jewish people versus about 1 in 10 non-Jews

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 1 in 10 Jewish people versus about 1 in 100 non-Jews

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 1 in 100 Jewish people versus about 1 in 10 non-Jews

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 1 in 2 Jewish people versus about 1 in 1,000 non-Jews

explanation.summary: About 1 in 10 Jewish people carry a Gaucher mutation, dramatically higher than the roughly 1 in 100 rate among non-Jews, a consequence of the founder effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gaucher disease is an example of the founder effect. About 1 in 10 Jewish people are carriers of a genetic mutation causing Gaucher disease, which is dramatically higher than non-Jews, where about 1 in 100 people is a carrier. Historically isolated Jewish communities descended from a group of founders in Eastern Europe, and mutations present in those founders were passed on and increased in prevalence over generations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1 in 1,000 greatly understates the Jewish carrier rate, which is about 1 in 10.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The carrier rates are not equal; the founder effect produced a roughly tenfold difference.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the figures; the carrier rate is higher, not lower, among Jewish people.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 1 in 2 overstates the Jewish carrier rate, and 1 in 1,000 understates the non-Jewish rate.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is diagnosed with Gaucher disease after enzyme testing. He has no neurologic symptoms, although his younger sibling, who has the same disease, developed chronic neurologic involvement in childhood. Which of the following best classifies the man's form of Gaucher disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heterozygous carrier state for Gaucher disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tay-Sachs disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Type 1, the non-neuronopathic form

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type 2, the acute infantile neuronopathic form

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 3, the chronic neuronopathic form

explanation.summary: Gaucher disease without neurologic involvement is Type 1 (non-neuronopathic); presentations can differ even within one family.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are 3 types of Gaucher disease based on symptoms: Type 1 (Non-Neuronopathic Form), Type 2 (Acute Infantile Neuronopathic Form), and Type 3 (Chronic Neuronopathic Form). An adult with no neurologic symptoms has the non-neuronopathic Type 1 form. Gaucher disease presents on a spectrum, and the symptoms and how the disease develops may not be the same for everyone, even for people in the same family.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The man is diagnosed with the disease itself, not merely the carrier state.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tay-Sachs disease results from hexosaminidase A deficiency and presents with seizures and a cherry-red macula; this patient has Gaucher disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type 2 is the acute infantile neuronopathic form, which involves neurologic disease in infancy, not an asymptomatic adult.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type 3 is the chronic neuronopathic form and better fits the sibling with chronic neurologic involvement, not this man.

questions.stem: A large population of insects with considerable allelic diversity is nearly wiped out by a flood, leaving a small surviving group. Several generations later, the regional climate shifts. Which of the following best explains why this population is now at particular risk of being unable to adapt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating among survivors increased the number of heterozygotes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gene flow from neighboring populations introduced maladaptive alleles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mutation-selection equilibrium eliminated all of the deleterious alleles

choices.label: D
choices.text: The surviving insects have all become homozygous dominant

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variation that selection would act on has already drifted out of the population

explanation.summary: A bottleneck reduces genetic variation, so a population may lack the variation selection needs to respond to new pressures.
explanation.whyCorrect: The bottleneck effect is a sharp reduction in population size and alleles due to environmental events such as famines, earthquakes, floods, fires, disease, and droughts. Reduced genetic variation means the population may not be able to adapt to new selection pressures, such as climatic change or a shift in available resources, because the genetic variation that selection would act on may have already drifted out of the population.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assortative mating decreases random mating; it is not described here and does not explain loss of adaptive capacity after a flood.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gene flow increases genetic variation and would improve, not reduce, the population's capacity to adapt; no migration is described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mutation-selection equilibrium is a balance that maintains variation; it is not the reason a bottlenecked population cannot adapt.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A bottleneck randomly reduces alleles; nothing indicates every survivor became homozygous dominant, and that is not the mechanism described.

questions.stem: A population of tan and brown/green bugs lives in a green environment. After nearly all of the brown/green bugs are accidentally stepped on by a human, the surviving population is predominantly tan. Which of the following best describes the effect of this event on the population's fitness for its environment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fitness decreased because the remaining bugs no longer camouflage as easily

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fitness increased because reduced variation stabilizes allele frequencies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fitness increased because the tan allele is dominant

choices.label: D
