choices.text: Fitness is unchanged because gene flow will restore the brown/green allele

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fitness is unchanged because the event was random rather than selective

explanation.summary: A bottleneck can change a population's fitness; tan survivors in a green environment camouflage poorly.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the bug example, a natural but random event rapidly decreased the number of brown/green alleles, producing genetic drift toward a greater frequency of tan alleles. The bottleneck effect may even change the fitness of the population: if the bugs typically live in a green environment, the remaining population does not camouflage as easily, so the fitness of the population for their environment has decreased.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduced variation does not raise fitness; it limits the population's ability to adapt.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dominance of an allele has nothing to do with fitness, which is the contribution of a genotype or phenotype to reproductive success.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No migration is described; the bugs are a small isolated population and gene flow cannot be assumed to restore lost alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although the event was random, its outcome (loss of camouflage) still lowers the population's fitness for a green environment.

questions.stem: Which of the following population-genetic processes increases genetic variation within a population rather than decreasing it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assortative mating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bottleneck effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Founder effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gene flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Genetic drift

explanation.summary: Gene flow increases genetic variation, whereas both types of genetic drift decrease it.
explanation.whyCorrect: While the two types of genetic drift (founder effect and bottleneck effect) decrease genetic diversity in a population, gene flow actually increases genetic variation. Gene flow is the transfer of genes (alleles) between populations, allowing the sharing and combination of gene pools of two different populations, which promotes and helps maintain genetic diversity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assortative mating decreases random mating within a population; it does not transfer alleles between populations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The bottleneck effect is a type of genetic drift that sharply reduces the number of individuals and alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The founder effect is a type of genetic drift in which a small separated group produces a subpopulation with reduced diversity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genetic drift in general is random change in allele frequency that decreases diversity and eventually leads to loss or fixation of alleles.

questions.stem: A sociologist observes that in a certain community, individuals strongly prefer to live with and marry partners who share their religion. Which of the following best classifies this pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Founder effect after separation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gene flow between populations

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phenotypic assortative mating

choices.label: D
choices.text: Random mating within the community

choices.label: E
choices.text: Socioeconomic assortative mating

explanation.summary: Preferring a partner who shares the same religion is the brick's example of socioeconomic assortative mating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Assortative mating refers to the desire for individuals to mate with others who are similar to them, decreasing random mating within a population. It may be phenotypic (related to appearance) or socioeconomic. A common example of socioeconomic assortative mating is individuals desiring to live with a partner who shares the same religion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The founder effect involves a small group separating from a larger population; it is not a mate-choice pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gene flow is the transfer of alleles between populations by migration and mating, not a within-community preference.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phenotypic assortative mating is related to appearance, such as attraction to faces resembling one's own; religion is not a physical trait.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Random mating is the Hardy-Weinberg assumption that this preference violates.

questions.stem: A study found that heterosexual males are more attracted to faces that resemble their own facial features. If this preference shapes who has children with whom in a population, which Hardy-Weinberg assumption is most directly violated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alleles do not mutate from generation to generation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mating occurs randomly

choices.label: C
choices.text: No selective forces favor one allele over another

choices.label: D
choices.text: The population is large enough that one birth does not alter allele proportions

choices.label: E
choices.text: There is no immigration or emigration

explanation.summary: Phenotypic assortative mating decreases random mating, violating the Hardy-Weinberg random-mating assumption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Assortative mating is a concept that deviates from the Hardy-Weinberg principle because it decreases random mating within a population. A 2011 study demonstrated phenotypic assortative preference by finding that heterosexual males are more attracted to faces that resemble their own facial features, so pairing is no longer random with respect to those traits.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mate preference does not change whether alleles mutate between generations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Assortative mating is about who mates with whom, not about one allele conferring a reproductive advantage over another.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Population size is unaffected by mate preference; the violated assumption concerns how mates are chosen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Attraction within a population does not involve individuals entering or leaving the population.

questions.stem: Tay-Sachs disease, an autosomal recessive disorder, is found at higher rates in Ashkenazi Jews. Historically, Jewish people were persecuted and exiled, resulting in smaller communities around the world. Which of the following best explains how this history increased the frequency of the Tay-Sachs allele?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bottleneck combined with nonrandom mating reduced genetic variation

choices.label: B
choices.text: An elevated mutation rate arose at the hexosaminidase A locus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gene flow between the scattered communities combined their gene pools

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mutation-selection equilibrium was reached at a high allele frequency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Natural selection favored heterozygotes for the Tay-Sachs allele

explanation.summary: Small, isolated Jewish communities formed a bottleneck, and nonrandom mating within them reduced variation and raised the Tay-Sachs allele frequency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Jewish people have been persecuted and exiled for much of their history, resulting in smaller communities around the world. This bottleneck of the smaller Jewish communities, combined with nonrandom mating within this smaller population, reduced the genetic variation and increased the frequency of disease-causing alleles for Tay-Sachs. This prevalence underlies the ACOG recommendation to offer screening to Ashkenazi Jews considering having children.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The elevated frequency reflects inheritance from a reduced founding pool, not an increased mutation rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gene flow would mix alleles and increase variation, whereas the high Tay-Sachs frequency resulted from a decrease in variation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mutation-selection equilibrium maintains deleterious alleles at a stable low frequency; it does not explain an unusually high frequency in one group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No heterozygote advantage is described for Tay-Sachs; heterozygote advantage is the HbS-malaria mechanism.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman whose mother is of Ashkenazi Jewish descent and whose father is not Jewish is planning a pregnancy with her partner. She asks whether she should be tested for Tay-Sachs carrier status. Based on the recommendation of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists Committee on Genetics, which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Screening is indicated only if she has a family history of Tay-Sachs disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Screening is not indicated because only one of her parents is Ashkenazi Jewish

choices.label: C
choices.text: Screening should be deferred until a pregnancy has been confirmed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Screening should be offered because of her mixed Jewish ancestry

choices.label: E
choices.text: Screening should be offered only to her partner rather than to her

explanation.summary: ACOG recommends offering Tay-Sachs screening to all Ashkenazi Jews or those of mixed Jewish ancestry who are considering having children.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because of the prevalence of Tay-Sachs in Ashkenazi Jews, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists Committee on Genetics recommends that screening be offered to all Ashkenazi Jews or those of mixed Jewish ancestry considering having children. A woman with one Ashkenazi Jewish parent who is planning a pregnancy falls within this recommendation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The recommendation is based on ancestry, not on family history of the disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The recommendation explicitly includes those of mixed Jewish ancestry, not only individuals with two Ashkenazi Jewish parents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The recommendation targets people considering having children, so screening is appropriate before conception.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It is the woman's Jewish ancestry that triggers the recommendation; her partner has no stated ancestry that would indicate screening.
